Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

Trace the changing character of peasant movements in colonial India.

How to frame it: Early revolts → Post-1857 → 20th century → Assessment

Model answer (95 words)

Early revolts such as the Sanyasi-Fakir, Faraizi and Moplah outbreaks combined peasant grievances with religious leadership and were violent and local. After 1857 movements — the Indigo revolt, Pabna and the Deccan riots — targeted planters, zamindars and moneylenders, often using legal methods and winning laws such as the Bengal Tenancy Act. In the 20th century, peasant struggles joined the national movement: Champaran, Kheda and Bardoli under Gandhi and Patel, Kisan Sabhas in UP, the AIKS (1936) demanding zamindari abolition, and Left-led Tebhaga and Telangana. Peasants thus moved from local protest to organised, political action.

5 marks · 50 words

What was the significance of the Indigo revolt?

How to frame it: Cause → Support → Result

Model answer (44 words)

In 1859–60 Bengal peasants refused to grow indigo for European planters. The revolt was disciplined and won intelligentsia support — Nil Darpan, the Hindoo Patriot. The Indigo Commission (1860) ruled cultivation voluntary. It showed peasants could resist colonial interests and inspired later nationalist politics.

2 marks · 15 words

What was the tinkathia system?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (12 words)

Champaran planters forced peasants to grow indigo on 3/20 of their land.

Part III · Unit I34Tribal Movements1774 – 1947

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Paharia, Kol, Santhal, Munda (Birsa), Bhil, Khond, Rampa, Naga, Tana Bhagat revolts

Mains: GS-I: Tribal uprisings — causes and character

Tier C. Santhal and Munda (Birsa) revolts are the most asked. Rajasthan tribal movements (Govind Guru, Bhil, Meena, Eki) are in R18.

The big picture

Tribal communities lived in forests and hills with their own land systems, chiefs and customs. Colonial rule brought outsiders — dikus (moneylenders, traders, landlords), revenue demands, forest laws and missionaries — which destroyed their autonomy, land and access to the forest. Tribal revolts were among the most frequent and violent in colonial India, often led by charismatic leaders who promised a golden age.

Exam focus

Explain the common causes (land, forest, dikus, missionaries) and use two or three examples in detail.

WhenWhat happened
1774–79Halba rebellion (Bastar)
1778Paharia rising (Rajmahal hills)
1820–37Ho and Munda risings
1831–32Kol uprising (Chotanagpur)
1817–46Bhil uprisings (Khandesh)
1837–56Khond uprisings (Odisha, Chakra Bisoi)
1855–56Santhal hul
1879–80Rampa rebellion (first)
1899–1900Ulgulan (Birsa Munda)
1913Mangarh massacre (Govind Guru, Bhils)
1914Tana Bhagat movement
1922–24Rampa rebellion (Alluri Sitarama Raju)
1927–32Naga movement (Jadonang, Rani Gaidinliu)

Core notes

I34.1 Causes

Before British rule most tribal communities lived largely outside the reach of the state. They held land jointly under their own chiefs, practised shifting cultivation (jhum), and depended on the forest for food, fuel, grazing and trade. Colonial rule broke this world apart in several ways at once.

Land became private property under revenue settlements, so it could be sold or seized for debt, and it passed to outsiders, the dikus: moneylenders, traders and landlords who came in with the new order. Forest laws (the Forest Acts of 1865, 1878 and 1927) declared forests state property, banned or restricted jhum, grazing and the collection of forest produce, and brought forced labour (begar) for forest officials. Moneylenders charged high interest and took land in payment. Missionaries attacked tribal customs, though some brought education. Chiefs lost their authority to courts and police that tribals did not understand.

Concept

Why tribal revolts took the form they did. Because the whole way of life was under threat, revolts were total: they targeted every outsider, Indian or European, and they looked to a charismatic leader who promised to restore a golden age, as Birsa Munda did. Strong ethnic solidarity made them fierce, but bows, arrows and axes could not stand against modern armies, and each revolt was local. Their lasting result was protective law: tenancy acts that barred the transfer of tribal land, and the "excluded areas" of 1935 that became the Fifth and Sixth Schedules.

I34.2 Major revolts

RevoltRegionLeaders / details
PahariaRajmahal hillsAgainst British expansion into their territory (1778)
Kol uprising (1831–32)Chotanagpur, Ranchi, SinghbhumBuddho Bhagat; against transfer of land to outsiders
BhilKhandesh (western ghats)Against Company rule (1817–19, 1825, 1831, 1846)
Khond (1837–56)Odisha hillsChakra Bisoi; against suppression of human sacrifice (meriah), taxes, outsiders
Santhal hul (1855–56)Rajmahal hills, Damin-i-Koh (Bihar–Bengal)Brothers Sidhu and Kanhu (also Chand, Bhairav); against zamindars, moneylenders and police; declared end of Company rule; suppressed by the army; Santhal Parganas district created (1855) with special laws
Munda ulgulan (1899–1900)Chotanagpur, south of RanchiBirsa Munda ("Dharti Aba"); against the destruction of khuntkatti (joint landholding) by jagirdars, thikadars and moneylenders, and missionaries; aimed at Munda raj; Birsa died in Ranchi jail (1900); led to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908); 15 November observed as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas
Tana Bhagat (1914)Chotanagpur (Oraons)Jatra Bhagat; religious reform; later joined Gandhian satyagraha
RampaGodavari hills (Andhra)1879; 1922–24 under Alluri Sitarama Raju against forest laws; killed in 1924
Naga / ZeliangrongManipur, NagalandJadonang; Rani Gaidinliu (arrested 1932; Nehru called her "Rani")
KukiManipur1917–19, against labour recruitment in World War I
Bhil (Rajasthan)Banswara, DungarpurGovind Guru, Mangarh (1913); Motilal Tejawat's Eki movement — R18

Other protests NCERT names: Songram Sangma's revolt in Assam (1906), the Bastar rebellion (1910), the forest satyagraha of the 1930s in the Central Provinces and the Warli revolt in Maharashtra (1940).

Paharias and Santhals ("the hoe and the plough"): the Paharias of the Rajmahal hills lived by shifting cultivation and forest produce and raided the plains. The British tried extermination in the 1770s; in the 1780s Augustus Cleveland proposed pacification, paying allowances to Paharia chiefs. Failing to settle the Paharias, the British brought in Santhals to clear and plough the lower slopes; by 1832 the Damin-i-Koh was marked out as Santhal land. Heavy taxes and moneylenders' takeovers led to the hul of 1855–56, after which the Santhal Parganas (about 5,500 square miles, from Bhagalpur and Birbhum districts) were created.

Birsa Munda's path: he went to a mission school and also spent time with a Vaishnav preacher, wearing the sacred thread. His movement first sought reform (no liquor, no witchcraft) and a return to a golden age (satyug); he was jailed 1895–97, then urged followers to destroy "Ravana" (the dikus and Europeans). They attacked police stations, churches and moneylenders' property under a white flag of Birsa Raj. He died in 1900 (officially of cholera).

I34.3 Character

  • Violent, armed with traditional weapons; easily crushed by modern armies.
  • Strong ethnic solidarity; outsiders, including Indian dikus, as enemies.
  • Messianic leaders (Birsa claimed divine mission); millenarian hopes of a golden age.
  • Results: protective laws (Santhal Parganas Tenancy, Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908), "excluded" and "partially excluded" areas (1935) — the base for the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution.
Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Causes: colonial land revenue and forest policy (I30); commercialisation and moneylenders (I31).
  • Alongside: peasant movements (I33); the Revolt of 1857 (I32).
  • After: the Fifth and Sixth Schedules and tribal policy in independent India (I45).
  • Rajasthan: Govind Guru and Mangarh, Motilal Tejawat and the Eki movement (R18).

What historians say

K.S. Singh (Birsa Munda and His Movement) is the standard study. Ranajit Guha used the Santhal hul in his theory of peasant insurgency. David Hardiman (The Coming of the Devi) studied Adivasi assertion in western India. Ramachandra Guha (The Unquiet Woods) linked tribal protest to colonial forestry.

  • The Santhal Parganas district was created after the hul.

Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

What were the causes and nature of tribal revolts in colonial India?

How to frame it: Causes → Examples → Character → Results

Model answer (92 words)

Colonial land settlements transferred tribal land to outsiders; Forest Acts restricted jhum, grazing and forest produce; moneylenders, traders and contractors (dikus) exploited tribals; missionaries and courts undermined custom and chiefs. Revolts followed — the Kol (1831), Khond, Santhal hul under Sidhu and Kanhu (1855), Birsa Munda's ulgulan (1899) and the Rampa revolt under Alluri Sitarama Raju. They were violent, based on ethnic solidarity and often led by messianic figures, and were crushed by superior arms. Yet they produced protective laws such as the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908) and the later Scheduled Areas.

5 marks · 50 words

Describe the Munda ulgulan.

How to frame it: Cause → Leader → Result

Model answer (41 words)

In 1899–1900 Birsa Munda led the Mundas of Chotanagpur against jagirdars, moneylenders and missionaries who destroyed the khuntkatti system, aiming at Munda raj. It was suppressed and Birsa died in jail (1900), but the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908) protected tribal land.

Who were the dikus?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (12 words)

Outsiders — moneylenders, traders, landlords — who exploited tribals in colonial India.

Part III · Unit I35Socio-Religious Reform Movements1815 – 1947

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj, Arya Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission, Theosophical Society, Aligarh, Satyashodhak, SNDP; social legislation

Mains: GS-I: 19th-century renaissance — reform movements, their nature and limitations

Tier A, one of the most-asked modern topics. RAS Mains asked on Mirat-ul-Akhbar (2016, 2 marks), the Indian Renaissance (2018, 10) and the Theosophists (2021, 10). Rajasthan links (Dayanand at Udaipur and Ajmer; Paropkarini Sabha; Walterkrit Sabha) are in R15.

The big picture

In the 19th century, educated Indians set out to reform their own society and religion. They were responding to a challenge and drawing on an inspiration. The challenge was colonial rule itself: British officials and Christian missionaries described Indian society as backward and used customs such as sati and caste to justify their rule. The inspiration came partly from the West (rational thought, liberal ideas of individual rights, modern science and the printing press) and partly from India's own past (the Upanishads, the Vedas, the Bhakti saints), which the reformers reread to show that the abuses were later corruptions, not the true tradition.

Two broad approaches emerged. Reformist movements (Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj, Aligarh) used reason and adapted religion to modern life. Revivalist movements (Arya Samaj, Deoband) called for a return to a purified original tradition. Both attacked sati, child marriage, purdah, idolatry and the ban on widow remarriage, and both promoted education. A third current, led by lower-caste reformers such as Phule, Narayana Guru, Periyar and Ambedkar, challenged the caste hierarchy itself. Together they laid the social and intellectual ground for Indian nationalism.

Exam focus

RAS asks about individual reformers and bodies (Rammohun's newspaper, the Theosophists) and about the character of the movement: was the "Indian Renaissance" Western-inspired or a response to a Western challenge (2018)? For every movement know: founder and year, ideas, method, social base and limits.

Core notes

I35.1 Why reform began: challenge and inspiration

Three changes made reform possible in the early 19th century. English education and contact with British officials introduced a small class of Indians, first in Calcutta and then in Bombay and Madras, to European ideas of reason, liberty and progress. Print allowed them to argue in newspapers, pamphlets and translated scriptures, and to reach a growing reading public. And the colonial state could pass laws, so reformers could appeal to it to ban practices they could not end by persuasion alone.

The reformers did not simply copy the West. They argued that Indian religion in its pure form, the Upanishads for Rammohun Roy and the Vedas for Dayanand, was rational and humane, and that sati, idolatry and caste rigidity were later corruptions. This let them defend Indian civilisation against missionary attack while still demanding change.

Concept

Reformist and revivalist. A reformist movement accepts change and uses reason and modern knowledge to judge tradition, keeping what passes the test (Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj, Aligarh). A revivalist movement looks back to a golden age and seeks to restore the original, pure tradition (Arya Samaj's "back to the Vedas", Deoband's return to the classical Islamic sciences). The line is not sharp: revivalists also opposed caste and child marriage, and reformists also quoted scripture. The difference lies in where they placed authority, in reason or in the original text. Revivalism gave confidence and pride, but it could also harden religious boundaries.

Debate

Was there an "Indian Renaissance"? The term compares 19th-century India with the European Renaissance: a rebirth of learning, reason and humanism. Nationalist writers used it with pride. Critics such as Sumit Sarkar argue that it was limited to a small, urban, upper-caste elite in a few cities, depended on colonial patronage and laws, and barely touched peasants, lower castes or women's own voices. The balanced answer to the 2018 Mains question: the movement was born of the Western challenge (conquest and missionary criticism) and drew on Western inspiration (rationalism, liberalism, print), but its content was shaped by Indian traditions, and its reach was narrow until lower-caste and nationalist movements carried it further.

I35.2 Bengal: Rammohun Roy and the Brahmo Samaj

Raja Rammohun Roy (1772–1833), often called the "father of the Indian Renaissance", knew Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English. He studied the Upanishads and argued that they taught belief in one formless God (monotheism), not idol worship; his Persian work Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin ("A gift to monotheists") and his Precepts of Jesus applied the same reasoning to other faiths. He founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815) and the Brahmo Sabha (1828), later the Brahmo Samaj.

His great campaign was against sati. He showed from the scriptures that sati was not required, described cases of widows forced onto the pyre, and petitioned the government; Lord William Bentinck banned it in 1829 (Regulation XVII). He also opposed polygamy, demanded property rights for women and supported English and scientific education (Hindu College, 1817; his own Vedanta College, 1825). He used the press: Sambad Kaumudi in Bengali and the Persian weekly Mirat-ul-Akhbar (1822), which he edited (RAS Mains 2016), and protested against the press regulation of 1823. The Mughal emperor Akbar II gave him the title "Raja" and sent him to England, where he died at Bristol in 1833.

After him, Debendranath Tagore revived the Samaj through his Tattvabodhini Sabha (1839), and Keshab Chandra Sen spread it across India with a more radical programme. Disputes followed. In 1866 Keshab's group formed the Brahmo Samaj of India, leaving Debendranath's Adi Brahmo Samaj. Keshab founded the Indian Reform Association (1870) and pressed for the Native Marriage Act (1872), which allowed inter-caste marriage and set minimum ages. When he then married his own under-age daughter to the prince of Cooch Behar, his followers broke away to form the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878); Keshab went on to found the New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan).

At Hindu College, the young teacher Henry Vivian Derozio inspired the Young Bengal group (1828–31) to question all authority and tradition, a radical rationalism that shocked orthodox society. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, a Sanskrit scholar, used the scriptures themselves to argue for widow remarriage; his campaign led to the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856. He also opened girls' schools, opposed polygamy and child marriage, and simplified Bengali prose (his primer Barna Parichay).

I35.3 Western India: Prarthana Samaj, Phule and women reformers

In Bombay, the Prarthana Samaj (1867), founded by Atmaram Pandurang with Keshab's encouragement, drew on the Bhakti saints of Maharashtra as much as on reason. Its leaders, M.G. Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar, worked for inter-caste dining, widow remarriage and women's education. Ranade founded the Widow Remarriage Association and the Indian National Social Conference (1887), which met alongside the Congress, and supported the Deccan Education Society.

Jyotiba Phule, from the Mali (gardener) caste, went further. He saw the caste system as a tool of Brahmin domination over the shudras and "untouchables", whom he presented as the original people of the land. With his wife Savitribai Phule he opened a girls' school at Pune in 1848. In 1873 he founded the Satyashodhak Samaj ("society of seekers of truth") and wrote Gulamgiri ("slavery"), dedicated to the Americans who had fought to free slaves, linking caste to slavery.

Others worked for women: Gopal Hari Deshmukh ("Lokahitawadi") wrote against orthodoxy; D.K. Karve opened a home for widows and founded the SNDT women's university (1916); Pandita Ramabai founded the Arya Mahila Samaj and the Sharada Sadan for widows; Behramji Malabari campaigned against child marriage, leading to the Age of Consent Act (1891). Among the Parsis, the Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha (1851; Naoroji Furdonji, Dadabhai Naoroji, S.S. Bengalee) reformed religion and women's position.

Concept

Women as the "site" of reform. Nearly every 19th-century debate (sati, widow remarriage, child marriage, education) was about women, yet women rarely spoke in it at first; men argued, and the British legislated. Historians such as Lata Mani point out that the sati debate was really about what scripture said, not about the widow's own wishes. This began to change as women such as Savitribai Phule, Pandita Ramabai and later the women's organisations of the 20th century spoke for themselves (unit I47).

I35.4 Arya Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission and the Theosophists

Swami Dayanand Saraswati (born at Tankara in Gujarat) founded the Arya Samaj at Bombay in 1875; its strongest base became Punjab, with Lahore as its centre. His call was "back to the Vedas": he held the Vedas to be the only true and infallible scripture, and rejected idol worship, ritualism, Brahmin monopoly, caste by birth and child marriage, while supporting widow remarriage and education for women. His ideas are set out in Satyarth Prakash (first edition 1875; a revised edition was prepared at Udaipur in 1882). The Samaj introduced shuddhi, a ritual to bring converts to other faiths back into Hinduism. After his death at Ajmer in 1883 (where the Paropkarini Sabha carries on his work), his followers founded DAV schools (Lahore, 1886; Lala Hansraj). In 1893 they split: the College group kept to Western-style education, while Swami Shraddhanand founded the Gurukul Kangri at Haridwar (1902) on the ancient model. Dayanand's stress on Vedic pride and self-reliance inspired nationalists such as Lala Lajpat Rai.

Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, a priest at the Dakshineswar temple near Calcutta, taught through his own experience that all religions are paths to the same God. His disciple Swami Vivekananda carried this message to the world at the Chicago Parliament of Religions (1893) and founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897). Vivekananda's "practical Vedanta" said that service to the poor is service to God, so the Mission ran schools, hospitals and famine relief. He scorned "kitchen religion" (obsession with ritual purity) and caste exclusion, and called on Indians to build strength and self-confidence; nationalists from Tilak to Subhas Bose drew on him.

The Theosophical Society (RAS Mains 2021) was founded in New York in 1875 by the Russian mystic Madame H.P. Blavatsky and the American Colonel H.S. Olcott. They came to India in 1879 and set up their headquarters at Adyar near Madras in 1882 (some textbooks give 1886). Its three aims were: a universal brotherhood of humanity without distinction of race, creed, sex or caste; the comparative study of religion, philosophy and science; and the investigation of unexplained laws of nature and the hidden powers of human beings. The Theosophists praised Hinduism, Buddhism and Zoroastrianism as stores of ancient wisdom and accepted karma and rebirth; Olcott also helped revive Buddhism in Sri Lanka.

Concept

Why Theosophy mattered in India. Here were educated Westerners saying that Indian religion was not superstition but deep wisdom, sometimes superior to that of the West. At a time when missionaries attacked Hinduism, this boosted the self-respect of educated Hindus. Annie Besant, a British reformer who joined in 1889 and settled in India, turned the Society towards education and politics: she founded the Central Hindu College at Benaras (1898), which became the core of Banaras Hindu University (1916), led the Home Rule League (1916) and became Congress president (1917) (unit I37). The limit: its mysticism and occult claims appealed to a small elite and did little to challenge caste in practice.

I35.5 Muslim, Sikh and Parsi reform

Muslim reform took two directions after 1857, when the community had lost political power and was viewed with suspicion by the British. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan led the Aligarh movement. He believed Muslims could recover only through Western education and cooperation with the British, and he reinterpreted the Qur'an in the light of reason and science. He founded the Scientific Society (1864) to translate Western works, the journal Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq, and the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental (MAO) school at Aligarh (1875), which became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920. Later he urged Muslims to keep away from the Congress, a stand that fed separatist politics.

The Deoband school (1866, Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi) took the opposite path: it trained ulema in the classical Islamic sciences, kept away from Western learning, and was anti-British; its ulema later supported the Congress. The Ahmadiya movement (1889, Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, Qadian) spread Western education but its claims about its founder made it controversial among Muslims. The earlier Wahabi (Waliullahi) movement of Syed Ahmad of Rae Bareli was a religious revival that turned into armed resistance to the British. Mumtaz Ali reread the Qur'an to argue for women's education.

Among the Sikhs, the Singh Sabha (1873, Amritsar) worked to purify Sikh practice and spread education (Khalsa College). In the 1920s the Akali movement took control of gurdwaras from corrupt hereditary mahants through non-violent agitation, leading to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act (1925) and the SGPC.

I35.6 Lower-caste movements: challenging caste itself

Upper-caste reformers had mostly tried to soften caste. From the late 19th century, leaders of the lower castes themselves demanded dignity and equal rights. Their methods ranged from religious reform to temple-entry campaigns and political organisation.

In Kerala, Sree Narayana Guru, from the Ezhava community, consecrated a Shiva idol at Aruvippuram (1888), challenging the Brahmin monopoly over temples, and founded the SNDP Yogam (1903); his message was "one caste, one religion, one God for man". Ayyankali organised the Pulayas through the Sadhu Jana Paripalana Sangham. The Vaikom satyagraha (1924–25), led by T.K. Madhavan and K.P. Kesava Menon and visited by Gandhi, demanded that lower castes be allowed to use the roads around the Vaikom temple; the Guruvayur satyagraha (1931–32, K. Kelappan) demanded temple entry.

In Tamil Nadu, E.V. Ramasamy (Periyar) left the Congress after seeing caste-based seating at a nationalist feast and started the Self-Respect movement (1925), attacking Brahmin dominance, caste and scripture. The Justice Party (1916) had already voiced non-Brahmin interests. In central India Ghasidas founded the Satnami movement among leatherworkers; in east Bengal Haridas Thakur's Matua sect worked among the Chandala cultivators. Veeresalingam Pantulu formed the Rajahmundry Social Reform Association (1871) for widow remarriage in the Telugu areas (RAS Prelims 2021); the Veda Samaj (Madras, 1864) followed the Brahmo model; the Paramhans Mandali (Bombay, 1840) worked against caste.

B.R. Ambedkar gave the movement its sharpest political form. He founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924), led the Mahad satyagraha (1927) for the right to draw water from a public tank, publicly burned the Manusmriti, led temple-entry movements between 1927 and 1935, and founded the Independent Labour Party (1936) and the All India Scheduled Castes Federation (1942). Gandhi worked within Hinduism, founding the Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932). The difference between the two, reform of caste from within or its rejection, ran through the national movement.

Orthodox reaction. Reform provoked resistance: the Sanatan Dharma Sabhas, the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal and the Brahman Sabha of Bengal defended caste and custom as commanded by scripture.

I35.7 Social legislation and assessment

LawYearAssociated with
Abolition of sati1829Bentinck, Rammohun Roy
Female infanticide banned1795, 1804, 1870—
Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act1856Dalhousie/Canning, Vidyasagar
Native Marriage Act1872Keshab Chandra Sen
Age of Consent Act1891Malabari
Sarda Act (Child Marriage Restraint)1929Harbilas Sarda (Ajmer) — girls 14, boys 18

Achievements. The reform movements spread a rational and humane outlook, improved the legal and social position of women, built schools and colleges, and weakened the hold of caste and ritual. By giving Indians pride in their heritage and confidence in their own ability to change, they prepared the ground for nationalism: many early Congress leaders came out of these bodies.

Limitations. Reform was largely confined to the urban, educated upper castes and barely reached peasants or lower castes. It leaned on colonial legislation, which was often weakly enforced (few widows actually remarried). Women were more often the subject of debate than its voice. And revivalist methods such as shuddhi, together with Aligarh's distance from the Congress, sometimes sharpened communal identities. The lower-caste movements exposed these limits and pushed reform from charity towards rights.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Background: British education policy and the press (I30); missionaries and the colonial critique of Indian society.
  • Ancient roots the reformers invoked: the Vedas and Upanishads (I04, I13); Buddhism and Jainism (I06); the Bhakti saints (I20).
  • Women: the women's movement and later laws (I47).
  • Nationalism: the Moderates and the Social Conference (I36); Besant's Home Rule League and the Extremists' use of religion (I37); Gandhi's work against untouchability (I39); communal politics and partition (I42).
  • Peasants and tribes: movements of the poor that reformers rarely reached (I33, I34).
  • Rajasthan: Dayanand at Udaipur and Ajmer, the Paropkarini Sabha, the Walterkrit Sabha, and Harbilas Sarda of Ajmer (R15).

What historians say

Sumit Sarkar critiqued the idea of a "Bengal Renaissance" as limited and dependent on colonial structures. Kenneth Jones classified movements as "transitional" and "acculturative". Gail Omvedt and Rosalind O'Hanlon studied Phule and anti-caste movements. Uma Chakravarti and Lata Mani (on sati debates) showed that women were often the site rather than the subject of reform debates.

Exam traps
  • Phule's Gulamgiri was published in 1873, not 1871 as some NCERT-based guides print.
  • Sarda Act (1929): girls 14, boys 18 — not 16 for girls, as some NCERT-based guides print.
  • William Carey, of the Serampore mission, was an English Baptist, not Scottish (William Adam was the Scottish missionary).
  • Arya Samaj founded at Bombay (1875), not Lahore.
  • Theosophical Society founded at New York (1875); Adyar later (1882; some textbooks give 1886).
  • Prarthana Samaj (Bombay) ≠ Brahmo Samaj (Calcutta).
  • Aligarh (reformist, pro-British) ≠ Deoband (orthodox, anti-British).
  • Satyarth Prakash: Dayanand; Gulamgiri: Phule.
  • The Brahmo Samaj did NOT hold the Vedas infallible; that was Dayanand's Arya Samaj.
  • Mirat-ul-Akhbar (Persian) and Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali) were both Rammohun's.

Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

The Indian Renaissance of the 19th century was the result of the challenges as well as the inspiration of the West. Examine critically.

How to frame it: Challenge: conquest, missionary critique → Inspiration: reason, liberalism, print, education → Indian roots → Limits → Conclusion

Model answer (92 words)

Colonial conquest and missionary attacks on sati, caste and idolatry challenged Indians to defend and reform their society. Western rationalism, liberal ideas, science, English education and print inspired reformers such as Rammohun Roy and Vidyasagar. Yet the content was Indian: Rammohun cited the Upanishads, Dayanand the Vedas, the Prarthana Samaj the Bhakti saints, and Vivekananda Vedanta. Critics note its narrow base among urban upper castes, its reliance on colonial laws and its neglect of women's own voices; Phule and Narayana Guru widened it. It was a Western stimulus answered in Indian terms.

10 marks · 100 words

Discuss in brief the growth of the ideology of Theosophists in the Theosophical Society in India.

How to frame it: Founding → Aims and ideas → Coming to India → Annie Besant → Impact and limits

Model answer (90 words)

Blavatsky and Olcott founded the Theosophical Society in New York in 1875 and moved to Adyar, Madras. Its aims were universal brotherhood without distinction of race, creed, sex or caste, comparative study of religion, philosophy and science, and inquiry into hidden laws of nature. It praised Hinduism and Buddhism as ancient wisdom and accepted karma and rebirth, raising Hindu self-confidence against missionary attack. Annie Besant founded the Central Hindu College (1898), later BHU, and led the Home Rule League (1916). Its occult side and elite base limited its social reach.

10 marks · 100 words

Evaluate the contribution of Swami Dayanand Saraswati to Indian society.

How to frame it: Ideas → Social reform → Education → Nationalism → Limits

Model answer (85 words)

Dayanand founded the Arya Samaj (1875) with the call "Back to the Vedas", rejecting idolatry, ritualism, caste by birth and Brahmin monopoly. He opposed child marriage and supported widow remarriage and women's education; his Satyarth Prakash set out these ideas. His followers built DAV schools and the Gurukul Kangri. By asserting Vedic self-respect and swadeshi, he inspired nationalists such as Lajpat Rai. His work in Rajasthan — Udaipur, Ajmer, the Paropkarini Sabha — influenced princes. Yet shuddhi and polemics against other faiths sharpened communal boundaries.

5 marks · 50 words

What were the limitations of the 19th-century reform movements?

How to frame it: Social base → Dependence → Communal side

Model answer (44 words)

Reform was confined to urban, educated upper castes and barely touched peasants or lower castes; it relied on colonial laws; revivalist movements sometimes sharpened communal identities; and women were often objects of the debates rather than participants. Phule and Narayana Guru exposed these limits.

2 marks · 15 words

Who was the editor of Mirat-ul-Akhbar?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (11 words)

Raja Rammohun Roy, who edited this Persian weekly from Calcutta (1822).

2 marks · 15 words

What was the Satyashodhak Samaj?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (11 words)

Jyotiba Phule's society (1873) against Brahmin dominance and for lower-caste rights.

Part III · Unit I36Early Nationalism and the Moderates1836 – 1905

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Pre-Congress associations; foundation of the INC; Moderate leaders, methods and demands

Mains: GS-I: Rise of nationalism; foundation of the Congress (safety-valve debate); assessment of the Moderates

Tier C. The safety-valve theory and the assessment of the Moderates are classic Mains questions.

The big picture

Modern Indian nationalism arose from the contradictions of colonial rule — economic exploitation, racial discrimination, administrative unification, modern education, the press and the reform movements. Political associations in the presidency towns (from the 1830s) led to the Indian National Congress (1885). Its early leaders, the Moderates (1885–1905), believed in British justice, used constitutional methods (petitions, resolutions, speeches) and built the economic critique of colonialism.

Exam focus

Assess the Moderates fairly: limited immediate gains but vital foundations — political education, economic critique, a national platform.

Core notes

I36.1 Causes of the rise of nationalism

Nationalism grew out of colonial rule itself. British economic policy hurt peasants, artisans and even the new Indian businessmen, so every class had a grievance against the same rulers. British rule also unified India as never before: one administration, one law, and railways, telegraph and post that let people and ideas move across the country. Western education gave a new middle class a common language, English, and the ideas of liberty, democracy and nationhood, which they turned against their rulers. The press (Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu, Kesari, Bangadarshan) spread political discussion, while Orientalist scholarship and the reform movements restored pride in India's past.

The trigger was British racial arrogance and reaction. Under Lytton (1876–80) came the Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act (1878), the lowering of the ICS age limit, the removal of cotton import duties and the lavish Delhi Durbar of 1877 held during a famine. The Ilbert Bill controversy (1883), when Europeans successfully agitated against Indian judges trying them, showed educated Indians that they would never be treated as equals and taught them the value of organised agitation.

I36.2 Pre-Congress associations

  • Bengal: Bangabhasha Prakasika Sabha (1836), Landholders' Society (1838, Dwarkanath Tagore), British India Society (1843), British Indian Association (1851), Indian Association (1876, Surendranath Banerjea, Ananda Mohan Bose) — the most important; agitated on ICS age; held the Indian National Conference (1883, 1885).
  • Bombay: Bombay Association (1852); Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870, M.G. Ranade, G.V. Joshi); Bombay Presidency Association (1885, Pherozeshah Mehta, Badruddin Tyabji, K.T. Telang).
  • Madras: Madras Native Association (1852); Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884, M. Viraraghavachari, G. Subramania Iyer, P. Ananda Charlu).
  • London: East India Association (1866, Dadabhai Naoroji).

I36.3 Foundation of the Congress

  • Founded on 28 December 1885 at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay (shifted from Poona due to cholera); 72 delegates; first president W.C. Bonnerjee; A.O. Hume, retired ICS officer, as organiser and first general secretary.
  • Viceroy Dufferin initially welcomed it, later called it a "microscopic minority".
  • Early presidents: Dadabhai Naoroji (1886, Calcutta; also 1893, 1906), Badruddin Tyabji (1887, Madras — first Muslim president), George Yule (1888 — first English president), Annie Besant (1917 — first woman), Sarojini Naidu (1925 — first Indian woman).
Debate

Safety-valve theory: Lala Lajpat Rai (Young India, 1916) and later R.P. Dutt argued that Hume founded the Congress, with Dufferin's blessing, as a safety valve to release Indian discontent and prevent revolt (Hume's "seven volumes" of secret reports). Bipan Chandra rejects this as a myth: Indian leaders used Hume as a "lightning conductor" to avoid official hostility, and the Congress was the culmination of a political awakening already under way. The "Cambridge school" (Anil Seal) saw it as a product of elite competition for patronage.

I36.4 The Moderates (1885–1905)

Leaders: Dadabhai Naoroji ("Grand Old Man of India"), Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjea ("Rashtraguru", "Surrender-not"), Gopal Krishna Gokhale (Servants of India Society, 1905; political guru of Gandhi), M.G. Ranade, Dinshaw Wacha, Badruddin Tyabji, R.C. Dutt, W.C. Bonnerjee, Madan Mohan Malaviya.

Methods: constitutional — petitions, prayers, protests ("3 Ps" — a later critics' label); resolutions, memoranda, meetings; British Committee of the INC (1889) and journal India in London.

Demands:

  • Economic: reduce land revenue; end the drain; protect Indian industry; reduce military expenditure; famine relief.
  • Constitutional: expansion and reform of councils; elected members; Indian control over the budget — self-government within the empire later (Naoroji's "swaraj" at Calcutta, 1906).
  • Administrative: Indianisation of services, simultaneous ICS exams, separation of judiciary and executive, repeal of the Arms Act, expansion of education.
  • Civil rights: freedom of speech, press and association.

Achievements: economic critique (drain theory); political education and a national platform; Indian Councils Act (1892); a resolution in the House of Commons (1893) for simultaneous ICS exams; Welby Commission (1895). Naoroji became the first Indian member of the British House of Commons (1892, Finsbury Central).

Limitations: narrow social base (urban educated middle class); faith in British justice; no mass mobilisation; little immediate success; led to the rise of the Extremists.

Concept

Why the Moderates used petitions, not protest. The Moderates were a small educated group facing a powerful state, at a time when the masses were not yet politically awake. Many sincerely believed that British rule had brought modern education, law and communications, and that the British people, once informed, would do justice to India. So they aimed first to educate both Indian and British opinion. Their great achievement was the economic critique of colonialism: Naoroji, Ranade, R.C. Dutt and Gokhale showed that British rule drained India's wealth, which destroyed the claim that it was for India's good. This laid the intellectual base on which the Extremists and Gandhi built mass movements.

Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

Assess the role of the Moderates in the national movement.

How to frame it: Leaders and methods → Demands → Achievements → Limitations → Conclusion

Model answer (91 words)

Moderates such as Naoroji, Gokhale, Banerjea and Ranade used petitions, resolutions and speeches, trusting British justice. They demanded lower land revenue, an end to the drain, Indianisation of services, expanded councils and civil liberties. Their drain theory exposed colonial exploitation; they gave Indians political education and a national platform, and won the Indian Councils Act (1892). But their base was the urban educated class, they avoided mass mobilisation and achieved little concrete success, which produced the Extremist reaction. Still, they laid the ideological foundation on which later mass movements were built.

5 marks · 50 words

Examine the safety-valve theory of the foundation of the Congress.

How to frame it: Theory → Critique

Model answer (46 words)

Lajpat Rai and R.P. Dutt argued that Hume founded the Congress with Dufferin's approval to release Indian discontent safely. Bipan Chandra rejects this: Indian leaders used Hume as a "lightning conductor", and the Congress grew out of a political awakening already under way in earlier associations.

Part III · Unit I37Swadeshi and the Extremists1905 – 1918

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Partition of Bengal; Swadeshi and boycott; Surat split; Muslim League; Morley-Minto; Lucknow Pact; Home Rule Leagues

Mains: GS-I: Swadeshi movement; Extremists vs Moderates; Home Rule movement

Tier B. Swadeshi movement and the Surat split are high-yield; the Lucknow Pact and Home Rule are frequent Prelims topics.

The big picture

By 1900 a younger generation of nationalists had lost faith in the Moderates' petitions. They were led by Lal, Bal and Pal (Lajpat Rai, Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal) and Aurobindo Ghosh, and became known as the Extremists. They demanded swaraj and wanted to win it through the strength of the people, not the goodwill of the British. Curzon's partition of Bengal (1905) gave them their chance: it set off the Swadeshi movement, the first mass movement of modern India. The movement brought new methods (boycott, swadeshi, national education) but also the Surat split (1907), repression, and the separate electorates of the Morley-Minto reforms. During the First World War the Lucknow Pact (1916) reunited the Congress and brought it together with the Muslim League, and the Home Rule Leagues kept agitation alive until Gandhi's arrival.

Exam focus

Mains asks why the Extremists emerged, why Bengal was partitioned (RAS Mains 2016), what Swadeshi achieved and why it declined. Prelims picks facts: dates of partition, Surat, Lucknow and the two Home Rule Leagues, and cultural details such as Abanindranath Tagore's Bharat Mata (RAS Pre 2024).

WhenWhat happened

Core notes

I37.1 Rise of the Extremists

Several forces pushed nationalists beyond the Moderate approach. First, two decades of petitions had won little, which convinced many that the British would concede only to pressure. Second, Curzon (Viceroy 1899–1905) seemed to go out of his way to offend educated Indians: the Calcutta Corporation Act (1899) cut elected members, the Indian Universities Act (1904) tightened government control of universities, the Official Secrets Act (1904) curbed the press, and finally he partitioned Bengal. Third, the famines and plague of 1896–1900, and harsh plague measures in Pune, caused deep anger; the plague commissioner Rand was shot in 1897 by the Chapekar brothers. Fourth, events abroad showed that Europeans could be beaten: Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa (1896) and Japan defeated Russia (1905), while nationalists struggled in Ireland, Egypt, Turkey and Persia. Finally, Vivekananda, Dayanand and Bankim had given Indians a new pride in their own culture.

Concept

Moderates and Extremists: the real difference. Both wanted Indian self-government and both used the economic critique. They differed on method and confidence. Moderates trusted British liberalism and appealed to it through petitions; Extremists believed freedom had to be taken, through self-reliance, passive resistance, boycott, swadeshi, national education and mass participation. Tilak declared, "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it," and used the Ganapati (1893) and Shivaji (1895) festivals and his papers Kesari and Mahratta to reach ordinary people. The use of religious festivals widened the movement's base but also gave it a Hindu tone that kept many Muslims away.

I37.2 Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi movement

Curzon announced the partition in July 1905, and it took effect on 16 October 1905. It created a new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam (capital Dacca) with a Muslim majority, while in western Bengal, joined to Bihar and Odisha, Bengali speakers became a minority. The official reason was administrative convenience, since Bengal was too large to govern. The real motive appears in the notes of Home Secretary Risley: "Bengal united is a power; Bengal divided will pull in several different ways." The aim was to weaken Bengal, the centre of Indian nationalism, and to divide Hindus and Muslims.

Bengal answered with the boycott resolution at the Calcutta Town Hall (7 August 1905). On 16 October people fasted and mourned, tied rakhis on one another as a symbol of unity, and sang Tagore's Amar Sonar Bangla. The movement used many methods. Foreign cloth was boycotted and burnt, and swadeshi enterprises were set up: P.C. Ray's Bengal Chemicals, the Banga Lakshmi cotton mills, and swadeshi match and soap factories. National education began with the Bengal National College (1906, Aurobindo principal) under the National Council of Education. Volunteer samitis such as Ashwini Kumar Dutta's Swadesh Bandhab Samiti (Barisal) spread the message, together with social boycott, festivals, folk theatre (jatras) and songs by Tagore, Rajanikanta Sen and Mukunda Das. In art, Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata (1905), the first image of India as a mother goddess.

The movement spread beyond Bengal: Tilak in Bombay and Poona, Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh in Punjab, Syed Haider Raza in Delhi, and V.O. Chidambaram Pillai, who founded the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company at Tuticorin.

Concept

Why Swadeshi declined, and why it still mattered. After 1908 the movement faded. The government crushed it with arrests and press laws; the Surat split divided the leadership; it had no lasting organisation; and it failed to win over the peasantry, especially the Muslim peasants of east Bengal, whose landlords were often Hindu and whose leaders, such as Nawab Salimullah, backed partition. Its leaders were removed: Tilak was sent to Mandalay, Aurobindo withdrew to Pondicherry and Pal retired. Yet Swadeshi was the first mass movement: it brought students, women and some workers into politics, boosted Indian industry and culture, and tested boycott, non-cooperation and passive resistance, the methods Gandhi later used on a national scale.

I37.3 Surat split (1907) and after

At the Calcutta session (1906), under Dadabhai Naoroji, the two groups agreed on compromise resolutions on swaraj, swadeshi, boycott and national education. A year later at Surat (1907) the compromise broke. The Extremists wanted Lajpat Rai or Tilak as president; the Moderates chose Rash Behari Ghosh, and the Extremists feared the four Calcutta resolutions would be dropped. The session broke up in chaos. At root, the Extremists had lost faith in the Moderates' ability to win anything by negotiating with the British.

The government used the split to "rally the Moderates" and crush the Extremists. It passed the Seditious Meetings Act (1907), the Newspapers Act (1908) and the Explosive Substances Act, and sentenced Tilak to six years in Mandalay (1908). At the same time it offered the Moderates the Morley-Minto Reforms (1909).

Meanwhile Muslim politics took its own course. The Aga Khan led the Simla deputation (1 October 1906) to Minto seeking separate electorates, and the Muslim League was founded at Dacca on 30 December 1906 under Nawab Salimullah, with the Aga Khan as first president. Morley-Minto granted separate electorates in 1909. Finally, at the Delhi Durbar (12 December 1911) George V announced the annulment of the partition and the transfer of the capital to Delhi.

I37.4 Lucknow Pact and the Home Rule movement

The First World War changed the mood. At the Lucknow session (1916), president A.C. Majumdar, the Moderates and Extremists reunited. In the Lucknow Pact the Congress and the League made joint demands for self-government and reforms, and the Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims. Tilak and Jinnah played key roles. The pact brought Hindu–Muslim cooperation but also gave the League legitimacy and accepted the principle of separate electorates.

The Home Rule Leagues (1916), on the Irish model, aimed at home rule, meaning self-government within the empire. Tilak's League (April 1916, Belgaum) covered Maharashtra (except Bombay city), Karnataka, the Central Provinces and Berar. Annie Besant's League (September 1916, Madras) covered the rest of India, with her papers New India and Commonweal and helpers such as George Arundale, B.P. Wadia and C.P. Ramaswami Aiyar. They worked through meetings, newspapers, libraries and pamphlets. Besant's internment (June 1917) caused nationwide protest; she was released and elected Congress president (1917). The movement declined after Montagu's August Declaration (1917), which promised the "gradual development of self-governing institutions, with a view to the progressive realisation of responsible government".

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before: the Moderates and the economic critique (I31, I36); reform and revivalist movements (I35).
  • Alongside: revolutionary nationalism grew from the Swadeshi samitis (I38); Morley-Minto and separate electorates (I29).
  • After: Gandhi's non-cooperation took up boycott and swadeshi (I39); separate electorates led towards the communal question and partition (I42).
  • Rajasthan: revolutionaries such as Arjunlal Sethi, Kesari Singh Barhath and Rao Gopal Singh (R19).

What historians say

Sumit Sarkar (The Swadeshi Movement in Bengal 1903–1908) identified four trends — moderate, constructive swadeshi, political extremism, revolutionary terrorism — and analysed why the movement failed to reach the Muslim peasantry. Bipan Chandra stressed its role in creating mass politics. Hugh Owen and H.F. Owen studied the Home Rule movement.

Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

Why was Bengal partitioned in 1905? Also highlight its consequences.

How to frame it: Official reason → Real motive → Consequences: Swadeshi → Communal consequences → Annulment

Model answer (103 words)

Curzon justified the partition as administrative convenience, since Bengal was too large to govern. The real aim, seen in Risley's notes, was to weaken Bengal, the centre of nationalism, and to divide Hindus and Muslims by creating a Muslim-majority Eastern Bengal and Assam. The consequences were the opposite of what was intended: it provoked the Swadeshi movement, with boycott, swadeshi industry, national education and the first mass participation in politics, and radicalised nationalism, leading to the Surat split and revolutionary activity. It also deepened communal division: the Muslim League was founded (1906) and separate electorates followed (1909). The partition was annulled in 1911.

10 marks · 100 words

Discuss the methods and significance of the Swadeshi movement.

How to frame it: Cause → Methods → Spread → Decline → Significance

Model answer (93 words)

Curzon's partition of Bengal (1905), meant to divide Bengali nationalists, sparked the Swadeshi movement. Its methods were boycott of British goods, swadeshi industries such as Bengal Chemicals, national education, samitis, festivals, songs and social boycott; it spread to Maharashtra, Punjab, Delhi and Tamil Nadu. It declined after 1908 because of repression, the Surat split, weak organisation and the failure to draw in peasants and Muslims. Yet it was the first mass movement, brought students and women into politics, encouraged indigenous industry and culture, and tested boycott and passive resistance later used by Gandhi.

5 marks · 50 words

Why did the Congress split at Surat in 1907?

How to frame it: Differences → Immediate cause → Result

Model answer (49 words)

Moderates and Extremists differed on goals and methods — reform versus swaraj, petitions versus boycott and mass action. At Surat the Moderates chose Rash Behari Ghosh as president and seemed set to dilute the Calcutta resolutions; the session broke up. The government repressed the Extremists and wooed the Moderates.

2 marks · 15 words

What was the Lucknow Pact?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (9 words)

1916 Congress–League agreement; joint demands; Congress accepted separate electorates.

Part III · Unit I38Revolutionary Nationalism1897 – 1934

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Anushilan, Jugantar; Abhinav Bharat; Ghadar; HRA/HSRA; Kakori; Bhagat Singh; Chittagong; revolutionaries abroad

Mains: GS-I: Revolutionary movements — phases, ideology, contribution

Tier B. Ghadar, HSRA and Bhagat Singh are the most-asked. Rajasthan revolutionaries (Barhat family, Arjun Lal Sethi, Rao Gopal Singh Kharwa) are in R19.

The big picture

Revolutionary nationalism was the belief that British rule could be ended only by force, and it came in two waves, each born of disappointment with mass politics. The first wave (1905–1918) grew out of the frustration of the Swadeshi years: secret societies in Bengal and Maharashtra turned to assassination of hated officials and to dacoity to raise funds, while revolutionaries abroad (India House, the Ghadar Party) tried to organise an armed revolt during the First World War. The second wave (1920s–1934) followed the sudden withdrawal of Non-Cooperation in 1922. It produced the HRA/HSRA in north India, which under Bhagat Singh moved towards socialism, and the Chittagong armoury raid in Bengal.

Exam focus

Mains asks for an outline of the movement's development (RAS Mains 2018) and an assessment of its contribution: it failed militarily but inspired patriotism and pushed national politics towards complete independence and socialism. Prelims matches conspiracy cases with people (RAS Pre 2021).

WhenWhat happened

Core notes

I38.1 Why young nationalists turned to revolution

The revolutionaries were mostly young, educated men and women who had joined the Swadeshi movement and watched it being crushed. When the government jailed leaders and banned meetings, and the Moderates offered nothing but petitions, some concluded that open politics was useless and that only violence could shake British rule. They did not yet know how to organise the masses, so they chose a shortcut: individual heroic action, such as killing an oppressive official, which they hoped would frighten the rulers and inspire the people. The same pattern repeated in the 1920s, when Gandhi's withdrawal of Non-Cooperation after Chauri Chaura left many young activists angry and looking for another path.

Concept

Revolutionary, not "terrorist". British records, such as the Sedition (Rowlatt) Committee Report of 1918, called these groups terrorists. Indian historians today avoid that word: the revolutionaries attacked officials and the state, not random civilians, and saw themselves as soldiers of a national war. Over time their ideas changed, from the religious nationalism of the first wave (oaths on the Gita, the cult of Kali) to the secular, socialist outlook of the HSRA.

I38.2 First wave in India

In Maharashtra the Chapekar brothers (Damodar and Balkrishna) killed the plague commissioner Rand in 1897, a response to the harsh plague measures in Poona. V.D. and Ganesh Savarkar founded Abhinav Bharat (1904), and the Nasik conspiracy case followed the murder of the collector Jackson (1909).

Bengal became the main centre. The Anushilan Samiti was founded by Pramathanath Mitra with Barindra Kumar Ghosh, Aurobindo's brother, and the Jugantar group grew around the paper of that name (1906); Pulin Behari Das led the Dacca Anushilan. In 1908 at Muzaffarpur, Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki threw a bomb meant for the judge Kingsford; it killed two Englishwomen instead, and Khudiram was hanged. The police then uncovered the Maniktala bomb factory, leading to the Alipore conspiracy case (1908), in which Aurobindo Ghosh was acquitted, defended by C.R. Das, and Barindra was sentenced. Jatindranath Mukherjee (Bagha Jatin) was the main accused in the Howrah conspiracy case (1910); he later planned a German-aided uprising and was killed at Balasore (1915).

In north India, a bomb was thrown at Viceroy Hardinge during his state entry into Delhi (1912), planned by Rash Behari Bose with Sachindranath Sanyal. In the resulting Delhi conspiracy case, Master Amir Chand, Avadh Behari, Bal Mukund and Basant Kumar Biswas were hanged.

I38.3 Revolutionaries abroad

Indians abroad could organise more freely. In London, Shyamji Krishna Varma founded India House (1905) and the journal Indian Sociologist; V.D. Savarkar wrote The Indian War of Independence of 1857 there, and Madan Lal Dhingra shot Curzon Wyllie (1909). In Europe, Madame Bhikaji Cama unfurled an Indian flag at Stuttgart (1907), with S.R. Rana and Virendranath Chattopadhyay active, and the Berlin Committee (1915) sought German help.

The largest effort was the Ghadar Party (1913, San Francisco), led by Lala Har Dayal with Sohan Singh Bhakna (president), Ramchandra, Barkatullah, Kartar Singh Sarabha and Bhai Parmanand. Its members were mostly Punjabi Sikh peasants and ex-soldiers working on the west coast of North America, where racial discrimination made them feel the humiliation of colonial rule sharply. The weekly Ghadar (from 1 November 1913) called for revolt. The Komagata Maru incident (1914), when a Japanese ship carrying Indian emigrants (chartered by Gurdit Singh) was refused entry at Vancouver and its passengers were fired on at Budge Budge near Calcutta on return, deepened the anger.

When the war began, Ghadarites returned to India and fixed 21 February 1915 for an armed revolt, but the plan was betrayed; the Lahore conspiracy cases followed and Kartar Singh Sarabha was hanged. The 5th Light Infantry mutinied at Singapore (February 1915). At Kabul a Provisional Government of India (1915) was set up with Raja Mahendra Pratap as president, Barkatullah as prime minister and Ubaidullah Sindhi.

I38.4 Second wave: HRA/HSRA

The Hindustan Republican Association (October 1924, Kanpur) was founded by Sachindranath Sanyal (author of Bandi Jeevan), Jogesh Chatterjee and Ram Prasad Bismil to establish a federal republic of the United States of India. To raise funds it robbed a government treasury train at Kakori near Lucknow (9 August 1925). Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, Roshan Singh and Rajendra Lahiri were hanged (1927); Chandrashekhar Azad escaped.

The group was rebuilt as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (September 1928, Feroz Shah Kotla, Delhi) by Chandrashekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Bhagwati Charan Vohra. The word "Socialist" marked a new goal: a socialist republic, not only freedom. Bhagat Singh had earlier helped found the Naujawan Bharat Sabha (1926, Lahore).

After Lala Lajpat Rai died following a police lathi charge during the Simon Commission protest, the group killed the police officer Saunders (December 1928, Lahore), mistaking him for Scott. On 8 April 1929 Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw harmless bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly against the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Disputes Bill, "to make the deaf hear", and courted arrest, using their trial to spread their ideas and the slogan "Inquilab Zindabad". Jatin Das died after a 64-day hunger strike in jail (1929). In the Lahore conspiracy case, Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were hanged on 23 March 1931 (Hussainiwala). Azad died fighting the police in Alfred Park, Allahabad (27 February 1931).

Concept

Bhagat Singh's idea of revolution. For Bhagat Singh, revolution meant the overthrow of exploitation, of man by man and nation by nation, not merely violence. He read Marx and Lenin, wrote Why I am an Atheist, and moved away from individual action towards the idea of a mass movement of workers and peasants. Bhagwati Charan Vohra's The Philosophy of the Bomb answered Gandhi's The Cult of the Bomb. This is why the HSRA is seen as a bridge between revolutionary nationalism and the socialist left.

I38.5 Bengal in the 1930s and assessment

In Bengal, Surya Sen ("Masterda") and his Indian Republican Army raided the Chittagong armoury (18 April 1930) and fought a battle at Jalalabad hill; Surya Sen was hanged in 1934. Binoy, Badal and Dinesh attacked the Writers' Building (1930). Women took a leading part: Pritilata Waddedar attacked the Pahartali European Club (1932), Kalpana Dutt joined Surya Sen, Bina Das fired at the Governor (1932), and Santi Ghosh and Suniti Chaudhury shot a magistrate in Comilla (1931).

Concept

Why they failed, and what they achieved. The revolutionaries failed to overthrow British rule because they were small secret groups without a mass base; they lacked arms; they relied on individual action; and the state, with its police and spies, crushed them ruthlessly. Yet their sacrifice inspired young Indians, kept nationalism alive during lulls in mass politics, pushed the Congress towards purna swaraj, and through Bhagat Singh brought socialist ideas into the national movement.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Roots: the Swadeshi samitis and the Extremists (I37).
  • Context: withdrawal of Non-Cooperation (I39); the Simon Commission and Lajpat Rai's death (I40); the Gandhi–Irwin Pact and the executions of 1931 (I41).
  • Later: Subhas Bose, the INA and the RIN mutiny (I42).
  • Rajasthan: the Barhath family, Arjunlal Sethi and Rao Gopal Singh of Kharwa (R19).

What historians say

Bipan Chandra and Manmathnath Gupta wrote on HSRA ideology; S. Irfan Habib (To Make the Deaf Hear) analysed Bhagat Singh's socialism. Peter Heehs (The Bomb in Bengal) studied early Bengal revolutionaries. Harish Puri wrote on the Ghadar movement. Older official records (Rowlatt/Sedition Committee Report, 1918) described revolutionaries as terrorists — a term avoided by most Indian historians today.

Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

Give an outline of the development of the revolutionary freedom movement in 20th century India.

How to frame it: Causes → First wave in India → Abroad → Second wave → Assessment

Model answer (107 words)

Frustration after the Swadeshi movement produced the first wave: Anushilan and Jugantar in Bengal, Abhinav Bharat in Maharashtra, the Muzaffarpur bomb and Alipore case (1908), and the bomb on Hardinge (1912). Abroad, India House, Madame Cama and the Ghadar Party planned a wartime revolt (1915) that was crushed; a Provisional Government was set up at Kabul. After Non-Cooperation was withdrawn, the HRA (1924) carried out the Kakori robbery, and the HSRA (1928) under Azad and Bhagat Singh adopted socialism, killed Saunders and bombed the Assembly (1929). Surya Sen led the Chittagong raid (1930). Without a mass base they failed militarily, but they inspired youth and radicalised nationalism.

10 marks · 100 words

Assess the contribution of Bhagat Singh and the HSRA to the national movement.

How to frame it: Origins → Actions → Ideology → Impact

Model answer (95 words)

The HSRA (1928), founded by Azad, Bhagat Singh and Sukhdev, renamed the HRA to aim at a socialist republic. After Lajpat Rai's death it killed Saunders; on 8 April 1929 Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt threw harmless bombs in the Assembly "to make the deaf hear" and used their trial for propaganda. Jatin Das's fast and the executions of 23 March 1931 roused the country. Bhagat Singh saw revolution as the end of exploitation, not mere violence, and introduced socialist thought. Though militarily ineffective, the HSRA inspired youth and radicalised the struggle for purna swaraj.

5 marks · 50 words

What was the Ghadar movement?

How to frame it: Founding → Plan → Result

Model answer (47 words)

Founded in San Francisco (1913) by Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna and others among Punjabi emigrants, the Ghadar Party planned an armed revolt in India for 21 February 1915 during the war. Betrayed, it was crushed in the Lahore conspiracy cases, but it spread secular, radical nationalism.

2 marks · 15 words

What was the Komagata Maru incident?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (15 words)

1914: ship of Indian emigrants refused at Vancouver; returning passengers fired on at Budge Budge.

Part III · Unit I39Gandhi's Early Movements and Non-Cooperation1915 – 1922

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Gandhi in South Africa; Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda; Rowlatt satyagraha; Jallianwala Bagh; Khilafat; Non-Cooperation; Chauri Chaura

Mains: GS-I: Gandhian methods; Non-Cooperation and Khilafat — significance and withdrawal

Tier A. RAS Mains asked on the objectives of Non-Cooperation (2016, 5 marks) and Gandhi's relevance across three decades (2024, 10); RAS Prelims 2023 asked who presided at Calcutta (1920). Non-Cooperation, its withdrawal, and Gandhian satyagraha are among the most-asked modern topics.

The big picture

Before 1915 the Indian national movement was led by educated men in the cities: the Moderates petitioned, and the Extremists of the Swadeshi years (unit I37) mobilised students and the middle class but could not reach the villages. Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948) changed this. In South Africa (1893–1914) he developed satyagraha, non-violent resistance based on truth. Returning to India in 1915, he tested it on local grievances (Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda), then nationally against the Rowlatt Act (1919). After the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh and the Khilafat grievance of Indian Muslims, he led the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22), the first all-India mass movement. It united Hindus and Muslims, brought peasants, workers, students and women into politics, and turned the Congress into a mass organisation. He withdrew it after violence at Chauri Chaura (February 1922), a decision still debated.

Exam focus

Know Gandhi's method (satyagraha, non-violence, constructive work, the struggle–truce–struggle pattern), the objectives and programme of Non-Cooperation (RAS Mains 2016) and the debate over its withdrawal. The 2024 question on Gandhi's relevance across three decades needs this unit plus Civil Disobedience (I41) and Quit India (I42).

Core notes

I39.1 Gandhi in South Africa and his method

Gandhi went to South Africa in 1893 as a young lawyer for Dada Abdullah's firm. Within weeks he was thrown off a first-class train compartment at Pietermaritzburg because he was Indian. The Indians there (traders, indentured labourers and their descendants) faced laws that made them carry passes, pay a special £3 tax and have their marriages declared invalid. Gandhi organised them: he founded the Natal Indian Congress (1894), the newspaper Indian Opinion (1903), and two community farms, the Phoenix Settlement (1904) and Tolstoy Farm (1910), where satyagrahis lived simply and trained. From 1906 he led campaigns against the registration law; thousands courted arrest. The Smuts–Gandhi agreement (1914) abolished the £3 tax and recognised Indian marriages. In South Africa Gandhi found his method, and he wrote Hind Swaraj (1909), a critique of modern industrial civilisation.

Concept

Satyagraha. Satyagraha means "holding firmly to truth". The satyagrahi resists injustice openly and without violence, refuses to obey unjust laws, and willingly accepts the punishment, even suffering, that follows. The aim is not to defeat or humiliate the opponent but to convert him by appealing to his conscience and by showing the strength of the resisters' will. Gandhi drew on the Gita, Jain non-violence (ahimsa), Tolstoy (The Kingdom of God is Within You), Ruskin (Unto This Last) and Thoreau (civil disobedience). Why did it work in India? Because it allowed unarmed people, including peasants and women, to take part without facing a hopeless armed contest with the British, and because it put the government in a dilemma: repress peaceful protest and lose moral authority, or tolerate it and lose control.

Gandhi's strategy had three further elements. Mass mobilisation: politics had to include peasants, workers, women and the poor. Constructive programme: between campaigns, workers spread khadi, Hindu–Muslim unity, the removal of untouchability, prohibition and basic education, building the nation from below and keeping the movement alive. And a rhythm of struggle–truce–struggle (S–T–S, Bipan Chandra's term): a mass campaign, then a pause to rest and consolidate, then a new campaign, since people cannot sustain sacrifice indefinitely.

I39.2 Early satyagrahas in India

On his return (9 January 1915), on Gokhale's advice Gandhi spent a year travelling across India. He then tested satyagraha on three local grievances, each involving a different group: indigo peasants, mill workers, and landowning peasants.

MovementIssueResult
Champaran (1917)Tinkathia indigo systemInquiry; tinkathia abolished; 25% refund
Ahmedabad (1918)Mill workers' plague bonus dispute; Gandhi's first hunger strike; Anasuya Sarabhai (mill owner Ambalal's sister) supported workers35% wage increase via tribunal
Kheda (1918)Revenue remission in crop failure; Patel, Indulal YagnikRevenue collected only from those able to pay

In Champaran (Bihar), European planters forced peasants under the tinkathia system to grow indigo on three-twentieths of their land. Raj Kumar Shukla, a local peasant, persuaded Gandhi to come. When ordered to leave the district, Gandhi refused and was ready to go to jail; the government withdrew the order and appointed an inquiry with Gandhi as a member, and the system was abolished with a partial refund. At Ahmedabad he supported mill workers demanding a higher wage after the plague bonus was withdrawn; when they wavered, he went on his first hunger strike in India, and the dispute went to a tribunal. At Kheda (Gujarat), peasants whose crops had failed demanded remission of land revenue; with Vallabhbhai Patel and Indulal Yagnik, Gandhi led a no-revenue campaign, and the government agreed to collect only from those able to pay.

These campaigns made Gandhi known, won him loyal lieutenants (Rajendra Prasad, Patel, Mahadev Desai, J.B. Kripalani), and showed that ordinary people would follow a leader who shared their hardships. In 1918 he also campaigned for army recruitment, hoping for self-government after the war, a stand later criticised.

I39.3 Rowlatt satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh

Indians had expected a reward for their support in the First World War. Instead they got the Rowlatt Act (Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, March 1919), based on the report of the Sedition Committee under Justice Rowlatt. It allowed detention without trial for up to two years and trial without jury, summed up in the slogan "no vakil, no dalil, no appeal" (no lawyer, no argument, no appeal). Gandhi formed the Satyagraha Sabha and called a nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919, the first all-India mass protest. There was violence in some places, and Gandhi called the campaign a "Himalayan blunder": he had launched it before people were trained in non-violence.

In Punjab, the arrest of Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal in Amritsar led to protests. On 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi), a crowd gathered in Jallianwala Bagh, an enclosed ground with a narrow entrance. General Reginald Dyer blocked the exit and ordered his troops to fire without warning until their ammunition ran out. The official toll was 379; the Congress estimate about 1,000. Punjab was placed under martial law under Lieutenant-Governor Michael O'Dwyer, with public floggings and humiliating orders.

The reaction transformed Indian opinion. Tagore renounced his knighthood; Gandhi later returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal (1920); Sankaran Nair resigned from the Viceroy's council. The official Hunter Committee censured Dyer only mildly, and the House of Lords praised him, while a Congress inquiry (Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, Gandhi and others) documented the horror. Many Indians who had trusted British justice now lost that faith. (Udham Singh later shot O'Dwyer at Caxton Hall, London, on 13 March 1940.)

I39.4 Khilafat and Non-Cooperation

Concept

The Khilafat question. The Ottoman Sultan of Turkey was also the Caliph (Khalifa), seen by many Sunni Muslims as the spiritual head of the Muslim world and guardian of the holy places. After the First World War, in which Turkey fought against Britain, the victorious Allies dismembered the Ottoman empire (Treaty of Sèvres, 1920). Indian Muslims saw this as an insult to their faith and a broken British promise. The Ali brothers (Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali), Maulana Azad, Hakim Ajmal Khan and Hasrat Mohani formed the Khilafat Committee (1919). Gandhi supported them as a chance to unite Hindus and Muslims against British rule. The issue was religious and foreign, but it brought Muslims into the national movement in large numbers for the first time.

Objectives (RAS Mains 2016). Non-cooperation had three stated aims: to undo the Punjab wrongs (Jallianwala Bagh and martial law), to redress the Khilafat wrong, and to win swaraj. Behind these lay Gandhi's idea that British rule survived only because Indians cooperated with it; if they withdrew that cooperation, peacefully and together, the government could not function. Gandhi promised "swaraj within a year" if the programme was fully carried out.

Launch. The Khilafat Committee adopted non-cooperation in June 1920, and Gandhi launched it on 1 August 1920, the day Tilak died. The Congress approved it at a special session at Calcutta (September 1920), presided over by Lala Lajpat Rai (RAS Prelims 2023), and confirmed it at Nagpur (December 1920), under C. Vijayaraghavachariar. Nagpur changed the Congress's goal to "swaraj by peaceful and legitimate means" and reorganised the party: Provincial Congress Committees on linguistic lines, a Congress Working Committee, and a four-anna membership that opened it to the poor.

Programme. In stages: surrender of titles and honours; boycott of government schools and colleges, law courts, the legislatures (the 1920 elections were boycotted) and foreign cloth; national schools and colleges (Jamia Millia Islamia, Kashi Vidyapith, Gujarat Vidyapith, Bihar Vidyapith); swadeshi and khadi, with bonfires of foreign cloth; the Tilak Swaraj Fund (Rs 1 crore); and, in a later stage, non-payment of taxes.

Participation. Lawyers gave up their practice (Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, Rajendra Prasad, Patel); thousands of students left government institutions; workers struck; and in many regions peasants and tribals turned the movement to their own grievances. In Awadh the sanyasi Baba Ramchandra led tenants against taluqdars' high rents, cesses and begar; panchayats organised nai–dhobi bandhs (denying landlords barbers and washermen); the Oudh Kisan Sabha (October 1920, with Jawaharlal Nehru) took up their cause; in 1921 taluqdars' houses and grain stores were attacked. In Andhra peasants refused taxes (Chirala-Perala, Pedanandipadu), and in Guntur tribals and poor peasants held forest satyagrahas, grazing cattle without fees. In Assam tea-garden workers, bound by the Inland Emigration Act (1859), which barred them from leaving without permission, left the plantations for home shouting "Gandhi Maharaj ki Jai". In Punjab the Akali movement ran alongside. In Madras the non-Brahman Justice Party did not boycott the council elections. The visit of the Prince of Wales (November 1921) was met with hartals and empty streets.

Concept

One movement, many meanings. NCERT stresses that each group read non-cooperation in its own way. For the urban middle class it meant boycott and khadi; for Awadh tenants, struggle against taluqdars; for tribals, the right to forests; for plantation workers, the freedom to go home. Many peasants believed Gandhi had miraculous powers (Shahid Amin's study of Gorakhpur). This breadth gave the movement its strength, but it also meant that local actions sometimes went beyond non-violence, which is what happened at Chauri Chaura.

I39.5 Chauri Chaura, withdrawal and significance

By early 1922 Gandhi was preparing mass civil disobedience, beginning with a no-tax campaign at Bardoli in Gujarat. On 5 February 1922, at Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur district, police fired on a procession; the crowd then set fire to the police station, killing 22 policemen. Gandhi called off the movement: the Congress Working Committee met at Bardoli and withdrew it on 12 February 1922, turning workers to the constructive programme. In March Gandhi was arrested and sentenced to six years' imprisonment.

Debate

Critics (Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, Subhas Bose, Jawaharlal Nehru) felt the withdrawal came at the peak and demoralised the movement. Bipan Chandra argues it was sound: the movement was showing fatigue, violence would invite crushing repression, and mass movements must have phases of rest (S–T–S strategy). Some Marxist historians (R.P. Dutt) saw it as Gandhi protecting propertied interests. A balanced answer: Gandhi withdrew both to protect the principle of non-violence, on which mass participation depended, and because he judged the movement could not win immediately; the cost was disappointment and the turn of some young people to revolutionary violence (I38) and of others to council entry (I40).

Significance. Swaraj did not come within a year, and the Khilafat issue disappeared when Turkey itself abolished the Caliphate in 1924. Yet Non-Cooperation changed Indian politics. It was the first all-India mass movement, carrying nationalism to villages, peasants, workers, women and Muslims. It made the Congress a mass organisation with a new constitution and a new goal. It built national schools and spread khadi as a symbol of self-reliance. Above all, it broke the fear of British power: ordinary Indians had defied the government, gone to jail in thousands, and learned that they could act together. The pattern it set, mass non-violent campaign followed by a pause and constructive work, was repeated in Civil Disobedience (1930–34) and Quit India (1942).

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before: the Moderates (I36) and the Swadeshi movement and Extremists (I37); the First World War and Home Rule leagues (I37); the reform movements whose ideas Gandhi drew on (I35).
  • Roots of Gandhi's ideas: Jain and Buddhist ahimsa (I06); the Gita (I13); Bhakti saints such as Narsi Mehta (I20).
  • After: revolutionaries and the turn to violence (I38); Swarajists and the 1920s (I40); Civil Disobedience (I41); Quit India and partition (I42).
  • Society: peasant and tribal movements (I33, I34); communal politics after Khilafat (I42).
  • Rajasthan: Gandhian methods in Bijolia and Begun (R17); Praja Mandals (R20); Rajasthan Seva Sangh (R19).

What historians say

Judith Brown (Gandhi's Rise to Power) explained Gandhi's rise through "sub-contractors" — local leaders who mobilised regions. Shahid Amin ("Gandhi as Mahatma") showed how peasants in Gorakhpur created their own image of Gandhi with miraculous powers; his Event, Metaphor, Memory studies Chauri Chaura. Gail Minault studied the Khilafat movement. Bipan Chandra analysed the S–T–S strategy.

Exam traps
  • Non-cooperation was launched on 1 August 1920 and approved at Calcutta (September) and Nagpur (December 1920); NCERT Class VIII says it "began in January 1921", meaning when it took off.
  • Calcutta special session (Sept 1920, Lajpat Rai) approved NCM; Nagpur (Dec 1920, Vijayaraghavachariar) ratified and reorganised.
  • Gandhi's "Himalayan blunder" refers to the Rowlatt satyagraha (1919).
  • Dyer ordered the firing; O'Dwyer was the Lt-Governor; Udham Singh killed O'Dwyer.
  • Kheda: revenue; Ahmedabad: wages; Champaran: indigo.
  • The withdrawal resolution was passed at Bardoli (12 February 1922); Chauri Chaura is in Gorakhpur district.
