Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

Mahatma Gandhi was relevant to each generation in his three decades of involvement in the Indian freedom struggle. Elucidate with proper examples.

How to frame it: 1910s: local satyagrahas → 1920s: Non-Cooperation → 1930s: Civil Disobedience → 1940s: Quit India → Constructive work and conclusion

Model answer (97 words)

Gandhi adapted his method to each phase. In 1917–18 he won local battles for indigo peasants, mill workers and Kheda farmers. In 1920–22 Non-Cooperation and Khilafat made nationalism a mass, Hindu–Muslim movement and remade the Congress. In 1930 the Salt March turned a daily necessity into a national symbol and drew in women. In 1942 "Do or Die" gave a new generation its call. Between campaigns his constructive programme of khadi, Harijan uplift and communal harmony kept workers active, and at Noakhali in 1946–47 he worked for peace. Each generation found in him a way to act.

5 marks · 50 words

With what objectives did Mahatma Gandhi launch the Non-Cooperation Movement?

How to frame it: Punjab wrongs → Khilafat → Swaraj → Idea behind

Model answer (49 words)

Gandhi launched it in August 1920 to redress the Punjab wrongs (Jallianwala Bagh and martial law), to right the Khilafat wrong done to Turkey, and to win swaraj within a year. He held that British rule rested on Indian cooperation, and that peaceful, united withdrawal would make it unworkable.

10 marks · 100 words

Evaluate the significance of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

How to frame it: Background → Programme → Participation → Withdrawal → Significance

Model answer (92 words)

The Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh and the Khilafat grievance led Gandhi to launch non-cooperation in August 1920, approved at Calcutta and Nagpur. Indians surrendered titles and boycotted schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth; national schools and khadi spread; peasants, workers, students and women joined. After Chauri Chaura (1922) Gandhi withdrew it. Though swaraj was not won, it was the first all-India mass movement: it carried nationalism to villages, forged Hindu–Muslim unity for a time, turned the Congress into a mass organisation with a new constitution and removed the fear of British power.

5 marks · 50 words

Why did Gandhi withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement?

How to frame it: Event → Reasons → Debate

Model answer (46 words)

After a crowd killed 22 policemen at Chauri Chaura (February 1922), Gandhi withdrew the movement, fearing violence would invite repression and betray non-violence. Critics like Nehru and Bose felt it was the movement's peak; Bipan Chandra argues the movement was already tiring and needed a pause.

2 marks · 15 words

What was the Rowlatt Act?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (12 words)

1919 law allowing detention without trial; "no vakil, no dalil, no appeal".

Part III · Unit I40The 1920s: Swarajists, Simon Commission, Nehru Report1922 – 1929

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Swaraj Party; no-changers; Simon Commission; Nehru Report; Jinnah's 14 points; Lahore session and purna swaraj; left-wing, youth and workers' movements

Mains: GS-I: National movement 1922–29; Nehru Report and communal question

Tier C. The Nehru Report, Simon boycott and the Lahore session are high-yield.

The big picture

After Non-Cooperation, the Congress split over the next step: the Swarajists (C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru) wanted to enter the councils and obstruct them from within, while the no-changers (Patel, Rajendra Prasad, Rajagopalachari) favoured Gandhi's constructive programme. Communal riots grew. The all-white Simon Commission (1927) united Indian parties in protest; the Nehru Report (1928) was the Indian answer, but it failed to resolve the communal question. The decade ended with the Lahore Congress (December 1929) declaring purna swaraj. Socialist ideas, youth leagues, trade unions and the Communist movement also took shape.

Exam focus

Show how the period was not a lull: council politics, constructive work, new ideologies and the radicalisation that led to Civil Disobedience.

WhenWhat happened

1922Gaya Congress; pro-changers vs no-changers

1923Delhi special session allows council entry

Core notes

I40.1 Swarajists and no-changers

  • Swaraj Party founded January 1923 by C.R. Das (president) and Motilal Nehru (secretary) after the Gaya session (December 1922) rejected council entry.
  • Aim: enter legislatures to obstruct and expose the "hollowness" of the 1919 reforms.
  • 1923 elections: majority in the Central Provinces, strong in Bengal and the Central Legislative Assembly; Vithalbhai Patel elected President (Speaker) of the Central Legislative Assembly (1925).
  • Achievements: defeated government budgets and bills; Public Safety Bill (1928) defeated; exposed the reforms.
  • Decline: death of C.R. Das (1925); split (Responsivists — Lajpat Rai, Malaviya, N.C. Kelkar); communalism; lure of office; walked out of legislatures (1926, 1930).
  • No-changers: constructive work — khadi, national schools, Hindu–Muslim unity, untouchability removal, ashrams (Sabarmati), Gandhi's All India Spinners' Association (1925); prepared cadres for later mass movements.
  • Gandhi's mediation kept the two groups within the Congress.

I40.2 New forces of the 1920s

  • Socialist ideas: Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Bose (Independence for India League, 1928); youth leagues.
  • Communists: M.N. Roy (CPI at Tashkent, 1920); CPI at Kanpur conference (December 1925); Kanpur Bolshevik (1924) and Meerut conspiracy (1929) cases.
  • Workers: Bombay Mill Hands Association (1890, N.M. Lokhande) — the first organised workers' body; AITUC (1920; Lala Lajpat Rai first president, N.M. Joshi); Trade Unions Act (1926); Trade Disputes Act (1929); Girni Kamgar Union strikes (Bombay, 1928).
  • Peasants: Bardoli (1928), Kisan sabhas.
  • Revolutionaries: HRA/HSRA (I38).
  • Communal organisations: Hindu Mahasabha (1915), RSS (1925), Tabligh and Tanzim movements; riots (Kohat 1924).
  • Caste movements: Self-Respect (1925), Ambedkar's Mahad satyagraha (1927).

I40.3 The workers' movement

Railways, coal mines and cotton and jute mills created a modern working class from the mid-19th century. Early efforts to help workers were philanthropic: Sasipada Banerjea started a workingmen's club (1870), and N.M. Lokhande ran the paper Deenbandhu (1880) and founded the Bombay Mill Hands Association (1890). The Factory Acts of 1881 and 1891, which limited child labour and working hours, were pushed by Lancashire mill owners who wanted to blunt Indian competition, so the early nationalists did not support them.

Workers entered national politics in the Swadeshi years, with strikes in railways and presses, at the Tuticorin coral mill led by V.O. Chidambaram Pillai, and in Bombay after Tilak's conviction (1908). After the First World War came Gandhi's Ahmedabad mill strike (1918), which won a 35% wage rise, and the All India Trade Union Congress, founded on 31 October 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as president and Dewan Chaman Lal as general secretary.

The government answered growing militancy with the Trade Unions Act (1926), which registered unions, and the Trade Disputes Act (1929), which restricted strikes. The long Bombay textile strike of 1928 under the Communist-led Girni Kamgar Union was followed by the Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929), in which 31 labour leaders, among them S.A. Dange, Muzaffar Ahmed and Philip Spratt, were tried. The Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley Commission, 1929–31) reported on working conditions. The movement split in 1929–31 between moderate, Congress and Communist groups, revived under the Congress ministries (1937–39), and joined the post-war upsurge of 1945–46, when dock workers refused to load ships for Indonesia and workers struck in support of the naval ratings.

I40.4 Simon Commission

  • Appointed November 1927 (two years early, under the 1919 Act's ten-year review) by the Conservative government — Birkenhead Secretary of State; chaired by Sir John Simon; seven British MPs, no Indian (Clement Attlee among them).
  • Congress (Madras session, 1927, president M.A. Ansari) decided to boycott it; also passed a resolution for complete independence; the Muslim League (Jinnah faction) and Hindu Mahasabha joined.
  • Landed at Bombay on 3 February 1928: hartal, black flags, "Simon Go Back".
  • Lala Lajpat Rai was injured in a lathi charge at Lahore (30 October 1928) and died on 17 November; "every blow on my body will be a nail in the coffin of British rule". Nehru and Pant were beaten in Lucknow.
  • Report (1930): abolish dyarchy, establish representative government in provinces, federation, retain separate electorates — basis of the 1935 Act; no mention of dominion status.
  • Birkenhead challenged Indians to produce an agreed constitution → the Nehru Report.
Concept

Why the Simon Commission united Indians. After Non-Cooperation ended in 1922, the national movement was divided: Swarajists against no-changers, Hindus against Muslims in riots, moderates against radicals. The Simon Commission ended this drift because it insulted everyone equally. It was to decide India's constitutional future, yet it had no Indian member, implying that Indians were unfit to judge their own needs. Congress, Jinnah's League and the Hindu Mahasabha boycotted it together. Birkenhead's challenge to produce an agreed constitution drew Indians into drafting one (the Nehru Report), and its failure on the communal question, together with the government's refusal to promise dominion status, pushed the Congress to declare purna swaraj and prepare for Civil Disobedience.

I40.5 Nehru Report and Jinnah's 14 points

  • All Parties Conference (1928) appointed a committee under Motilal Nehru (members included Tej Bahadur Sapru, Subhas Bose, Ali Imam, M.S. Aney, Mangal Singh, Shuaib Qureshi; Jawaharlal Nehru as secretary).
  • Recommendations (August 1928):
    1. Dominion status (not complete independence).
    2. Joint electorates with reservation of seats for Muslims at the centre and in provinces where they were a minority (not where a majority).
    3. Linguistic provinces.
    4. 19 fundamental rights, including equal rights for women and adult suffrage.
    5. Responsible government at the centre and in provinces; federal structure with residuary powers at the centre.
    6. Secular state.
  • Opposition: the young radicals (Nehru, Bose) wanted complete independence; Jinnah's amendments (one-third seats in the central legislature, residuary powers to provinces, reservation in Punjab and Bengal) were rejected at the Calcutta convention (December 1928) under Hindu Mahasabha pressure.
  • Jinnah's 14 points (March 1929): federal constitution with residuary powers to provinces, provincial autonomy, one-third Muslim representation at the centre, separate electorates, Muslim majorities in Punjab, Bengal and NWFP, safeguards for religion and culture.
  • The Calcutta Congress (1928) gave the government one year to accept the Nehru Report or face civil disobedience.

I40.6 The road to purna swaraj

  • Irwin Declaration (31 October 1929): dominion status as the "natural issue" of India's progress; a Round Table Conference promised. Delhi Manifesto by Indian leaders demanded assurances; Irwin could not give them.
  • Lahore session (December 1929), president Jawaharlal Nehru:
    • Purna swaraj (complete independence) declared as the goal.
    • Round Table Conference to be boycotted; Congress members to resign from legislatures.
    • CWC authorised to launch civil disobedience.
    • Tricolour hoisted on the banks of the Ravi at midnight of 31 December 1929.
    • 26 January 1930 celebrated as Independence Day (Purna Swaraj Day) — later chosen as Republic Day.
Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before: Non-Cooperation and Chauri Chaura (I39); the 1919 Act and its ten-year review (I29).
  • Alongside: Bhagat Singh and the HSRA (I38); Bardoli (I33).
  • After: Dandi and Civil Disobedience (I41); the 1935 Act built on the Simon report (I29).
  • Sessions: the Congress sessions table in I36.
  • Rajasthan: political awakening and early associations in the princely states (R19).

What historians say

Bipan Chandra sees the 1920s as a phase of consolidation preparing for the next struggle. Sumit Sarkar (Modern India) emphasises new social forces (workers, peasants, Left). Ayesha Jalal (The Sole Spokesman) argues Jinnah sought a strong Muslim position within a federation and that the Nehru Report's rejection of his amendments was a turning point.

  • The Swaraj Party was founded in January 1923 by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru.
  • C.R. Das was the first president of the Swaraj Party.
  • Vithalbhai Patel became President of the Central Legislative Assembly in 1925.
  • The AITUC was founded in 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as president.
  • The CPI was formally founded at the Kanpur conference in December 1925.
  • The Meerut conspiracy case began in 1929.

  • Clement Attlee was a member of the Simon Commission.

  • The Nehru Report recommended dominion status and joint electorates.

  • The Irwin Declaration was made on 31 October 1929.

Exam traps

  • Madras (1927) passed an independence resolution; Lahore (1929) made purna swaraj the official goal.
  • Simon Commission had seven British MPs, no Indians.
  • Swaraj Party: C.R. Das (president), Motilal Nehru (secretary).

Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

Discuss the recommendations of the Nehru Report and the reasons for its failure.

How to frame it: Context → Recommendations → Opposition → Result

Model answer (94 words)

In reply to Birkenhead's challenge and the Simon Commission, an All Parties committee under Motilal Nehru proposed (1928) dominion status, responsible government, joint electorates with reserved seats for minorities, linguistic provinces, nineteen fundamental rights, adult suffrage and a secular state. Young radicals wanted complete independence, while Jinnah's amendments — one-third central seats and residuary powers to provinces — were rejected under Hindu Mahasabha pressure. Jinnah responded with his 14 points. The report thus failed to settle the communal question, but it set out a democratic constitutional framework and led to the purna swaraj demand.

5 marks · 50 words

Why was the Simon Commission boycotted?

How to frame it: Composition → Reaction

Model answer (45 words)

Appointed in 1927 to review the 1919 reforms, it had seven British MPs and no Indian — an insult to Indian self-respect. Congress, the Jinnah League and others boycotted it with hartals and "Simon Go Back"; Lajpat Rai died after a lathi charge in Lahore.

2 marks · 15 words

What was decided at the Lahore session of 1929?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (13 words)

Purna swaraj as the goal; civil disobedience authorised; 26 January 1930 Independence Day.

  • Nehru Report Aug 1928; Jinnah 14 points Mar 1929.
  • Irwin Declaration 31 Oct 1929; Lahore Dec 1929 — purna swaraj; 26 Jan 1930.

Part III · Unit I41Civil Disobedience to the 1937 Ministries1930 – 1939

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Dandi March; Civil Disobedience; Round Table Conferences; Gandhi-Irwin Pact; Karachi session; Communal Award; Poona Pact; 1937 elections; Tripuri crisis

Mains: GS-I: Civil Disobedience — features and comparison with NCM; Poona Pact; Congress ministries

Tier C. Civil Disobedience (and its comparison with NCM), the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and the Poona Pact are very frequent.

The big picture

After the Lahore declaration, Gandhi launched Civil Disobedience with the Dandi March (March–April 1930). Unlike Non-Cooperation, it involved deliberately breaking laws — salt, forest, tax laws. Mass participation, including women, was larger than ever. The British combined repression with negotiation: the Round Table Conferences, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) and, after the second phase, the Communal Award (1932), which Gandhi resisted by a fast, leading to the Poona Pact. The 1935 Act followed; in the 1937 elections the Congress formed ministries in most provinces and governed for 28 months.

Exam focus

Common questions: why salt? CDM vs NCM; Gandhi-Irwin Pact's merits; Poona Pact; record of the Congress ministries.

WhenWhat happened
31 January 1930Gandhi's 11 demands to Irwin
12 March – 6 April 1930Dandi March (Sabarmati to Dandi, 78 volunteers)
April 1930Peshawar: Khudai Khidmatgars; Garhwali soldiers refuse to fire; Chittagong raid; Rajaji's Vedaranyam march
May 1930Dharasana salt works raid (Sarojini Naidu)
November 1930 – January 1931First Round Table Conference
5 March 1931Gandhi-Irwin Pact (Delhi Pact)
23 March 1931Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru executed
March 1931Karachi session: fundamental rights and economic policy
September – December 1931Second Round Table Conference
January 1932Civil Disobedience resumed; Gandhi arrested
16 August 1932Communal Award (Ramsay MacDonald)
September 1932Gandhi's fast; Poona Pact (24 September)
November – December 1932Third Round Table Conference
1934CDM formally withdrawn; Congress Socialist Party founded
1936Lucknow and Faizpur sessions
1937Elections; Congress ministries (July)
1938Haripura (Bose)
1939Tripuri crisis; Bose resigns, forms Forward Bloc; ministries resign (October–November)

Core notes

I41.1 Dandi March and Civil Disobedience

  • 11 demands (January 1930) to Irwin — included halving land revenue, abolishing the salt tax, reducing military expenditure, releasing political prisoners, protective tariffs — ignored.
  • Why salt? A tax on a basic necessity touching every Indian, especially the poor; easy to break; non-communal; symbol of injustice.
  • Dandi March: 12 March 1930 from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 volunteers, 240 miles (about 385 km) to Dandi; broke the salt law on 6 April 1930.
  • Spread:
    • Tamil Nadu: C. Rajagopalachari — Trichinopoly to Vedaranyam.
    • Malabar: K. Kelappan (Calicut to Payyanur).
    • NWFP: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan ("Frontier Gandhi") — Khudai Khidmatgars (Red Shirts); Garhwal Rifles under Chandra Singh Garhwali refused to fire on the crowd at Peshawar.
    • Dharasana (Gujarat): Sarojini Naidu, Imam Saheb and Manilal Gandhi led non-violent raid on the salt works; brutal beating reported by the American journalist Webb Miller.
    • Sholapur (textile workers' parallel government); Manipur and Nagaland (Rani Gaidinliu); no-chowkidari tax (Bihar, Bengal); forest satyagraha (Maharashtra, Karnataka, Central Provinces); no-revenue (Gujarat, UP).
  • Features: breaking of laws; large participation of women; merchants and business groups; peasants; weaker Muslim participation than in NCM (except NWFP); boycott of foreign cloth and liquor.
  • Who joined and why (NCERT): rich peasants (Patidars of Gujarat, Jats of UP), hit by the Depression's price fall, fought against revenue and were let down when the movement was suspended in 1931 without revenue cuts; poor tenants wanted unpaid rent remitted. Business wanted protection from imports and a rupee–sterling ratio that discouraged them; it had organised in the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress (1920) and FICCI (1927); Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G.D. Birla backed the movement. Workers joined in large numbers mainly around Nagpur (railway strikes 1930, dock strikes 1932), but the Congress kept workers' demands off its programme to avoid alienating industrialists. Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay persuaded Gandhi to let women join the salt protests.
  • Limits: Dalit groups (especially in Maharashtra and Nagpur) kept away, as did most Muslim organisations after the Khilafat–Non-Cooperation alliance ended.

I41.2 Round Table Conferences and Gandhi-Irwin Pact

ConferenceCongress?Outcome
First (Nov 1930 – Jan 1931)BoycottedPrinces agreed in principle to federation; little else
Second (Sept – Dec 1931)Gandhi as sole Congress representative (Sarojini Naidu attended separately); Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for depressed classesDeadlock on the communal question; Gandhi returned empty-handed
Third (Nov – Dec 1932)BoycottedLed to the White Paper (1933) and the 1935 Act

Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931):

  • Government: release political prisoners not convicted of violence; return confiscated property not yet sold; lenient treatment of resigned officials; allow making salt for consumption in coastal villages; permit peaceful picketing; withdraw emergency ordinances.
  • Congress: suspend Civil Disobedience; attend the Second Round Table Conference.
  • Not granted: inquiry into police excesses; commutation of Bhagat Singh's death sentence (criticised by the youth).
  • Significance: the government negotiated with the Congress as an equal.

Karachi session (March 1931, president Vallabhbhai Patel): endorsed the pact; resolutions on Fundamental Rights and National Economic Programme (drafted with Nehru) — free speech, equality, universal adult franchise, free primary education, rent and revenue reduction, state control of key industries.

I41.3 Second phase, Communal Award and Poona Pact

  • Willingdon's repression; CDM resumed (January 1932); Gandhi arrested; Congress banned; movement withdrawn (April 1934).
  • Communal Award (16 August 1932) by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald: separate electorates for Muslims, Europeans, Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians — and the depressed classes (who also got a vote in general constituencies).
  • Gandhi saw separate electorates for depressed classes as dividing Hindu society; began a fast unto death in Yerwada jail (20 September 1932).
  • Poona Pact (24 September 1932) between Gandhi (through Malaviya and others) and Ambedkar: separate electorates abandoned; joint electorate with reserved seats for depressed classes — 148 seats in provincial legislatures (instead of 71 under the Award); 18% of general seats in the central legislature; primary election by depressed class voters for a panel of four candidates.
  • Gandhi then launched an all-India anti-untouchability campaign: Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932), weekly Harijan (1933).

I41.4 CDM compared with NCM

AspectNon-Cooperation (1920–22)Civil Disobedience (1930–34)
GoalSwaraj (undefined), Khilafat, Punjab wrongsPurna swaraj
MethodNon-cooperation — withdrawal (boycott)Deliberate violation of laws
MuslimsLarge participation (Khilafat)Limited (except NWFP)
Middle class (lawyers, students)StrongLess
Women, peasants, businessSomeMuch larger
WorkersSignificantLess
EndingWithdrawn after Chauri ChauraPact (1931), then repression and withdrawal (1934)

I41.5 1937 elections and Congress ministries

  • Congress Socialist Party (1934): Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Minoo Masani.
  • Lucknow (1936, Nehru) and Faizpur (1936 — first village session) sessions; Congress decided to contest elections under the 1935 Act.
  • 1937 elections: Congress won absolute majorities in five provinces (Madras, Bihar, Orissa, Central Provinces, United Provinces) and was the largest party in Bombay; later formed ministries in eight (including NWFP and Assam). The Muslim League did poorly even in Muslim seats.
  • Work of the ministries (28 months): civil liberties restored; political prisoners released; agrarian laws (tenancy, debt relief); prohibition; basic education (Wardha); improvements in health; National Planning Committee (1938, Nehru).
  • Limitations: limited powers under the Governors; caution on radical agrarian reform; tensions with the Left and kisan sabhas.
  • Jinnah's League attacked the ministries (Pirpur Report, 1938); celebrated "Day of Deliverance" (22 December 1939) when they resigned.
  • Haripura (1938) and Tripuri (1939): Subhas Bose re-elected (defeating Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Gandhi's candidate); Gandhi: "Pattabhi's defeat is my defeat"; Bose resigned and formed the Forward Bloc (May 1939).
  • Ministries resigned (October–November 1939) in protest against India being declared a party to World War II without consultation.
Concept

Why the 1937 ministries mattered. For the first time Indians governed most of British India's provinces. The 28 months showed that the Congress could run a government: it released prisoners, restored civil liberties, passed tenancy and debt-relief laws and began basic education. This raised the Congress's prestige and showed the British that power could be handed over. But office also exposed limits and divisions: the Governors kept wide powers, the ministries moved cautiously on land reform, the Left grew impatient, and the Muslim League's attacks on "Congress rule" (the Pirpur Report) helped it build support among Muslims. Both trends shaped the 1940s.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before: the Lahore resolution (I40); Non-Cooperation compared (I39).
  • Alongside: Bhagat Singh's execution and the pact (I38); the Communal Award and Ambedkar's movement (I35).
  • Constitutional link: the 1935 Act under which the ministries worked (I29).
  • After: war, Quit India and independence (I42).
  • Rajasthan: after the Haripura session (1938), Praja Mandals spread in the Rajput states (R20).

What historians say

Judith Brown (Gandhi and Civil Disobedience) studied the movement's regional variations. Sumit Sarkar highlighted business support and its limits. Bipan Chandra defended the Gandhi-Irwin Pact as a truce in the S–T–S strategy, not a surrender. Eleanor Zelliot and Gail Omvedt analysed Ambedkar's position on the Poona Pact, which he later criticised.

Prelims fact bank

  • Gandhi placed 11 demands before Irwin in January 1930.
  • The Dandi March began on 12 March 1930 with 78 volunteers.
  • Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930.
  • C. Rajagopalachari led a salt march from Trichinopoly to Vedaranyam.
  • Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan organised the Khudai Khidmatgars.
  • Chandra Singh Garhwali's soldiers refused to fire at Peshawar.
  • Sarojini Naidu led the Dharasana salt raid.
  • The Congress boycotted the first and third Round Table Conferences.
  • Gandhi was the sole Congress representative at the Second Round Table Conference.
  • The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931.
  • The Karachi session of 1931 passed the resolution on Fundamental Rights and Economic Programme.
  • Vallabhbhai Patel presided over the Karachi session.
  • The Communal Award was announced on 16 August 1932 by Ramsay MacDonald.
  • The Poona Pact was signed on 24 September 1932.

  • Gandhi founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh in 1932.
  • The Congress Socialist Party was founded in 1934.

  • Congress formed ministries in 1937.
  • Subhas Bose formed the Forward Bloc in 1939.
  • The Muslim League observed the Day of Deliverance on 22 December 1939.
Exam traps
  • Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay (NCERT Class XII) persuaded Gandhi to admit women to the salt protests; some guides credit Sarojini Naidu.
  • Dandi March: 12 March – 6 April 1930.
  • Poona Pact: joint electorate with reserved seats (148), not separate electorates.
  • Karachi (1931) president: Patel; Lahore (1929): Nehru; Tripuri (1939): Bose.
  • Congress absolute majority in five provinces, ministries in eight.
  • Gandhi-Irwin Pact did not save Bhagat Singh.

Previous-year questions (RAS)

Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

How did the Civil Disobedience Movement differ from the Non-Cooperation Movement?

How to frame it: Goal → Method → Participation → Ending → Conclusion

Model answer (90 words)

Non-Cooperation (1920–22) sought an undefined swaraj and redress of Khilafat and Punjab wrongs; Civil Disobedience (1930–34) aimed at purna swaraj. NCM withdrew cooperation through boycotts; CDM deliberately broke laws — salt, forest and tax laws. Muslim participation was high in NCM because of Khilafat but limited in CDM except in the NWFP; lawyers and students were prominent in NCM, while CDM drew far more women, peasants and business groups. NCM was withdrawn after Chauri Chaura; CDM ended in the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and then repression. CDM was broader and more defiant.

5 marks · 50 words

What was the Poona Pact? Why was it significant?

How to frame it: Background → Terms → Significance

Model answer (44 words)

Against the Communal Award's separate electorates for depressed classes, Gandhi fasted in Yerwada; Ambedkar agreed (24 September 1932) to joint electorates with 148 reserved provincial seats. It kept Hindu society electorally united, increased depressed class representation and began the reserved-seat model of the Constitution.

2 marks · 15 words

Why did Gandhi choose salt?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (13 words)

Salt tax hit every Indian, especially the poor; easy, non-communal law to break.

Part III · Unit I421939–1947: War, Quit India, INA, Partition1939 – 1947

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: August Offer; individual satyagraha; Cripps Mission; Quit India; INA; Wavell Plan; RIN mutiny; Cabinet Mission; Direct Action; Mountbatten Plan; Independence Act

Mains: GS-I: Quit India — significance; INA; Cabinet Mission; causes of partition

Tier B. Quit India, Cripps and Cabinet Mission, and "causes of partition" are among the most-asked questions of modern history.

The big picture

The Second World War changed everything. When the Viceroy declared India at war without consultation, the Congress ministries resigned. British offers (August Offer, Cripps Mission) fell short; Gandhi launched the Quit India Movement (August 1942), the most intense mass uprising of the freedom struggle. Abroad, Subhas Bose led the Indian National Army. After the war, the INA trials, the RIN mutiny and mass unrest convinced Britain to leave. The Cabinet Mission (1946) tried to keep India united, but Congress–League deadlock, Direct Action and communal violence led to the Mountbatten Plan and partition on 15 August 1947.

Exam focus

The two analytical questions: significance of Quit India, and why partition happened.

WhenWhat happened
3 September 1939Linlithgow declares India at war
October–November 1939Congress ministries resign
22 December 1939League's Day of Deliverance
March 1940Lahore Resolution of the Muslim League; Ramgarh Congress (Azad)
8 August 1940August Offer
October 1940Individual satyagraha (Vinoba Bhave first, Nehru second)
January 1941Bose escapes from Calcutta
March–April 1942Cripps Mission
8 August 1942Quit India resolution (Bombay, Gowalia Tank)
9 August 1942Leaders arrested
1942–44Parallel governments: Ballia, Tamluk, Satara
February 1943Gandhi's 21-day fast
21 October 1943Bose forms the Provisional Government of Free India (Singapore)
1943Bengal famine
1944INA in Imphal–Kohima; C.R. formula; Gandhi–Jinnah talks
June 1945Wavell Plan; Simla Conference
November 1945INA trials at Red Fort
February 1946RIN mutiny (Bombay)
March–June 1946Cabinet Mission (plan of 16 May)
16 August 1946Direct Action Day; Calcutta killings
2 September 1946Interim Government (Nehru)

3 June 1947Mountbatten Plan

Core notes

I42.1 War, August Offer, individual satyagraha, Cripps

  • Congress position (Wardha, September 1939): support the war against fascism if India is declared free and a Constituent Assembly promised; Linlithgow refused — ministries resigned.
  • Lahore Resolution (March 1940, Muslim League): "independent states" for Muslim-majority areas in the north-west and east — later called the Pakistan Resolution. (The name "Pakistan" was coined by Choudhry Rahmat Ali, 1933.)
  • August Offer (8 August 1940, Linlithgow): dominion status as the objective (undated); expansion of the Viceroy's Executive Council; a body to frame a constitution after the war; minorities' consent for any future constitution (a veto to the League). Congress rejected it.
  • Individual satyagraha (October 1940): limited, symbolic; anti-war speech; Vinoba Bhave first, Nehru second, Brahma Datt third; "Delhi Chalo".
  • Cripps Mission (March–April 1942), after Japan's advance (fall of Singapore, Rangoon):
    • Dominion status after the war; constitution-making body elected by provincial legislatures and nominated by princes; provinces could opt out and form a separate union; defence with Britain during the war.
    • Rejected by Congress (no immediate transfer, princes nominated, provincial option threatened unity; Gandhi is said to have called it "a post-dated cheque" — the addition "on a crashing bank" is of doubtful origin) and by the League (Pakistan not explicitly accepted).

I42.2 Quit India Movement (1942)

  • Causes: failure of Cripps; rising prices and shortages; Japanese threat and fear of a "scorched earth" policy; discrimination in evacuating Indians from Malaya and Burma; loss of faith in British rule.
  • Resolution passed by the AICC at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, on 8 August 1942; Gandhi's mantra "Do or Die" (Karo ya Maro).
  • Operation Zero Hour: Gandhi and all top leaders arrested early on 9 August; Congress banned.
  • Leaderless phase: spontaneous uprisings; attacks on railways, telegraph lines, police stations; underground leaders — Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Aruna Asaf Ali (hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank), Usha Mehta (Congress Radio), Achyut Patwardhan, Sucheta Kripalani.
  • Parallel governments: Ballia (Chittu Pandey, August 1942), Tamluk (Midnapore — Jatiya Sarkar, 1942–44; Matangini Hazra killed), Satara (Prati Sarkar, 1943–46, Y.B. Chavan, Nana Patil; volunteer corps (seba dals) and village units (tufan dals), people's courts; mainly kunbi peasants with Dalit support, it lasted until the 1946 elections despite later Congress disapproval).
  • Repression: over 1 lakh arrested; firing, aerial strafing; collective fines.
  • Attitudes: Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha and Communists (after the USSR joined, "People's War") stayed away; Ambedkar opposed it; princes supported the British.
  • Gandhi's 21-day fast (February 1943) against government blame for violence.
  • Significance: demand for independence became non-negotiable; youth, students, peasants and women participated massively; showed that British rule could not continue without consent; though crushed by 1944, it made withdrawal a question of time.

In Assam, Kanaklata Barua was shot dead at Gohpur in September 1942 while leading a procession to hoist the national flag at the police station.

I42.3 Subhas Bose and the INA

  • Bose escaped house arrest (January 1941), reached Berlin via Kabul; Free India Centre and radio; Indian Legion.
  • First INA (1942): Mohan Singh with Japanese help from Indian prisoners of war; Rash Behari Bose's Indian Independence League (Tokyo, Bangkok conference 1942).
  • Bose reached Singapore (July 1943); took command of the Azad Hind Fauj; slogans "Delhi Chalo", "Jai Hind", "Give me blood and I will give you freedom".
  • Provisional Government of Free India (21 October 1943, Singapore); Andaman and Nicobar islands handed over (renamed Shaheed and Swaraj); Rani Jhansi Regiment (Captain Lakshmi Swaminathan).
  • INA brigades (Gandhi, Nehru, Azad, Subhas) fought in the Imphal–Kohima campaign (1944); flag hoisted at Moirang (Manipur); retreat after Japanese defeat.
  • Bose reportedly died in an air crash at Taipei (18 August 1945).
  • INA trials (Red Fort, November 1945): Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sahgal, Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon — Hindu, Sikh and Muslim; defended by Bhulabhai Desai, Tej Bahadur Sapru, Nehru, Asaf Ali, K.N. Katju; nationwide agitation; sentences remitted.

I42.4 Post-war upsurge

  • Desai–Liaquat Pact (January 1945): an informal understanding between Bhulabhai Desai (Congress leader in the Central Assembly) and Liaquat Ali Khan (League) for an interim government at the centre with equal numbers of Congress and League nominees and 20% of seats for minorities. Neither party adopted it, but the idea of Congress–League parity passed into the Wavell Plan.
  • Wavell Plan / Simla Conference (June 1945): Executive Council of Indians except the Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief; parity of caste Hindus and Muslims; failed over Jinnah's claim to nominate all Muslim members.
  • Labour Party won in Britain (July 1945, Attlee).
  • Elections (1945–46): Congress swept general seats; League won most Muslim seats — polarisation.
  • RIN mutiny (18 February 1946, HMIS Talwar, Bombay): against racial discrimination and poor food; spread to 78 ships and 20 shore establishments; supported by strikes; called off on Patel and Jinnah's advice. Also RIAF strikes and Jabalpur army unrest.
  • Peasant and worker struggles: Tebhaga, Telangana, Punnapra-Vayalar; postal strike; princely state movements.
Concept

Why the British decided to leave. By 1946 the foundations of British rule had given way. The war had left Britain economically exhausted and dependent on the USA, and the new Labour government had no wish to hold India by force. More important, the British could no longer rely on the instruments of control: the INA trials (1945) roused sympathy across communities and even within the Indian army, the RIN mutiny (February 1946) and unrest in the air force and police showed that Indian forces might not obey, and the bureaucracy was tired and short of British recruits. Quit India had shown that ruling without consent meant constant repression. The question was no longer whether Britain would leave, but how, and whether India would stay united.

I42.5 Cabinet Mission (1946)

  • Members: Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State), Stafford Cripps, A.V. Alexander.
  • Plan of 16 May 1946:
    1. Rejected a full Pakistan.
    2. Union of India (provinces and states) with control over defence, foreign affairs and communications; all other powers to provinces.
    3. Grouping of provinces: Group A (Hindu-majority — Madras, Bombay, UP, Bihar, CP, Orissa), Group B (Punjab, NWFP, Sindh), Group C (Bengal, Assam); groups could frame their own constitutions.
    4. Constituent Assembly elected by provincial assemblies (389 members: 292 provinces, 4 chief commissioners' provinces, 93 princely states).
    5. Interim Government of Indian leaders.
  • Disagreement on grouping: Congress saw it as optional; the League as compulsory. Nehru's statement (July 1946) that the Congress was not bound by the plan led the League to withdraw acceptance.
  • Direct Action Day (16 August 1946): Calcutta killings; violence spread to Noakhali (Gandhi's peace mission), Bihar, Garhmukteshwar, Punjab.
  • Interim Government (2 September 1946) under Nehru; the League joined in October (Liaquat Ali Khan — finance) but obstructed. Constituent Assembly met on 9 December 1946; League boycotted.

I42.6 Mountbatten Plan and partition

  • Attlee's statement (20 February 1947): British would leave by June 1948.
  • Mountbatten as Viceroy (March 1947); 3 June Plan: partition; provincial assemblies of Punjab and Bengal to vote on division; referendum in NWFP and Sylhet; Sindh to decide; princely states free to join either (paramountcy lapses); boundary commission; date advanced to 15 August 1947.
  • Radcliffe boundary awards (published 17 August 1947).
  • Indian Independence Act (royal assent 18 July 1947) — see I29.
  • Partition violence: an estimated 0.5–1 million killed (estimates vary up to 2 million); 10–15 million displaced.
  • About 30,000 abducted women were "recovered" (22,000 Muslim women in India, 8,000 Hindu and Sikh women in Pakistan) in an operation that ran until 1954.
  • Gandhi spent 15 August in Calcutta (Beliaghata), fasting for peace; assassinated on 30 January 1948.

I42.7 Why partition happened

  1. British policy of divide and rule: separate electorates (1909), Communal Award, recognising the League as the sole Muslim voice (August Offer, Cripps, Simla veto).
  2. Growth of communalism: Hindu and Muslim communal organisations; two-nation theory.
  3. Congress limitations: failure to win over Muslim masses after the 1930s; rejection of coalitions in UP (1937); underestimation of the League.
  4. Jinnah's leadership and the League's mass mobilisation after 1937; the Lahore Resolution; 1946 election victory.
  5. Direct Action and communal violence made a united India seem unworkable; Congress leaders accepted partition to obtain a strong centre and quick transfer of power.
  6. British haste to leave (Attlee's deadline; Mountbatten's advanced date).
  7. Numbers NCERT uses: in 1937 (franchise about 10–12% of the population) the League won only 4.4% of the Muslim vote; in 1946 the Congress took 91.3% of the non-Muslim vote and the League 86.6% of the Muslim vote. Iqbal's League presidential address (Allahabad, 1930) spoke of a "North-West Indian Muslim state", still within a loose federation. In December 1938 the Congress Working Committee barred its members from the Hindu Mahasabha (founded 1915). In Punjab the cross-community landholders' Unionist Party was strong from 1923 to 1947.
Debate

Ayesha Jalal argues Jinnah used the Pakistan demand as a bargaining counter for parity in a federal India and that the Congress's insistence on a strong centre made partition unavoidable. Bipan Chandra stresses colonial communal policy and the failure to contain communalism. Anita Inder Singh and Yasmin Khan (The Great Partition) emphasise the contingency of 1946–47 and the role of violence.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before: the 1937 ministries and their resignation (I41); separate electorates and the Communal Award (I29, I41); revolutionaries and the INA's roots (I38).
  • Constitutional link: the Indian Independence Act, 1947 (I29).
  • After: integration of the princely states (I43); the Constituent Assembly and the Nehru era (I45).
  • Rajasthan: Praja Mandals in 1942 (R20); the integration of Rajasthan (R21).

What historians say

See the debate box. Sumit Sarkar and Gyanendra Pandey (Remembering Partition) study the violence. Urvashi Butalia (The Other Side of Silence) and Ritu Menon recorded women's experiences. Leonard Gordon wrote a standard biography of the Bose brothers; Peter Fay studied the INA.

Exam traps
  • The Muslim League accepted the Cabinet Mission plan on 6 June 1946; the Mission's interim-government statement was 16 June. NCERT's timeline swaps the two dates.
  • 1937 was not the first provincial election: councils had been elected under the 1919 Act from 1920. It was the first under the 1935 Act with provincial autonomy (NCERT says "for the first time").
  • Both the League (June 1946) and the Congress initially accepted the Cabinet Mission plan; the League withdrew its acceptance in July 1946. Statements that neither accepted it are wrong.
  • Cripps (1942): provincial option; Cabinet Mission (1946): grouping, rejected Pakistan.
  • Quit India resolution 8 August; arrests 9 August (August Kranti Day).
  • First INA: Mohan Singh; Bose took over in 1943.
  • Wavell Plan (1945) failed at Simla over League's nomination claim.
  • Independence Act royal assent 18 July 1947.

Mains answer writing

2 marks · 15 words

Highlight the role of Aruna Asaf Ali in the Quit India Movement.

How to frame it: Flag at Gowalia Tank → Underground leader

Model answer (17 words)

She hoisted the Congress flag at Gowalia Tank on 9 August 1942 and led the movement underground.

10 marks · 100 words

Assess the significance of the Quit India Movement.

How to frame it: Causes → Course → Parallel governments → Repression → Significance

Model answer (100 words)

After the Cripps failure, wartime hardship and the Japanese threat, the Congress passed the Quit India resolution on 8 August 1942; Gandhi gave the call "Do or Die". Leaders were arrested next morning, and the movement became a spontaneous uprising: railways and police stations were attacked, underground leaders such as JP, Lohia and Aruna Asaf Ali organised resistance, and parallel governments arose in Ballia, Tamluk and Satara. It was crushed by 1944 with massive repression. Yet it made independence the only acceptable demand, involved youth, peasants and women on an unprecedented scale and showed Britain could not rule without consent.

5 marks · 50 words

What were the main proposals of the Cabinet Mission Plan?

How to frame it: Union → Grouping → Assembly → Interim government

Model answer (44 words)

The 1946 plan rejected Pakistan and proposed a Union handling defence, foreign affairs and communications, with residuary powers to provinces grouped into A, B and C; a Constituent Assembly elected by provincial assemblies; and an interim government. Disputes over grouping led to its collapse.

2 marks · 15 words

What was the RIN mutiny?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (13 words)

February 1946 revolt of Indian naval ratings in Bombay against discrimination; widely supported.

Part IV · Unit I43Integration of the Princely States1947 – 1950

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Instrument of Accession; Standstill Agreement; Patel and V.P. Menon; Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir; Goa, Pondicherry

Mains: GS-I: Post-independence consolidation — integration of princely states

Tier B. Patel's role and the three problem states are standard questions. The integration of Rajasthan (seven stages) is in R21.

The big picture

At independence there were about 565 princely states covering roughly two-fifths of the subcontinent's area. With the lapse of paramountcy (Indian Independence Act, 1947), each was legally free to join India or Pakistan or remain independent. Through the diplomacy of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon (States Department, July 1947), almost all acceded before 15 August 1947 by signing the Instrument of Accession (surrendering defence, external affairs and communications). Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir were the exceptions. A second stage (1948–50) merged or integrated the states into unions and provinces, and democratised them.

Exam focus

Explain the method (persuasion, popular pressure, and force when needed), the three problem cases and the two-stage process. RAS Mains has asked twice about Hyderabad (2016, 2023), including the role of the Razakars.

WhenWhat happened

25 July 1947Mountbatten addresses the Chamber of Princes
15 August 1947Most states have acceded
September 1947Junagadh accedes to Pakistan
20 February 1948Junagadh plebiscite
22 October 1947Tribal raiders invade Kashmir
26 October 1947Hari Singh signs the Instrument of Accession
1 January 1948India refers Kashmir to the UN
November 1947Standstill Agreement with Hyderabad
13–17 September 1948Operation Polo (Hyderabad)
1948–1949Unions: Saurashtra, Matsya, Vindhya Pradesh, Madhya Bharat, PEPSU, Rajasthan, Travancore-Cochin

1961Goa liberated (Operation Vijay)
1971Privy purses abolished (26th Amendment)

Core notes

I43.1 The problem: the lapse of paramountcy

Under British rule the princes had accepted the Crown's paramountcy: the British controlled their defence and foreign relations, and in return protected their thrones. The Indian Independence Act (1947) declared that paramountcy would lapse and would not pass to India or Pakistan. In law, therefore, each of about 565 states could join either dominion or try to stay independent. Some rulers, such as those of Travancore, Hyderabad and Bhopal, hoped to do just that. Had they succeeded, India would have been broken into pieces, with states in its middle controlling railways, rivers and roads.

Concept

Accession first, merger later. Patel's method worked in two stages. First, a state only acceded: through the Instrument of Accession it handed India just three subjects, defence, external affairs and communications, and kept everything else. This asked little of the rulers, so almost all signed before 15 August 1947. Second, in 1948–50, the states were merged into provinces or grouped into unions, and their administrations were made democratic. Asking for little at first made the second, far larger step possible.

I43.2 The approach

The States Department was set up on 5 July 1947 with Patel as minister and V.P. Menon as secretary. A Standstill Agreement kept existing arrangements (customs, posts, railways) running while the Instrument of Accession settled the political question. Patel appealed to the princes' patriotism and to their self-interest: they were assured privy purses, titles and private property. Mountbatten used his influence with them, notably in his address to the Chamber of Princes (25 July 1947). Below them, popular movements (praja mandals and the States People's Conference) pressed reluctant rulers. Travancore (where the dewan C.P. Ramaswami Aiyar briefly declared independence), Bhopal and Jodhpur hesitated before acceding.

I43.3 The three problem states

StateSituationResolution
JunagadhHindu majority, Muslim Nawab (Mahabat Khan III); acceded to Pakistan (September 1947); not contiguous to PakistanPopular revolt (Samaldas Gandhi's provisional government, Arzi Hukumat); Indian troops; Nawab fled; plebiscite (February 1948) — overwhelming vote for India
HyderabadLargest state; Hindu majority; Nizam Osman Ali Khan wanted independence; Standstill Agreement (November 1947); Razakars (Kasim Razvi, Ittehad-ul-Muslimeen) terrorised the population; Telangana peasant struggleOperation Polo ("police action", 13–17 September 1948); Nizam acceded; became Rajpramukh (1950)
Jammu and KashmirMuslim majority, Hindu ruler Hari Singh; sought independence (standstill with Pakistan); National Conference under Sheikh Abdullah opposed the ruler and the Muslim LeagueTribal raiders backed by Pakistan invaded (22 October 1947); Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession (26 October 1947); Indian troops airlifted; India referred the matter to the UN (1 January 1948); ceasefire (1 January 1949) left part of the state under Pakistan's control; Article 370
Concept

Why the Razakars blocked Hyderabad's accession. The Nizam wanted independence, and the Razakars, the armed volunteers of Kasim Razvi's Ittehad-ul-Muslimeen, gave him the force to resist pressure. They terrorised the largely Hindu population and attacked trains and villages, while Razvi pushed the Nizam to reject any settlement. This made negotiation under the Standstill Agreement impossible, and violence was also feeding the communist-led Telangana peasant struggle. India therefore ended the deadlock by force through Operation Polo (September 1948).

I43.4 Second stage: merger and democratisation

Once the states had acceded, small states were merged into neighbouring provinces (for example the Orissa and Chhattisgarh states, 1948). Larger groups formed unions of states: Saurashtra (1948), Matsya (1948), Vindhya Pradesh, Madhya Bharat, PEPSU (Patiala and East Punjab States Union), Rajasthan (in stages, completed 1949; Ajmer added 1956) and Travancore-Cochin (1949). Some, such as Himachal Pradesh, Tripura, Manipur, Bhopal, Kutch and Bilaspur, were administered by the centre.

Rulers became Rajpramukhs (heads) of the unions and received privy purses, guaranteed under Article 291. The 1950 Constitution made the former princely unions Part B states under Rajpramukhs, a category ended by the States Reorganisation Act (1956). When a 1970 presidential order derecognising the princes was struck down by the Supreme Court (Madhav Rao Scindia case), the privy purses were abolished by the 26th Amendment (1971).

Concept

Why integration succeeded so fast. Within about two years, hundreds of states that had existed for centuries disappeared into the Indian Union. Several factors explain this. The princes had no real independent strength: paramountcy had protected them, and without it they faced their own people. The praja mandal movements had already weakened their hold. Patel combined generous terms (privy purses, titles, posts as Rajpramukhs) with a clear message that India would not tolerate independent states in its territory, and he used force only where persuasion failed, as in Hyderabad. V.P. Menon's administrative skill turned agreements into working governments. Note the contrast in principle: in Junagadh India insisted that the people's will, shown by plebiscite, outweighed the ruler's choice, while in Kashmir it was the ruler's accession, supported by Sheikh Abdullah's popular National Conference, that brought the state to India.

I43.5 French and Portuguese territories

France handed over its settlements peacefully: Chandernagore by plebiscite (1949), merged with West Bengal (1954); Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam de facto in 1954 and de jure in 1962. Portugal refused. Volunteers liberated Dadra and Nagar Haveli (1954), the Goa Liberation satyagraha (1955) was fired upon, and finally Operation Vijay (18–19 December 1961) ended Portuguese rule in Goa, Daman and Diu.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before: paramountcy and the princes under the Crown (I29, I30); the States People's Conference and praja mandals (R19, R20); the Cabinet Mission and the Independence Act (I42).
  • Rajasthan: integration in seven stages, 1948–56 (R21).
  • After: the reorganisation of states on linguistic lines, 1956 (I44).

What historians say

V.P. Menon (The Story of the Integration of the Indian States) is the insider account. Ramachandra Guha (India after Gandhi) and Bipan Chandra, Mridula Mukherjee, Aditya Mukherjee (India since Independence) give balanced narratives. Ian Copland (The Princes of India in the Endgame of Empire) analysed the princes' strategies.

Part IV · Unit I44Linguistic Reorganisation of States1948 – 1987

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Dhar Commission; JVP Committee; Potti Sriramulu; States Reorganisation Commission; creation of new states

Mains: GS-I: Linguistic reorganisation — process, rationale and effect on national unity

Tier B. Frequently asked as an analytical question ("Did linguistic states weaken or strengthen national unity?").

The big picture

The Congress had accepted linguistic provinces since the Nagpur session (1920). After independence and partition, leaders feared that linguistic states would encourage division. The Dhar Commission and the JVP Committee (1948–49) advised caution. Popular agitation — especially the death of Potti Sriramulu after a fast for Andhra (1952) — forced the creation of Andhra (1953) and the States Reorganisation Commission (1953–55). The States Reorganisation Act (1956) created 14 states and 6 union territories, largely on linguistic lines. Further reorganisation followed (Bombay, Punjab, the north-east, and later Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Telangana).

Exam focus

Conclude with the accepted view: linguistic states, by accommodating diversity, strengthened democracy and national unity.

December 1953States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, K.M. Panikkar, H.N. Kunzru)
1955SRC report
1 November 1956States Reorganisation Act in force: 14 states, 6 UTs; Andhra Pradesh formed
1960Bombay divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat
1963Nagaland
1966Punjab, Haryana (and Chandigarh UT); hill areas to Himachal
1971Himachal Pradesh a state
1972Manipur, Tripura, Meghalaya states (Meghalaya autonomous 1970)
1975Sikkim (36th Amendment)

2000Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand
2014Telangana

Core notes

I44.1 Early hesitation

  • Dhar Commission (1948, S.K. Dhar): favoured administrative convenience over language; opposed immediate linguistic reorganisation.
  • JVP Committee (December 1948 – April 1949; Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya): emphasised unity, security and economic progress; advised postponement but conceded that strong public demand might be accepted (e.g. Andhra, excluding Madras city).
  • The 1950 Constitution classified states as Part A, B, C, D — not on linguistic lines.

I44.2 The Andhra movement and the SRC

  • Potti Sriramulu, a Gandhian, fasted for a separate Andhra state from 19 October 1952 and died on 15 December 1952 after 58 days; violent protests followed.
  • Nehru announced Andhra; formed on 1 October 1953 (capital Kurnool).
  • States Reorganisation Commission (December 1953): Fazl Ali (chairman), K.M. Panikkar, H.N. Kunzru; report (September 1955) — accepted language as the main basis but rejected "one language, one state" as the sole principle; also considered unity, security, financial and administrative viability.
  • States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (with the 7th Amendment): abolished the four-category classification; 14 states and 6 union territories; Kerala, Mysore (Karnataka), Andhra Pradesh (with Telangana), Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan (with Ajmer) reshaped.

Safeguards for national unity. The SRC put unity and security first and rejected "one language, one state" as the sole principle. To keep states from turning inward, it recommended that the all-India services take at least half their new recruits from outside the state, that about a third of High Court judges come from outside the state, and that linguistic minorities be protected, with teaching in the mother tongue at the primary stage. These led to Articles 350A (mother-tongue instruction) and 350B (a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities), added by the 7th Amendment (1956). The 1956 Act also set up five zonal councils to encourage co-operation between neighbouring states.

Concept

Why leaders hesitated, and why they gave way. In 1947–49 partition had just shown how identity could divide the country, the princely states were still being integrated, and leaders feared that language-based states would breed regional loyalties stronger than the national one. Hence the caution of the Dhar Commission and the JVP Committee. But language was how ordinary people dealt with government, courts and schools, and the demand had been Congress policy since 1920. Potti Sriramulu's death showed that refusing it was more dangerous than granting it. Reorganisation with safeguards turned a possible source of separatism into a base for democratic participation.

I44.3 Later reorganisations

YearChangeBackground
1960Bombay split into Maharashtra and GujaratSamyukta Maharashtra Samiti and Mahagujarat movements; Bombay city to Maharashtra
1963NagalandNaga insurgency (Phizo)
1966Punjab and Haryana; Chandigarh UTPunjabi Suba movement (Master Tara Singh, Sant Fateh Singh); Shah Commission
1971–72Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura, MeghalayaNorth-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act 1971
1975Sikkim36th Amendment after a referendum
1987Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, GoaMizo Accord (1986, Laldenga)
2000Chhattisgarh (1 Nov), Uttarakhand (9 Nov), Jharkhand (15 Nov)Development and tribal identity, not language
2014Telangana (2 June)Long movement (1969 agitation; K. Chandrashekar Rao); Srikrishna Committee
2019J&K reorganised into two UTsArticle 370 provisions revoked

I44.4 Assessment

  • Fears: regional chauvinism, inter-state disputes (Belgaum, water), threat to unity.
  • Outcome: made administration accessible in people's languages; deepened democracy; removed a major source of discontent; regional identities proved compatible with national identity.
  • Later states show that development, ethnicity and administrative viability have replaced language as the main basis.
Debate

Bipan Chandra and Ramachandra Guha argue that linguistic reorganisation strengthened unity by accommodating diversity; critics point to persistent border and water disputes and the rise of regionalism. Most scholars today see it as a democratic success.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before: the Nagpur Congress's linguistic committees (I39); integration of the princely states (I43).
  • Alongside: the Nehru era and planning (I45).
  • Constitution: Articles 3, 350A and 350B; the 7th Amendment.
  • Rajasthan: Ajmer merged into Rajasthan in 1956, the final stage of integration (R21).

What historians say

Paul Brass (Language, Religion and Politics in North India) studied language movements. Ramachandra Guha (India after Gandhi, ch. "Ideas of India") and Bipan Chandra et al. (India since Independence) treat reorganisation as a key step in nation-building. Selig Harrison (India: The Most Dangerous Decades, 1960) predicted linguistic states would lead to fragmentation — a prediction that did not come true.

  • Fazl Ali chaired the States Reorganisation Commission.
  • K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru were members of the SRC.
  • The States Reorganisation Act came into force on 1 November 1956.
  • The 1956 reorganisation created 14 states and 6 union territories.
  • Bombay was divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat in 1960.
  • Nagaland became a state in 1963.
  • Punjab and Haryana were separated in 1966.
  • Sikkim became a state by the 36th Amendment in 1975.
  • Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa became states in 1987.
  • Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were formed in 2000.
  • Telangana was formed on 2 June 2014.
Exam traps
  • Andhra (1953) was the first linguistic state after independence; Orissa (1936) before independence.
  • JVP = Jawaharlal, Vallabhbhai, Pattabhi.
  • SRC report 1955; Act in force 1 November 1956.
  • Andhra Pradesh (1956) ≠ Andhra state (1953).

Mains answer writing

5 marks · 50 words

What were the suggestions given by the State Reorganisation Commission to strengthen the national unity?

How to frame it: Unity first → All-India services → High Court judges → Linguistic minorities

Model answer (52 words)

The SRC (1955) put unity and security first and rejected "one language, one state" as the sole basis. It recommended that half of new all-India service recruits and about a third of High Court judges come from outside the state, and safeguards for linguistic minorities, including mother-tongue primary teaching (Articles 350A, 350B).

10 marks · 100 words

Did the linguistic reorganisation of states weaken national unity? Discuss.

How to frame it: Background → Process → Fears → Outcome → Conclusion

Model answer (92 words)

The Congress had promised linguistic provinces since 1920, but after partition the Dhar Commission and the JVP Committee advised caution for the sake of unity. Potti Sriramulu's death forced the creation of Andhra (1953); the Fazl Ali Commission led to the 1956 Act creating 14 states and 6 UTs, followed by Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab and others. Critics feared regional chauvinism, and border and water disputes did arise. Yet administration in people's languages deepened democracy, removed a major grievance and showed that regional and national identities could coexist. On balance it strengthened unity.

5 marks · 50 words

What was the States Reorganisation Commission?

How to frame it: Members → Recommendations → Result

Model answer (45 words)

Appointed in December 1953 under Fazl Ali, with K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru, it accepted language as the main basis of reorganisation while weighing unity, security and viability. Its 1955 report led to the States Reorganisation Act (1956), creating 14 states and 6 union territories.

Part IV · Unit I45Nation-Building in the Nehru Era and Planning1947 – 1964

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Constituent Assembly; Planning Commission; Five-Year Plans; land reforms; Non-Alignment; Panchsheel; 1962 war; Bhoodan

Mains: GS-I: Post-independence consolidation — planning, land reforms, foreign policy; Nehru's legacy

Tier B. Planning (Mahalanobis model), land reforms and Non-Alignment are frequently asked. Links to Economy and International Relations.

The big picture

India at independence faced partition refugees, communal violence, integration of states, poverty and illiteracy. Under Jawaharlal Nehru (Prime Minister 1947–64), the new state built its foundations: a democratic Constitution (1950), universal adult franchise (first elections 1951–52), a planned mixed economy with emphasis on heavy industry, land reforms, institutions of science and education, and a foreign policy of Non-Alignment. The 1962 war with China was the major setback.

Exam focus

Assess the Nehru era as a whole: achievements in democracy, institution-building and industrialisation; shortcomings in agriculture, land reform and defence.

WhenWhat happened
1946–49Constituent Assembly (constitution adopted 26 November 1949)
26 January 1950Constitution in force; India a republic
March 1950Planning Commission (Nehru chairman)
1951First Five-Year Plan begins; Bhoodan begins (Pochampalli, 18 April)
1951–52First general elections
1952National Development Council; Community Development Programme (2 October)
1954Panchsheel agreement with China
1955Bandung Conference; Avadi session — "socialistic pattern of society"
1956Industrial Policy Resolution; Second Plan (Mahalanobis)
1957Kerala: first elected Communist government
1959Balwant Rai Mehta panchayati raj launched at Nagaur (2 October)
1961Belgrade: first NAM summit; Goa liberated
October–November 1962Sino-Indian war
27 May 1964Death of Nehru

Core notes

I45.1 Constitution and democracy

  • Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946; Rajendra Prasad president; B.R. Ambedkar chairman of the Drafting Committee; adopted 26 November 1949; in force 26 January 1950.
  • Making the Constitution (NCERT Class XII): M.N. Roy first proposed a constituent assembly (1934). Members were chosen by the provincial legislatures elected in 1945–46, not by universal franchise; about 82% were also Congress members, and the League boycotted it. Sachchidananda Sinha was provisional president before Rajendra Prasad. Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution (13 December 1946) and proposed the tricolour with the navy-blue wheel; Patel worked behind the scenes on key reports; B.N. Rau was constitutional adviser. Drafting Committee members included K.M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswamy Aiyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Mohammad Saadulla, B.L. Mitter and D.P. Khaitan.
  • Debates: separate electorates were rejected (Patel blamed them for Partition; Begum Aizaz Rasul called them self-destructive for minorities); K. Santhanam defended states' rights while Ambedkar wanted a Centre stronger than under the 1935 Act; the Congress had accepted Hindustani in the 1930s, but the compromise made Hindi the official (not national) language, with English continuing for 15 years.
  • First general elections (October 1951 – February 1952): universal adult franchise; Election Commission under Sukumar Sen; Congress won a large majority.
  • Strengthening of parliamentary institutions, an independent judiciary, a free press, civilian control of the military.
  • Hindu Code Bills (1955–56) reformed Hindu personal law.
  • Panchayati Raj (Balwant Rai Mehta Committee, 1957): three-tier system first launched at Nagaur, Rajasthan (2 October 1959).

I45.2 Planning and the mixed economy

  • Background: Bombay Plan (1944, industrialists), Gandhian Plan (S.N. Agarwal), People's Plan (M.N. Roy), National Planning Committee (1938, Nehru).
  • Planning Commission (March 1950) — extra-constitutional, advisory; National Development Council (1952).
  • Industrial Policy Resolutions 1948 and 1956 (the "economic constitution"): Schedule A (state), Schedule B (mixed), Schedule C (private) — public sector to occupy the "commanding heights".
PlanFocusResult
First (1951–56)Agriculture, irrigation, power; Harrod–Domar model (drafted chiefly by the economist K.N. Raj); Bhakra-Nangal, Damodar Valley, HirakudSuccessful — growth above target
Second (1956–61)Rapid heavy industrialisation; P.C. Mahalanobis model; steel plants at Bhilai (USSR), Rourkela (West Germany), Durgapur (UK)Foreign exchange crisis; industry grew
Third (1961–66)Self-reliance; agriculture and industryFailed — 1962 and 1965 wars, droughts; Plan holiday (1966–69)

Institutions: IITs (Kharagpur 1951), AIIMS (1956), Atomic Energy Commission (1948, Homi Bhabha), CSIR, ISRO's predecessor INCOSPAR (1962, Vikram Sarabhai), UGC (1953).

Education commissions: the University Education Commission (1948–49) under S. Radhakrishnan and the Secondary Education Commission (1952–53) under A. Lakshmanaswami Mudaliar.

Concept

Why Nehru chose planning and heavy industry. In 1947 India was poor, mostly agricultural, and dependent on imported machines. Private capital was too small and too cautious to build steel plants, dams and power stations, and nationalists believed colonial rule had kept India industrially backward on purpose. So the state would plan and invest. The First Plan (Harrod–Domar model) stressed agriculture, irrigation and power after partition's food crisis. The Second Plan (Mahalanobis model) argued that long-run growth needed India to make its own capital goods, machines that make machines, so it put the public sector into steel and heavy industry. This built an industrial base, but it starved agriculture of attention until the food crisis of the mid-1960s.

I45.3 Land reforms and rural development

  1. Abolition of zamindari (intermediaries) — largely completed by the mid-1950s; first and Ninth Schedule amendments protected the laws.
  2. Tenancy reforms: security of tenure, regulation of rent, ownership rights — weakly implemented.
  3. Ceiling on landholdings — evaded through benami and fictitious transfers; little surplus land.
  4. Consolidation of holdings — successful in Punjab, Haryana, western UP.
  5. Cooperative farming (Nagpur session, 1959) — opposed and abandoned.
  • Community Development Programme (2 October 1952) and National Extension Service (1953).
  • Bhoodan (land-gift) movement of Vinoba Bhave, begun at Pochampalli (Telangana, 18 April 1951); later Gramdan; about 4 million acres pledged, much of it poor land.

I45.4 Foreign policy

  • Non-Alignment: independence from Cold War blocs; Bandung (1955); Belgrade (1961) first NAM summit — Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno, Nkrumah.
  • Panchsheel (29 April 1954) with China: mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, peaceful coexistence; "Hindi–Chini bhai bhai".
  • Roles in Korea (NNRC chairmanship), Indo-China (ICSC), Suez (1956), decolonisation, disarmament.
  • 1962 war: background — Tibet (Dalai Lama's asylum, 1959), McMahon Line and Aksai Chin disputes, "forward policy"; China attacked in October 1962 in NEFA and Ladakh; India defeated; Defence Minister V.K. Krishna Menon resigned; Henderson Brooks–Bhagat report.
  • Relations with Pakistan: Kashmir, Indus Waters Treaty (1960, World Bank mediation).

I45.5 Assessment of the Nehru era

Achievements: democratic institutions survived; secularism; integration; planned industrial base; scientific and educational institutions; independent foreign policy and global standing.

Shortcomings: agriculture neglected (food imports, PL-480); incomplete land reforms; licence-permit raj bureaucracy; slow poverty reduction; illiteracy; defeat in 1962; Kashmir unresolved.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before: the National Planning Committee (I41); partition and the Constituent Assembly (I42); integration of the states (I43).
  • Alongside: linguistic reorganisation (I44); science and technology (I46); women and the Hindu Code Bill (I47).
  • Roots: zamindari created by colonial settlements, now abolished (I30); peasant movements (I33).
  • Rajasthan: land reform and jagirdari abolition in Rajasthan (R21, R23).

What historians say

Bipan Chandra, Mridula and Aditya Mukherjee (India since Independence) offer a positive assessment of Nehruvian nation-building. Ramachandra Guha (India after Gandhi) emphasises the "unnatural nation" that survived. Sunil Khilnani (The Idea of India) analyses Nehru's vision. Critics such as B.R. Shenoy (1950s) questioned the Mahalanobis strategy; Jagdish Bhagwati criticised the licence raj.

  • K. Santhanam of Madras was the chief defender of states' rights in the Constituent Assembly.
  • Gandhi Sagar, the first of four dams on the Chambal, was completed in 1960.
  • The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.
  • Sukumar Sen was the first Chief Election Commissioner.
  • The University Education Commission (1948–49) was chaired by S. Radhakrishnan; the Secondary Education Commission (1952–53) by A. Lakshmanaswami Mudaliar.
  • The first general elections were held in 1951–52.
  • The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950.
  • The National Development Council was set up in 1952.
  • The First Five-Year Plan was based on the Harrod–Domar model.
  • The Second Five-Year Plan was based on the Mahalanobis model.
  • Bhilai steel plant was built with Soviet help.
  • The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 is called the economic constitution of India.
  • The Community Development Programme began on 2 October 1952.
  • Vinoba Bhave began the Bhoodan movement at Pochampalli in 1951.
  • Panchayati raj was first launched at Nagaur on 2 October 1959.
  • The Panchsheel agreement was signed with China in 1954.
  • The first NAM summit was held at Belgrade in 1961.
  • The Avadi session (1955) adopted the socialistic pattern of society.
  • The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960.
  • The Sino-Indian war was fought in 1962.
Exam traps

10 marks · 100 words

Assess the achievements and limitations of planning in the Nehru era.

How to frame it: Framework → Plans → Achievements → Limitations

Model answer (96 words)

Nehru set up the Planning Commission (1950) and, through the 1956 Industrial Policy Resolution, gave the public sector the commanding heights of a mixed economy. The First Plan (Harrod–Domar) built irrigation and power and exceeded targets; the Second (Mahalanobis) created heavy industry — Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur — and institutions such as the IITs and the Atomic Energy Commission. But agriculture was neglected, leading to food imports; land reform remained incomplete; the licence raj bred inefficiency; and the Third Plan failed amid war and drought. Planning laid an industrial and scientific base but did not end poverty.

Non-Alignment meant independence from Cold War blocs while judging issues on merit. Nehru promoted it at Bandung (1955) and the Belgrade NAM summit (1961), with Panchsheel and peacekeeping roles in Korea and Indo-China. The 1962 war with China exposed its security limits.

Part IV · Unit I46Science and Technology; Economic Reforms of 19911947 – 2000s

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Atomic energy and space programmes; Green and White Revolutions; IT; 1991 crisis and LPG reforms

Mains: GS-I: Post-independence India — science and technology, economic reforms

Tier C. This closes the RAS history syllabus's "post-independence" section. Detailed science and economy content belongs in GS-III notebooks; here the historical narrative is enough.

The big picture

Independent India invested early in science and technology — atomic energy (Homi Bhabha), space (Vikram Sarabhai), agricultural research (M.S. Swaminathan) — as tools of self-reliance. The Green Revolution (late 1960s) ended dependence on food imports; Operation Flood made India the largest milk producer. The planned, regulated economy, however, ran into crisis: in 1991 India faced a balance-of-payments emergency, leading to liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation (LPG) under P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh.

Exam focus

Know the pioneers, the milestones and the causes, content and impact of the 1991 reforms.

I46.1 Science and technology

Atomic energyHomi J. Bhabha — TIFR (1945), Atomic Energy Commission (1948), Trombay (BARC, named 1967); three-stage nuclear programme (thorium); Apsara reactor (1956); Pokhran-I (1974, peaceful nuclear explosion); Pokhran-II (1998); NPT not signed
SpaceVikram Sarabhai — INCOSPAR (1962), Thumba launch (1963), ISRO (1969); Satish Dhawan; Aryabhata (1975, Soviet launch); SLV-3 (1980, A.P.J. Abdul Kalam project director); INSAT, PSLV, GSLV; Chandrayaan, Mangalyaan
DefenceDRDO (1958); IGMDP (1983, Abdul Kalam) — Prithvi, Agni, Trishul, Akash, Nag
AgricultureGreen Revolution — HYV seeds (Norman Borlaug's dwarf wheat), irrigation, fertilisers; M.S. Swaminathan; C. Subramaniam (agriculture minister); Punjab, Haryana, western UP
DairyOperation Flood (1970), Verghese Kurien, NDDB, Amul (Anand model) — White Revolution
Telecom and ITSam Pitroda — C-DOT (1984); software growth (Bangalore), Software Technology Parks (1991)

Green Revolution effects: food self-sufficiency; but regional and inter-personal inequality, soil and water degradation, wheat bias, rise of rich farmers.

CSIR laboratories: the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (1942) built a chain of national laboratories after independence, among them the Central Electrochemical Research Institute at Karaikudi (Tamil Nadu, 1953).

I46.2 The 1991 crisis

  • Causes: fiscal deficits through the 1980s; rising external debt; Gulf War (1990–91) oil price rise and loss of remittances; political instability; collapse of the USSR (a major trade partner); foreign exchange reserves fell to about two weeks of imports; credit rating downgraded.
  • Emergency steps: gold pledged (Bank of England, Union Bank of Switzerland); IMF loan with conditions; rupee devalued (July 1991).
Concept

Why the planned economy reached a crisis. The Nehruvian model protected Indian industry behind high tariffs and licences, and gave the public sector the lead. This built an industrial base, but over time protected firms had little reason to become efficient, licences bred delay and corruption, and exports stayed weak, so India earned little foreign exchange. In the 1980s growth was financed by government borrowing at home and abroad. When the Gulf War raised oil prices and cut remittances, and the Soviet Union, a major trading partner, collapsed, India could no longer pay for its imports. The crisis gave the government the reason, and the IMF conditions the pressure, to dismantle the licence raj.

I46.3 The LPG reforms

  • Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, Finance Minister Manmohan Singh; New Industrial Policy (24 July 1991).
  • Liberalisation: industrial licensing abolished for most industries; MRTP restrictions eased; reduced reservation for the public sector.
  • Privatisation: disinvestment in public sector undertakings; private entry into reserved sectors.
  • Globalisation: import tariffs cut; quantitative restrictions removed; rupee made convertible on the current account (1993–94); foreign direct and portfolio investment encouraged; WTO (1995).
  • Financial sector: Narasimham Committee (1991) — banking reforms; SEBI given statutory powers (1992).
  • Tax reform: Raja Chelliah Committee.

Impact: higher growth rates (especially services and IT), larger foreign exchange reserves, expansion of the middle class; but critics point to jobless growth, agrarian distress, regional inequality and limited gains for the poor.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before: planning, the Mahalanobis model and the first science institutions (I45).
  • Ancient roots: India's scientific tradition, Aryabhata and zero (I14).
  • Alongside: women in independent India (I47).
  • Rajasthan: the nuclear tests at Pokhran (1974, 1998) were held in Jaisalmer district.

Jagdish Bhagwati and Arvind Panagariya (India: The Emerging Giant) defend liberalisation; Jean Drèze and Amartya Sen (An Uncertain Glory) stress human development gaps. Itty Abraham (The Making of the Indian Atomic Bomb) and Gyan Prakash (Another Reason) study science and nationalism.
