Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

What were the causes and main features of the economic reforms of 1991?

How to frame it: Causes → Liberalisation → Privatisation → Globalisation → Impact

Model answer (93 words)

In 1991 large fiscal deficits, rising external debt, the Gulf War oil shock, lost remittances and the Soviet collapse left India with reserves for barely two weeks of imports. The Rao government, with Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister, pledged gold, took IMF help and devalued the rupee. The New Industrial Policy abolished most licensing and eased MRTP limits; public sector shares were disinvested; tariffs were cut, the rupee made current-account convertible and foreign investment invited; banking and capital markets were reformed. Growth and reserves rose, though critics note jobless growth and agrarian distress.

5 marks · 50 words

What were the achievements and limitations of the Green Revolution?

How to frame it: Achievements → Limitations

Model answer (42 words)

HYV seeds, irrigation and fertilisers, promoted by Swaminathan and C. Subramaniam from the mid-1960s, made India self-sufficient in food grains, mainly wheat. But gains were concentrated in Punjab, Haryana and western UP and among richer farmers, and caused soil and groundwater degradation.

2 marks · 15 words

Who was Homi Bhabha?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (13 words)

Father of India's nuclear programme; founded TIFR and headed the Atomic Energy Commission.

Part IV · Unit I47Women's Reform Movement and Women's Empowerment1829 – 2001

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Social reform for women in the 19th century: sati, widow remarriage, female infanticide, child marriage, education; Women reformers: Savitribai Phule, Pandita Ramabai, Tarabai Shinde, Rukhmabai, D.K. Karve, Begum Rokeya; Women's organisations: WIA (1917), NCWI (1925), AIWC (1927); women in the freedom struggle; After 1947: constitutional guarantees, Hindu Code laws, Towards Equality (1974), NCW (1992), 73rd and 74th Amendments; Rajasthan link: Deorala (1987) and the Sati (Prevention) law; the Women's Development Programme and the Bhanwari Devi case leading to Vishaka (1997)

Mains: GS-I Part B: Post-independent India — Women empowerment and women reform movement; GS-I Part B: Socio-religious reform movements in the 19th and 20th century

Tier C. New in the 2026 syllabus, so there is no RAS PYQ yet. Expect a 10-mark question on the course of the women's movement from social reform to empowerment, and short questions on laws, reports and reformers. Links: I35 (reform movements), I42 (women in Quit India), Law notebook (Domestic Violence Act, POSH Act).

The big picture

The women's question in India moved through three stages. First (c. 1820–1900), male reformers sought legal change for women: the ban on sati (1829), the Widow Remarriage Act (1856) and the Age of Consent Act (1891), with schools for girls. Women such as Savitribai Phule and Pandita Ramabai began speaking for themselves. Second (1900–1947), women organised: the Women's Indian Association (1917) and the All India Women's Conference (1927) demanded education, suffrage and legal reform, while thousands joined the Salt Satyagraha and Quit India. Third (after 1947), the Constitution promised equality, the Hindu Code laws (1955–56) reformed family law, the report Towards Equality (1974) showed how far reality lagged behind, and a new autonomous women's movement pressed for laws on dowry, rape and violence, leading to the National Commission for Women (1992) and one-third reservation in local bodies (73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992).

Exam focus

Answer frame: reform for women → movement by women → rights and empowerment through the state and law; end with a Rajasthan example (Deorala 1987, Bhanwari Devi and Vishaka 1997).

Core notes

I47.1 Stage 1: social reform for women (19th century)

IssueReformerOutcome
SatiRaja Rammohan RoyBengal Regulation XVII, 1829 (Bentinck)
Widow remarriageIshwar Chandra VidyasagarHindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856
Female infanticideBritish officials; reformersBengal regulations (1795, 1804); Female Infanticide Prevention Act, 1870
Child marriageBehramji Malabari; the Rukhmabai case (1884–88)Age of Consent Act, 1891 (12 years); Sarda Act, 1929
EducationPhules, Bethune, Vidyasagar, KarveGirls' schools (Pune 1848, Calcutta 1849); widows' home (1896) and women's university (1916) by Karve

Women's own voices. Savitribai Phule taught at the first girls' school and wrote poetry against caste and gender oppression. Tarabai Shinde's Stri Purush Tulana (1882) attacked double standards. Pandita Ramabai founded the Arya Mahila Samaj (1882) and Sharada Sadan (1889) for widows. Rukhmabai refused to accept a child marriage and became one of India's first women doctors. Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain wrote Sultana's Dream (1905) and worked for Muslim girls' education in Bengal.

I47.2 Stage 2: women organise (1900–1947)

  • Organisations: Women's Indian Association (1917, Madras), National Council of Women in India (1925), and the All India Women's Conference (1927, Pune), which began with education and moved on to suffrage and legal reform.
  • Politics: Annie Besant presided over the Congress in 1917 and Sarojini Naidu in 1925, the first Indian woman to do so. Women won a limited franchise in the provinces in the 1920s and under the 1935 Act.
  • Freedom struggle: mass participation in the Salt Satyagraha (1930); in Quit India, Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank (9 August 1942) and Usha Mehta ran the underground Congress Radio; the INA's Rani of Jhansi Regiment was led by Lakshmi Swaminathan.
  • Karachi resolution (1931) promised equal rights regardless of sex: the bridge to the Constitution.
Concept

From reform "for" women to a movement "by" women. The 19th-century reforms were mostly led by men, and they framed women as victims to be rescued through laws and schools. Those schools, however, produced educated women who began to speak for themselves, first in writing (Tarabai Shinde, Pandita Ramabai) and then through their own organisations. The national movement, especially Gandhi's mass campaigns, drew women into public life in large numbers, which made it hard to deny them political rights. By the 1930s women's bodies such as the AIWC were demanding the vote and legal equality as rights, not favours, and the Karachi resolution (1931) committed the Congress to them. This is the line that runs into the Constitution.

I47.3 Stage 3: rights and empowerment after 1947

  • Constitution: equality (Art. 14), no discrimination on grounds of sex with special provisions allowed for women (Art. 15(1), 15(3)), equal opportunity (Art. 16), equal pay for equal work (Art. 39(d)), maternity relief (Art. 42), and the duty to renounce practices derogatory to women (Art. 51A(e), added in 1976).
  • Hindu Code laws (1955–56): monogamy and divorce, daughters' inheritance, guardianship and adoption. The Special Marriage Act (1954) allowed civil marriage.
  • Other laws: Dowry Prohibition Act (1961), Maternity Benefit Act (1961), Equal Remuneration Act (1976).
  • Towards Equality (1974): the Committee on the Status of Women in India found falling sex ratios and widespread disadvantage; it gave rise to women's studies and a new women's movement.
  • Autonomous women's movement (1970s–80s): campaigns against dowry deaths and custodial rape (the Mathura case led to the 1983 criminal law amendment).
  • Institutions: National Commission for Women (1992, under the 1990 Act); 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) reserving at least one-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities for women; National Policy for the Empowerment of Women (2001).

I47.4 Rajasthan link

  • Deorala, Sikar (1987): the sati of Roop Kanwar led to the Rajasthan Sati (Prevention) law and the central Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987.
  • Women's Development Programme (1984): village-level workers (sathins) campaigned against child marriage. The gang-rape of Bhanwari Devi, a sathin, in 1992 led to the Supreme Court's Vishaka guidelines (1997), later the basis of the POSH Act 2013 (Law notebook).
  • Rajasthan's women reformers and Praja Mandal activists are covered in the Rajasthan History notebook (R19, R20).
Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Roots: the socio-religious reform movements (I35); Bentinck and the ban on sati (I30).
  • Freedom struggle: women in Civil Disobedience (I41) and Quit India (I42).
  • After 1947: the Hindu Code laws and the Nehru era (I45).
  • Rajasthan: women in the Praja Mandals (R20); changing social patterns in Rajasthan (R23).

What historians say

Geraldine Forbes (Women in Modern India, 1996) traces the move from reform for women to women's organisations. Radha Kumar (The History of Doing, 1993) documents campaigns from the 19th century to the 1990s. Uma Chakravarti and Lata Mani argue that 19th-century reform debated women more than it listened to them; Mani shows the sati debate was really about scripture and colonial authority. Vina Mazumdar, member secretary of the 1974 committee, describes Towards Equality as the starting point of women's studies in India.

Exam traps

Trace the evolution of the women's movement in India from social reform to empowerment.

Model answer (101 words)

In the 19th century reformers sought laws for women: the sati ban (1829), widow remarriage (1856) and the Age of Consent Act (1891), with girls' schools started by the Phules. Women then organised through the WIA (1917) and AIWC (1927) and joined the Salt and Quit India movements. After 1947 the Constitution promised equality and the Hindu Code laws reformed family law, but Towards Equality (1974) exposed the gap, sparking campaigns against dowry and rape. The NCW (1992) and one-third reservation in local bodies followed. Rajasthan's Bhanwari Devi case produced the Vishaka guidelines (1997): reform became empowerment through law and participation.

Part VIndian Heritage (Indus to the British era)

4 units10 verified PYQs44 self-test questions

Part V · Unit I48Architecture: Indus to the British Erac. 2600 BCE – 1931 CE

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Harappan town planning: Mohenjodaro, Dholavira, Lothal; Mauryan pillars, stupas and rock-cut caves; post-Mauryan stupas and chaityas; Temple architecture: Gupta beginnings; Nagara, Dravida and Vesara styles; Pallava, Chola, Chandela, Odisha, Hoysala; Indo-Islamic architecture: Sultanate, provincial styles, Vijayanagara, Mughal; Colonial architecture: Indo-Saracenic, New Delhi

Mains: GS-I Part B: Indian heritage — architecture from the Indus to the British era

Tier A. Indian heritage (IH1) carried 55.5 marks across the five Mains papers 2016–2024, the sixth most-tested line. Architecture questions: Mauryan pillars (2023, 10 marks), indigenous impact on Mughal architecture (2024, 5 marks); the 2023 "continuity of culture" question (10 marks) is best answered with examples from this unit and I49–I51. Rajasthan forts, temples and havelis are in the Art, Culture and Heritage notebook (book 6).

The big picture

Indian architecture is best read as continuity with change. Each age kept what worked and added something new, and three forces drove the change: religion (what kind of building worship needed), power (rulers built to show their authority and earn legitimacy) and technique (new materials and ways of spanning space). The Harappans built planned cities of baked brick. The Mauryas began building in stone: polished pillars, the first stupas and rock-cut caves. Buddhist stupas and chaityas grew in the post-Mauryan centuries. The Gupta period gave the first structural temples, which matured into the Nagara (north), Dravida (south) and Vesara (Deccan) styles. From the 13th century the Indo-Islamic tradition brought the true arch, the dome and lime mortar; Indian craftsmen blended these with brackets, chhatris and lotus motifs, a synthesis that peaked under the Mughals. The British added neo-classical, neo-Gothic and Indo-Saracenic buildings and a new capital at New Delhi.

Exam focus

RAS asks you to argue about architecture: were Mauryan pillars Indian? How did Indian traditions shape Mughal buildings? Is Indian culture continuous? For any answer, use this order: structure (plan, material, technique) → features → one or two named monuments with patron and date → what they show about continuity or synthesis.

c. 1010Brihadeeswara (Rajarajeshwara) temple, Thanjavur, completed under Rajaraja I
c. 950–1050Chandela temples at Khajuraho (Kandariya Mahadeva)
12th–13th centuryHoysala temples at Belur and Halebidu
13th centurySun temple at Konark under Narasimhadeva I (Eastern Ganga); Qutub Minar begun by Aibak, completed by Iltutmish
1311Alai Darwaza built by Alauddin Khalji
1565–72Humayun's tomb, Delhi, commissioned by Bega Begum; architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas
1571–85Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar's capital
1590Govind Deva temple, Vrindavan, built by Raja Man Singh of Amber

1888Victoria Terminus, Bombay, designed by F.W. Stevens

Core notes

I48.1 Harappan cities: planning before monuments

The Harappans left no temples or palaces that we can identify with certainty. Their achievement was the planned city. Streets ran on a rough grid, houses opened onto side lanes, and covered drains ran along the streets with inspection holes. Bricks, whether baked or sun-dried, followed a standard ratio of 1:2:4 across hundreds of sites, which points to a shared system of rules. Most cities had a raised citadel in the west and a larger lower town where most people lived.

Each major site is remembered for one structure. Mohenjodaro has the Great Bath, a watertight tank of fitted bricks sealed with bitumen, probably used for ritual bathing, and a large building often called a granary. Lothal in Gujarat has a brick basin usually read as a dockyard, linked to trade. Dholavira in Kutch was divided into three parts (citadel, middle town, lower town) and cut large stone reservoirs to store rainwater in a dry land. The concern with water, drainage and order is the first lasting theme of Indian building: the later stepwells, temple tanks and Mughal water channels continue it.

I48.2 Mauryan stone and the Buddhist stupa

Indian building after the Harappans was mostly in wood and brick, which has perished. The Mauryas made the shift to stone on a large scale, for reasons of power and religion: Ashoka wanted his dhamma carried across the empire in lasting form.

His pillars are single shafts of Chunar sandstone with a mirror polish. The shaft is plain, round and tapering, with no base; on top, carved from a separate block, sits a capital: an inverted lotus (often called bell-shaped), a round abacus, and one or more animals. The four lions of the Sarnath capital are India's national emblem; the abacus below them carries a wheel, a lion, an elephant, a bull and a horse.

Debate

Were the pillars Indian or Persian? The polish and the bell capital reminded early scholars of the columns of the Achaemenid (Persian) palace at Persepolis, so they argued for Persian influence, perhaps through craftsmen who came to India after Alexander destroyed the Persian empire. Others point to basic differences. Persian columns stand on bases; Mauryan shafts rise straight from the ground. Persian shafts are built of segments; Mauryan ones are monolithic. Persian columns hold up roofs; Mauryan pillars stand free as monuments. The animals, the lotus and the wheel are Indian motifs, and the purpose, to carry a king's moral message, is Indian. John Irwin traced them to an older Indian cult of the sacred pillar. The balanced view, which the 2023 Mains question wants you to argue: some foreign technique may have been absorbed, but the form and purpose are indigenous.

Ashoka also had the Barabar caves near Gaya cut into hard granite and polished inside, for the Ajivikas; the Lomas Rishi cave has a carved doorway that copies a wooden hut with a curved roof. This was the start of rock-cut architecture: buildings carved out of the hill rather than built up. In the next centuries Buddhist monks cut chaityas (prayer halls with a stupa at the far end) and viharas (monasteries) into the Western Ghats at Bhaja, Karle and later Ajanta, keeping wooden-style ribs and beams in stone.

Concept

The stupa. A stupa is a solid mound built over relics of the Buddha or a saint; it is a memorial, not a building you enter. Its parts: the hemispherical mound (anda); above it a square railing-like harmika (abode of the gods); a mast (yashti) carrying an umbrella (chhatri), a sign of honour; a railing (vedika) round the mound marking a path for walking round it (pradakshina); and gateways (toranas). Ashoka built the brick core of the Sanchi stupa; the stone casing and the four carved toranas came later, under the Shungas and Satavahanas. Inscriptions record hundreds of donors: kings, monks, nuns, merchants and guilds (the ivory workers of Vidisha paid for carving on one gateway). The stupa shows how Buddhism spread through ordinary patrons, not only kings. The parasol on top survives in the chhatri of later Indian and Mughal buildings, and the Sanchi dome inspired Rashtrapati Bhavan.

The early carvings never show the Buddha as a person: an empty seat, a tree, a wheel or a stupa stands for him (see I49). Sanchi's northern gateway tells the Vessantara Jataka, and figures such as the shalabhanjika (a woman holding a tree) and Gajalakshmi show that popular beliefs about fertility and good fortune were absorbed into Buddhist art.

I48.3 The Hindu temple: from shrine to styles

Why did temples appear so late, around the 5th century CE? Vedic religion centred on the open-air sacrifice and needed no building. As devotion (bhakti) to images of Vishnu and Shiva grew in the Gupta period, the image needed a house. The first temples were small and simple: Sanchi Temple 17 and the temple at Tigawa are a square sanctum with a flat roof and a pillared porch. The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh (Uttar Pradesh) shows an early tower, and the brick temple at Bhitargaon shows the same idea in brick. Every later temple grew from this core.

Concept

Parts of a Hindu temple. The garbhagriha ("womb house") is a small dark sanctum that holds the main image. Over it rises a tower: a shikhara in the north, a vimana in the south. In front is a mandapa, a hall for worshippers, sometimes several in a row. A path round the sanctum allows pradakshina. The temple stands on a plinth, often on a raised platform (jagati). It was designed as a model of the cosmos, with the god at the centre and the tower as the mountain of the gods (Meru), so the worshipper moves from the busy hall into darkness and the presence of the deity. This is why temples grew taller and more elaborate but never changed the sanctum.

From the 7th century, regional styles grew apart. The texts name three, and the difference lies mostly in the tower and the layout.

StyleRegionFeaturesExamples
NagaraNorth IndiaCurved tower (shikhara) over the sanctum with a ribbed stone disc (amalaka) and a pot (kalasha) on top; often on a high platform; usually no enclosure wallKhajuraho (Kandariya Mahadeva), Konark, Lingaraja at Bhubaneswar
DravidaTamil countryStepped pyramidal tower (vimana); enclosure wall; gateway towers (gopurams) that later grow taller than the vimana; a water tank in the complexShore Temple, Brihadeeswara, Meenakshi temple (Madurai)
VesaraDeccanA mix of the two; star-shaped plans under the HoysalasAihole and Pattadakal (Chalukya), Belur and Halebidu (Hoysala)

The north. At Khajuraho the Chandelas built sandstone temples on high platforms whose towers rise in a cluster of smaller towers like a mountain range; the Kandariya Mahadeva is the finest. In Odisha the temple is called a deul and its hall a jagamohana; the Lingaraja at Bhubaneswar and the Konark Sun temple of Narasimhadeva I (13th century) are the peaks; Konark is built as the Sun god's chariot, with carved stone wheels and horses.

The south. The Pallavas moved from rock to structure at Mahabalipuram. The five rathas are each carved from a single rock, while the Shore Temple (Narasimhavarman II, Rajasimha) is built of cut stone. The Chola king Rajaraja I completed the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur around 1010: its vimana, about 66 metres high, was the tallest of its time and announced the king's power as much as the god's. Later, under the Pandyas, Vijayanagara and the Nayakas, the gopurams of the enclosure walls grew taller than the central tower, and temples became walled towns with halls, tanks and markets (Madurai, Srirangam).

The Deccan sat between the two traditions and mixed them. At Aihole the Chalukyas experimented: the Durga temple has an apsidal (rounded-end) plan. At Pattadakal temples in the northern and southern styles stand side by side. The Hoysalas (12th–13th centuries) built at Belur and Halebidu on star-shaped plans in soft soapstone, which allowed very fine carving.

I48.4 Indo-Islamic architecture: arch, dome and synthesis

Concept

Trabeate and arcuate. Trabeate (post-and-beam) building lays horizontal beams across vertical supports; it was the Indian method, and its spans were short. Arcuate building carries the load on true arches and domes, in which wedge-shaped stones are held in place by a central keystone, so larger spaces can be roofed. The spread of the arcuate method after the 13th century was helped by lime mortar, which set hard with stone chips into a kind of concrete. Before that, Indian masons built corbelled arches, laying each course of stone a little further out than the one below until they met; these look like arches but do not work like them.

The Sultanate. The first mosques were built quickly from the material of older temples, and Indian masons used their own methods: the arches of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque in Delhi (Aibak) are corbelled, and its screen is carved with Indian creepers beside Quranic verses. The Qutub Minar was begun by Aibak and completed by Iltutmish. The Alai Darwaza (1311), the gateway Alauddin Khalji added to the mosque, has the first true arches and true dome in India, in red sandstone with white marble decoration. The Tughlaqs built massive, plain buildings with sloping (battered) walls, as at Tughlaqabad. The Lodis built octagonal tombs in gardens, which the Mughals would develop. Rulers also built for the public: Iltutmish's reservoir Hauz-i-Sultani at Delhi, tanks, wells, sarais and bazaars all earned legitimacy.

The provinces. When the Sultanate broke up, regional kingdoms built in their own manner, which shows how local tradition shaped Islamic forms. Gujarat (Jama Masjid, Ahmedabad) used carved pillars and brackets from its temple tradition; Jaunpur built the Atala Masjid with a huge gateway screen; Bengal used brick and curved roofs; in the Deccan, Bijapur built the Gol Gumbaz, one of the largest domes in the world. Vijayanagara built Dravida temples with tall gopurams, musical pillars and kalyana mandapas (Vitthala temple, Hampi), while its Lotus Mahal and elephant stables use the arches and domes of the neighbouring sultanates.

The Mughals. Babur laid out gardens; the full style begins with Humayun's tomb (1565–72), built by his widow Bega Begum to a design by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas. It brings together a Persian plan and Indian materials and features: a central double dome, a tall arched portal (pishtaq), the hasht bihisht ("eight paradises") plan of a central hall ringed by eight rooms, red sandstone edged with white marble, chhatris on the roof, all set in a charbagh. Akbar built forts at Agra and Lahore and a new capital at Fatehpur Sikri (1571–85), where Indian trabeate halls (Panch Mahal, Jodha Bai's palace) sit beside arched gateways such as the Buland Darwaza, built to mark the conquest of Gujarat. Under Jahangir, Nur Jahan built the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daula at Agra, covered in white marble inlaid with coloured stones. Shah Jahan favoured white marble, cusped arches and inlay: the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and Jama Masjid at Delhi. Under Aurangzeb building slowed; the Bibi ka Maqbara at Aurangabad and the Badshahi Mosque at Lahore are the main works.

Concept

The charbagh and the riverfront garden. A charbagh is a walled garden divided into four by water channels, an image of the gardens of paradise described in the Quran; Babur writes of laying them out at Agra. In Humayun's tomb the tomb sits at the centre. The Mughals developed a variant, the riverfront garden, which puts the main building on a terrace at the river's edge. The Taj Mahal uses it: the tomb stands by the Yamuna with the garden to its south, so it is seen against open sky. In Kashmir gardens were terraced down hillsides (Shalimar Bagh).

Court symbolism. Buildings were also statements of rule. Shah Jahan's audience halls in the Red Fort were pillared halls (chihil sutun, "forty pillars"). Behind the throne in the Diwan-i-Am, inlaid panels show Orpheus playing the lute, a European image of harmony used to suggest just rule. This stone inlay, called pietra dura in Italy, was called parchin kari in Mughal India.

Indigenous impact on Mughal architecture (Mains 2024). The Mughal style is Indian as much as Persian. Indian elements include chhatris, carved brackets and sloping eaves (chhajjas), overhanging balconies (jharokhas), lotus and kalash finials, and trabeate pillared halls at Fatehpur Sikri drawing on Gujarat and Malwa styles. The curved Bangla roof was copied from Bengal's thatched huts. The builders were largely Indian craftsmen from Rajasthan and Gujarat, and the red sandstone and Makrana marble came from Rajasthan. Influence ran both ways: the Govind Deva temple at Vrindavan (Raja Man Singh of Amber, 1590) uses red sandstone and intersecting arches like Fatehpur Sikri, and Rajput palaces at Amber and elsewhere adopted Mughal gardens and halls.

Bengal temples (late 15th to 19th century) show the same local inventiveness. Built in brick and terracotta, they copied the double roof (dochala) or four-part roof (chauchala) of village huts; their outer walls are covered in terracotta panels. The finest are at Vishnupur (Bankura district). Many were paid for by artisan and trading groups who prospered with European trade.

I48.5 Colonial architecture: buildings of empire

The British built to show that they were the new, modern rulers. Their buildings in the presidency towns of Bombay, Calcutta and Madras followed three main styles, and their choice of style itself made a political claim.

Neo-classical buildings, with geometric fronts and tall columns based on Roman models, suggested the order and reason of an empire like Rome's: the Town Hall in Bombay (1833), Elphinstone Circle (now Horniman Circle), built in the cotton boom of the 1860s, and the Writers' Building in Calcutta. Neo-Gothic buildings, with steep roofs, pointed arches and rich decoration from medieval European churches, were favoured in Bombay: the University, the High Court and above all Victoria Terminus (F.W. Stevens, 1888). Indian donors paid for some of them: Cowasjee Jehangir Readymoney (University Hall) and Premchand Roychand (the Rajabai clock tower, named after his mother).

Indo-Saracenic buildings ("Indo" for Hindu, "Saracen" for Muslim) appeared in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. They set European plans under Indian domes, chhatris, jalis and arches, to present the British as the lawful heirs of India's past rulers: the Madras High Court, the Mysore Palace, the Taj Mahal Hotel (built by Jamsetji Tata) and the Gateway of India, built to mark the 1911 visit of George V and completed in 1924. Even the bungalow, the typical British house in India, took its name and form from the Bengali bangla hut.

The capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911. Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker designed New Delhi, inaugurated in 1931. The Viceroy's House (now Rashtrapati Bhavan) is classical in plan but carries a dome inspired by the Sanchi stupa, chhatris and jalis: an empire borrowing India's oldest forms to claim permanence. The Victoria Memorial in Calcutta (William Emerson, opened 1921) is built of white Makrana marble from Rajasthan, the stone of the Taj Mahal.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before: Harappan cities (I03); the Mauryas and Ashoka's dhamma (I07); Buddhism, Jainism and the Ajivikas (I06).
  • Dynasties behind the buildings: Shungas, Satavahanas and Kushanas (I08), Guptas (I10), Chalukyas, Pallavas and Rashtrakutas (I11), Cholas (I12), Chandelas and other Rajputs (I15), the Delhi Sultanate (I17, I18), Vijayanagara and the Bahmanis (I19), the Mughals (I21, I22).
  • Art: the sculpture on stupas, caves and temples, and the Kailasa temple at Ellora (I49); dance poses carved at Chidambaram, Konark and Khajuraho (I50); the texts on architecture (I51).
  • Religion: bhakti and the temple as the home of the god (I20); Sufi shrines (dargahs) such as Nizamuddin beside Humayun's tomb.
  • Colonial era: the presidency towns and British rule (I26, I30); the 1911 transfer of the capital after the reversal of the Bengal partition (I37).
  • Rajasthan: Makrana marble and Rajasthani craftsmen in Mughal buildings; Rajput forts, palaces, temples (Dilwara, Ranakpur), stepwells and havelis are in book 6.

What historians say

Percy Brown (Indian Architecture, 2 volumes) set the Buddhist–Hindu and Islamic periods that most textbooks still use. Stella Kramrisch (The Hindu Temple) explains the temple as a cosmic diagram. Ebba Koch (Mughal Architecture) shows how the Mughals combined Timurid and Indian elements. On Mauryan pillars, John Irwin argued for an Indian pillar cult older than Ashoka, while older writers stressed Persian influence; the NCERT Class 11 text An Introduction to Indian Art presents both views. Thomas Metcalf (An Imperial Vision) reads Indo-Saracenic buildings as a claim by the British to be India's rightful rulers.

Prelims fact bank

  • Harappan bricks follow a standard 1:2:4 ratio.
  • The Great Bath is at Mohenjodaro; the dockyard is at Lothal.
  • Dholavira was a three-part city with stone reservoirs.
  • Mauryan pillars are monolithic Chunar sandstone with a mirror polish.
  • The Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka is India's national emblem.
  • The Barabar caves were dedicated to the Ajivikas.
  • The parts of a stupa are the anda, harmika, yashti, chhatri, vedika and toranas.
  • Chaityas at Bhaja and Karle are rock-cut Buddhist prayer halls.
  • The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh is a Gupta temple with an early shikhara.
  • The Durga temple at Aihole (Chalukya) has an apsidal (rounded-end) plan.
  • Pattadakal has Chalukya temples in both the northern and southern styles.
  • The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram was built under Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha).
  • The Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur was completed around 1010 under Rajaraja I.
  • The Konark Sun temple was built under Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty.
  • In Odisha temples the sanctum tower is the deul and the hall is the jagamohana.
  • Hoysala temples at Belur and Halebidu have star-shaped plans.
  • The Alai Darwaza (1311) has the first true arches and dome in India.
  • Nagara temples have a curvilinear shikhara; Dravida temples have a pyramidal vimana and gopurams.
  • Gol Gumbaz is at Bijapur.
  • Humayun's tomb (1565–72) has a double dome, a hasht bihisht plan and a charbagh garden.
  • The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daula at Agra was built by Nur Jahan.
  • Pietra dura inlay was called parchin kari in Mughal India.
  • The Govind Deva temple at Vrindavan was built by Raja Man Singh of Amber in 1590.
  • Dochala and chauchala temples of Bengal copy the roofs of thatched huts; Vishnupur has the best examples.
  • Victoria Terminus in Bombay was designed by F.W. Stevens and completed in 1888.
  • New Delhi was designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker and inaugurated in 1931.
  • The Victoria Memorial, Calcutta, is built of Makrana marble from Rajasthan.
Exam traps
  • Victoria Terminus is NCERT's main example of neo-Gothic, not Indo-Saracenic; the Gateway of India is Indo-Saracenic.
  • The Gateway of India marks the 1911 visit of George V but was completed only in 1924.
  • Qutub Minar was begun by Aibak and completed by Iltutmish; Firoz Tughlaq repaired the top storeys.
  • The Quwwat-ul-Islam arches are corbelled; the first true arch is in the Alai Darwaza.
  • The Shore Temple is structural; the five rathas are monolithic rock-cut shrines.
  • Ashoka built the brick core of Sanchi; the stone toranas are post-Mauryan.
  • Gol Gumbaz is at Bijapur (Adil Shahi), not Golconda.
  • NCERT Class 7 says Kandariya Mahadeva was built in 999 by Dhanga; most scholars date it c. 1025–50 under Vidyadhara. Safe Prelims answer: Chandela, Khajuraho.
  • Humayun's tomb was built by his widow Bega Begum (1565–72), not by Humayun or Akbar.
  • Vesara is the Deccan hybrid style, not a separate southern style.
  • In later Dravida temples the gopuram (gateway) is taller than the vimana (sanctum tower); do not mix the two terms.

Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

Mauryan pillars are of indigenous origin. Explain.

How to frame it: Describe the pillars → Persian influence view → Indian features: no base, monolithic, free-standing → Indian motifs and purpose → Conclusion

Model answer (106 words)

Ashoka's pillars are monolithic Chunar sandstone shafts with a mirror polish, crowned by an inverted lotus, an abacus and animals, as at Sarnath. Their polish and bell capital led some scholars to see Persian influence. But the differences are basic: Persian columns stand on bases, are built in segments and support roofs, whereas Mauryan shafts have no base, are single blocks and stand free. The bull, elephant and lion, the lotus and the dharma-chakra are Indian motifs, and the pillars carried Ashoka's dhamma message. Irwin traced them to an older Indian pillar cult. Foreign ideas may have been absorbed, but the form and purpose are Indian.

10 marks · 100 words

Continuity of culture is a unique feature of Indian civilization. Explain with examples from architecture.

How to frame it: Define continuity with change → Harappan to later water works → Stupa to temple to Mughal → Synthesis, not replacement → Conclusion

Model answer (100 words)

Indian culture has changed without breaking. Harappan concern with water and drains survives in temple tanks, stepwells and Mughal water channels. The stupa's parasol lives on in the chhatri of Rajput, Mughal and even British buildings, and Rashtrapati Bhavan's dome recalls Sanchi. The temple kept the same sanctum from the Gupta period to Vijayanagara while its towers grew. New arrivals did not replace older forms but merged with them: the Mughals combined the Persian dome and garden with Indian brackets, jharokhas and the Bangla roof, and the Govind Deva temple took Mughal arches. Continuity through synthesis is the Indian pattern.

5 marks · 50 words

Examine the indigenous impact on Mughal architecture.

How to frame it: Indian elements → Examples → Craftsmen

Model answer (39 words)

Mughal buildings used Indian chhatris, brackets, chhajjas, jharokhas and lotus finials, and trabeate halls at Fatehpur Sikri (Panch Mahal, Jodha Bai's palace) in the Gujarat and Malwa manner, and the Bengal-style Bangla roof. Rajasthani and Gujarati craftsmen built them.

2 marks · 15 words

What is a gopuram?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (12 words)

The tall gateway tower in the enclosure wall of a Dravida-style temple.

Revision card

Remember
  • Harappan: grid, drains, 1:2:4 bricks; Great Bath (Mohenjodaro), dockyard (Lothal), reservoirs (Dholavira).
  • Mauryan: polished monolithic pillars (no base, free-standing), Sanchi core, Barabar caves (Ajivikas); indigenous-origin arguments.
  • Stupa: anda, harmika, yashti, chhatri, vedika, toranas; chaityas at Bhaja and Karle.
  • Temples: Gupta (Sanchi 17, Deogarh) → Nagara / Dravida / Vesara; Shore Temple, Brihadeeswara c. 1010, Khajuraho, Konark, Aihole, Pattadakal, Belur.
  • Indo-Islamic: corbelled (Quwwat-ul-Islam) → true arch (Alai Darwaza 1311); Gol Gumbaz; Vitthala temple; Humayun's tomb 1565–72, Fatehpur Sikri, Itimad-ud-Daula, Taj (riverfront garden).
  • Exchange: Bangla roof, Gujarat–Malwa at Fatehpur Sikri, Govind Deva temple 1590, Bengal dochala/chauchala (Vishnupur).
  • Colonial: neo-classical (Town Hall 1833), neo-Gothic (VT 1888), Indo-Saracenic (Gateway 1924); New Delhi 1931 (Lutyens, Baker).

Self-test

  1. What is the ratio of Harappan bricks, and what does it suggest?
    Show answer

    1:2:4; a shared system of standards across many sites.

  2. Which site has a Harappan dockyard?
    Show answer

    Lothal.

  3. Give three features that distinguish Mauryan pillars from Persian columns.
    Show answer

    No base; monolithic shaft; free-standing rather than supporting a roof.

  4. For which sect were the Barabar caves cut?
    Show answer

    The Ajivikas.

  5. Why did structural Hindu temples appear only around the Gupta period?
    Show answer

    Vedic worship was an open-air sacrifice; the growth of devotion to images of Vishnu and Shiva created the need for a house for the god.

  6. How does a true arch differ from a corbelled arch?
    Show answer

    A true arch uses wedge-shaped stones locked by a keystone; a corbelled arch steps courses of stone inward until they meet.

  7. Name the three temple styles and their regions.
    Show answer

    Nagara (north), Dravida (south), Vesara (Deccan).

  8. Under whom was the Brihadeeswara temple completed?
    Show answer

    Rajaraja I (c. 1010).

  9. What is the hasht bihisht plan, and where does it first appear in Mughal India?
    Show answer

    A central hall ringed by eight rooms; Humayun's tomb.

  10. How does the Taj Mahal's garden differ from a standard charbagh?
    Show answer

    It is a riverfront garden: the tomb stands at the river's edge, not at the centre, with the garden to its south.

  11. Why did the British adopt the Indo-Saracenic style?
    Show answer

    To present themselves as the lawful successors of India's earlier rulers by using Indian domes, chhatris and arches.

  12. Connect the Sanchi stupa to New Delhi.
    Show answer

    The dome of the Viceroy's House (Rashtrapati Bhavan) was inspired by the Sanchi stupa.

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Harappan sculpture: bronze, stone and terracotta; seals; Mauryan and post-Mauryan sculpture; Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati schools; Gupta and early medieval sculpture: Sarnath, Elephanta, Ellora, Mahabalipuram; Chola bronzes; Painting: Bhimbetka, Ajanta, Bagh; Pala manuscripts; Mughal, Deccani and Pahari schools; Modern trends: Company painting, Raja Ravi Varma, the Bengal School

Mains: GS-I Part B: Indian heritage — sculpture and painting

Tier A, the most-tested part of IH1. RAS Mains asked about the Dancing Girl (2016, 2 marks), Gandhara vs Mathura (2016, 5), Mughal painting (2016, 10), Arjuna's Penance (2018, 2) and Harappan bronzes (2018, 5). Rajasthani painting schools are in book 6.

The big picture

Indian sculpture and painting form one long story in which three forces keep reshaping the art: religion (what had to be shown), patronage (who paid, and why) and contact with other cultures (Persian, Greek, Central Asian, European). Sculpture begins with the small bronzes and stone figures of the Harappans, becomes a polished court art under the Mauryas and a storytelling art on the stupas, and then, in the first centuries CE, creates the image of the Buddha in three schools: Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati. The Gupta sculptors fixed a classical ideal that Pallava, Rashtrakuta and Chola artists carried into rock and bronze. Painting runs from the rock shelters of Bhimbetka to the murals of Ajanta, then shrinks onto manuscript pages, and flowers again in the Mughal workshop, whose style spread to Rajput and Pahari courts. Colonial rule brought new patrons and techniques and, in reaction, the national Bengal School.

Exam focus

Every RAS question on this unit so far has asked you to describe a work (Dancing Girl, Arjuna's Penance), compare schools (Gandhara and Mathura) or trace a tradition (Mughal painting). So for each work, know what it is made of, who made it and what it shows; for each school, know its patron, material and style; and for each tradition, know how it changed and why.

Core notes

I49.1 Harappan sculpture: small but skilled

Harappan art was small in scale. There are no colossal statues or temple images; what survives is a set of figures a few centimetres high, seals and clay figurines. Their value lies in their skill. The best known is the bronze Dancing Girl from Mohenjodaro, about 10.5 cm tall. She stands nude, one hand on her hip and the other arm, covered almost to the shoulder with bangles, resting on her leg; she wears a necklace, and her head is tilted with a confident, relaxed air. Its attributes, in a 2-mark answer: bronze, cast by the lost-wax method, naturalistic pose and full of movement. Other bronzes include a buffalo and a ram, and a hoard from Daimabad in Maharashtra (a chariot with a rider, an elephant, a rhinoceros and a buffalo), usually placed in the late Harappan period, though its date is debated.

Concept

The lost-wax (cire perdue) method. The artist models the figure in wax, coats it in clay and heats it; the wax melts and runs out, leaving a hollow mould into which molten metal is poured. When it cools the clay is broken away, so each casting is unique. The Harappans used it for the Dancing Girl, the Chola artists of the 10th–11th centuries for their bronzes, and craftsmen in Bastar and elsewhere still use it. It links the oldest and the most celebrated Indian bronzes.

In stone, the steatite Priest-King (about 17.5 cm) wears a shawl with a trefoil (three-lobed) pattern over the left shoulder, a fillet round the head and a carefully trimmed beard; the half-closed eyes suggest meditation. Two small torsos from Harappa, one in red sandstone, show a feel for the soft modelling of the body that later Indian sculpture would develop. Terracotta mother-goddess figurines and toys were common household objects, and thousands of square seals, mostly steatite, carry animals (the "unicorn", the humped bull, the elephant) and short inscriptions; the so-called "Pashupati" seal shows a seated figure surrounded by animals.

I49.2 Mauryan court art and the storytelling stupas

Under the Mauryas, sculpture split into two streams. Court art was made for the emperor: the monolithic pillars of polished Chunar sandstone, with animal capitals such as the four lions of Sarnath, carry Ashoka's message. Their mirror-like polish and bell-shaped capitals have led some scholars to suggest Persian (Achaemenid) influence, a view others dispute. Popular art was made for local patrons: large standing figures of yakshas and yakshis, nature spirits worshipped across India, such as the Parkham Yaksha near Mathura and the polished Didarganj Yakshi from Patna (dated to the Mauryan period by many, later by others). These heavy, frontal figures became the model for the later Indian image of the god.

From the 2nd century BCE the railings and gateways of the stupas at Bharhut and Sanchi turned sculpture into storytelling. Panels show the Jatakas and the life of the Buddha, crowded with townspeople, animals and trees, and paid for by monks, nuns, merchants and guilds whose donations are inscribed beside them.

Concept

From symbol to image. In the earliest Buddhist art the Buddha himself is never shown. A seat, footprints, a tree, a wheel or a stupa stands for him (this is called aniconism). In the first centuries CE this changed. Devotional worship (bhakti) of the Buddha grew with Mahayana Buddhism, Kushana kings patronised art on a large scale, and the image-making traditions of the yakshas and of Greek art were both at hand. The result was the Buddha image, created almost at the same time in Gandhara and Mathura.

I49.3 Three schools of the Buddha image

Why did three schools look so different? Each grew where a different patron, stone and artistic tradition met. Gandhara, in the north-west on the trade routes to Central Asia, had absorbed Greek and Roman art since Alexander's time, so its Buddha looks like a Greek god in a monk's robe. Mathura grew from the local yaksha tradition and served all faiths, so its figures are Indian in body and spirit. Amaravati, in the Krishna valley under the Satavahanas, continued the storytelling of the stupa railings.

FeatureGandharaMathuraAmaravati
Region and patronsNorth-west (Kushanas)Mathura (Kushanas)Andhra (Satavahanas, Ikshvakus)
MaterialGrey-blue schist, stuccoSpotted red sandstoneWhite marble-like limestone
InfluenceGreco-Roman (Hellenistic)Indian, from yaksha figuresIndian, narrative

The fundamental difference between Gandhara and Mathura, the 2016 Mains question, is one of origin: Gandhara adapted a foreign (Hellenistic) style to Indian themes, while Mathura developed an indigenous style from Indian folk sculpture. The other differences, stone, robe, face and subject, follow from that.

The Gupta classical ideal (4th–6th centuries) joined the best of both. The seated Buddha of Sarnath, in the preaching posture with a transparent robe and calm, inward-looking face, and the standing Buddhas of Mathura balance physical beauty with spiritual calm. That balance is why the Gupta period is called "classical". Brahmanical sculpture rose beside it: the great Varaha panel at Udayagiri (near Vidisha) shows Vishnu as a boar lifting the earth, and the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh has panels of Vishnu resting on the serpent Shesha.

I49.4 Rock and bronze: Pallavas, Rashtrakutas and Cholas

After the Guptas the centres of sculpture moved south and to the Deccan, where kings carved whole hillsides. Arjuna's Penance, also read as the Descent of the Ganga, at Mahabalipuram (Pallava, 7th century) is a huge open-air relief on two boulders. A natural cleft between them once carried water, standing for the river Ganga; around it gods, sages, nagas and animals gather, an ascetic stands on one leg in penance (identified as Arjuna seeking Shiva's weapon, or as Bhagiratha bringing down the Ganga), and a cat mimics his pose while mice gather around it. In a 2-mark answer: Pallava, 7th century, Mahabalipuram, a rock-cut relief of the descent of the Ganga.

At Elephanta, near Mumbai (c. 6th century), the main cave's three-headed Shiva (Mahesamurti) shows the god as creator, preserver and destroyer. At Ellora, 34 caves of Buddhist, Hindu and Jain faiths sit side by side; the Kailasa temple (Cave 16), carved from the top down out of a single rock under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (8th century), is a whole temple sculpted rather than built.

Concept

Reading the Chola Nataraja. The 10th–11th century bronzes of the Chola temples, cast by the lost-wax method, show Shiva as the Lord of Dance (ananda tandava). Each element has a meaning: the ring of fire (prabhamandala) is the cosmos; the drum (damaru) in one hand sounds creation, the fire in another is destruction; a third hand gives protection (abhaya mudra) and the fourth points to the raised foot, which offers release; the other foot crushes the dwarf Apasmara, ignorance. One image holds the full cycle of creation, preservation and destruction. The bronzes were made to be carried in temple processions.

I49.5 Painting: from rock walls to the Mughal workshop

The earliest painting. The rock shelters of Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh), found by V.S. Wakankar in 1957 and a UNESCO site since 2003, carry paintings from the Mesolithic onwards in red and white: hunting, dancing and animals. They show that painting in India is as old as settled life.

Ajanta. The about 30 rock-cut caves of Ajanta (Maharashtra) were made in two phases, from the 2nd century BCE and again in the 5th century under the Vakatakas. The murals, in mineral colours on dry lime plaster, show Jataka stories and the Buddha's life with flowing lines, shaded bodies and expressive faces; the Bodhisattva Padmapani of Cave 1 is the most famous. The murals of Bagh (Madhya Pradesh) are related.

Concept

The six limbs of painting (shadanga). A later commentary on the Kamasutra lists six principles a painter must master: rupabheda (variety of form), pramana (proportion), bhava (emotion), lavanya yojana (grace), sadrishya (likeness) and varnikabhanga (use of colour and brush). They explain why Indian painting values expression and grace over exact copying of nature.

Manuscript painting. From about the 10th century painting shrank onto pages. In eastern India the monasteries of the Palas produced palm-leaf Buddhist manuscripts, such as the Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita, with small, gently shaded figures. In western India, Jain manuscripts such as the Kalpasutra used bright red, blue and gold, angular figures and a typical face in profile with the further eye projecting. When paper replaced palm leaf, page sizes and pictures grew.

Mughal painting (the 2016 10-mark question) was born of the meeting of Persian and Indian art. Humayun, in exile at the Safavid court, met the Persian masters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad and brought them to India. Akbar set up a large royal workshop (tasvirkhana) where they trained Indian painters such as Daswanth and Basawan. Its first great work, the Hamzanama (about 1,400 large paintings), and later the Razmnama (a Persian Mahabharata) and the Akbarnama are crowded, lively narratives, with several artists working on each page: one drew the outline, another coloured it, a third did the faces. Under Jahangir, himself a keen naturalist, painting turned to single portraits and studies of nature. Ustad Mansur (titled Nadir-ul-Asr) painted birds and animals such as a zebra and a Siberian crane; Abul Hasan (Nadir-uz-Zaman) court scenes; Bishandas, sent with Jahangir's embassy to Persia, painted portraits of Shah Abbas. European prints brought by the Jesuits added shading, perspective and the halo round the emperor's head. Under Shah Jahan painting became formal and richly decorated (the Padshahnama); under Aurangzeb court patronage shrank, and many painters moved to Rajput and Pahari courts.

Concept

Atelier and miniature. An atelier (karkhana or tasvirkhana) was a royal workshop where many artists worked under a master, often on one painting together, and were paid and ranked by the court. A miniature is a small, finely detailed painting made for a book or an album and viewed in the hand, not on a wall. The two ideas explain the Mughal style: teamwork under imperial taste, and close detail meant for private viewing.

The courts that followed. Deccani painting at Bijapur, Golconda and Ahmadnagar mixed Persian, Turkish and local styles, with rich colours and gold. Rajasthani painting (Mewar, Bundi, Kishangarh and others) is covered in book 6. In the hill states of the Himalaya (Pahari painting), Basohli in the late 17th century used bold, intense colours and favoured Bhanudatta's Rasamanjari; Nadir Shah's sack of Delhi (1739) sent more Mughal-trained artists to the hills, and from the mid-18th century Guler and Kangra painted Vaishnava themes, especially the Gita Govinda, in soft blues and greens with a lyrical line.

I49.6 Colonial and national art

British rule changed who paid for art. Indian painters working for British officials produced Company painting at Patna, Murshidabad, Lucknow and Tanjore: watercolours of Indian trades, festivals, plants and animals in a European manner. In Calcutta, painters near the Kalighat temple made cheap, bold Kalighat pats for pilgrims. Raja Ravi Varma of Travancore mastered European oil painting and gave Hindu gods and heroines of the Ramayana and Mahabharata a realistic look; his lithographic press in Bombay (1894) printed cheap oleographs that brought these images into ordinary homes.

The Bengal School reacted against both Western academic art and Ravi Varma's realism. Encouraged by E.B. Havell, principal of the Calcutta Government School of Art, Abanindranath Tagore turned to Mughal, Ajanta and Japanese models (the wash technique he learned from Japanese artists linked to Okakura Kakuzo) to build an "Indian" style. His Bharat Mata (1905), an ascetic, four-armed figure painted during the Swadeshi movement, made art part of nationalism. His pupil Nandalal Bose carried the school forward at Santiniketan.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Architecture (I48): the stupas, rock-cut caves and temples that hold this sculpture; parts of a stupa; Mughal buildings.
  • Religion: Buddhism and the stupa (I06); Bhagavatism and Vaishnava art (I08, I10); the Bhakti themes of Pahari painting, such as the Gita Govinda (I20).
  • Dynasties: Mauryas (I07), Kushanas and Satavahanas (I08), Guptas (I10), Pallavas and Rashtrakutas (I11), Cholas (I12), the Mughals (I21–I23).
  • Performing arts (I50): dance poses in temple sculpture, the Nataraja, and ragamala paintings that show ragas as scenes.
  • Nationalism (I37): Bharat Mata and the Swadeshi movement.
  • Rajasthan: Mewar, Bundi, Kishangarh and other Rajasthani schools, which grew from Mughal contact (book 6).

What historians say

Ananda Coomaraswamy argued that the Buddha image was an Indian creation at Mathura, against Alfred Foucher, who credited Gandhara and Greek influence; most scholars now accept that both arose around the same time. Percy Brown and Milo Beach (Mughal and Rajput Painting) trace the Mughal atelier. Partha Mitter studies colonial art and the Bengal School.

Exam traps
  • Dancing Girl is bronze; the Priest-King is steatite (stone).
  • Mathura made Buddhist, Jain and Hindu images; Gandhara was mainly Buddhist.
  • Abul Hasan was titled Nadir-uz-Zaman; Mansur was Nadir-ul-Asr.
  • The Kailasa temple is Ellora Cave 16 (Rashtrakuta), not Elephanta.
  • The Bengal School rejected Ravi Varma's European realism; Ravi Varma was not part of it.
  • Pala manuscripts are Buddhist and on palm leaf; western Indian manuscripts of the same age are mainly Jain.

Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

Write a detailed note on Mughal painting.

How to frame it: Origins under Humayun → Akbar's atelier → Jahangir: portraits and nature → Shah Jahan and decline → Legacy

Model answer (94 words)

Humayun brought Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad from Persia. Akbar organised a large atelier where Persian masters trained Indian painters such as Daswanth and Basawan; works like the Hamzanama and Razmnama are lively, crowded narratives that blend Persian line with Indian colour. Jahangir preferred single portraits and nature studies: Mansur painted birds and animals, Abul Hasan court scenes, and European perspective and shading appeared. Under Shah Jahan painting became formal and ornate. Aurangzeb withdrew patronage, so painters moved to Rajput and Pahari courts, where the Mughal style shaped Kishangarh, Kangra and other schools.

5 marks · 50 words

Explain the fundamental difference between the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.

How to frame it: Origin → Material → Buddha image → Subjects

Model answer (55 words)

The basic difference is origin: Gandhara adapted Hellenistic style to Buddhist themes, while Mathura grew from the indigenous yaksha tradition. So Gandhara used grey schist and showed a Greek-looking Buddha with wavy hair and heavy folds; Mathura used red sandstone, a smiling, energetic Buddha in a thin robe, and served Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical patrons.

5 marks · 50 words

Write a short note on bronze images found from Harappan sites.

How to frame it: Technique → Examples → Significance

Model answer (39 words)

Harappans cast bronzes by the lost-wax method. The Dancing Girl of Mohenjodaro is the best known; a buffalo and a ram are also known, and Daimabad yielded a chariot with animals. They show skill in alloying and lifelike modelling.

2 marks · 15 words

Briefly describe the "Arjun's Penance" sculpture.

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (13 words)

A 7th-century Pallava open-air relief at Mahabalipuram showing the descent of the Ganga.

Self-test

  1. By what method was the Dancing Girl made, and how does it work?
    Show answer

    The lost-wax method: a wax model is coated in clay and heated, the wax runs out and molten metal is poured into the hollow mould.

  2. Which site yielded a Harappan bronze chariot?
    Show answer

    Daimabad.

  3. Why was the Buddha first shown by symbols and only later as a human image?
    Show answer

    Early Buddhism avoided images of the Buddha; the rise of devotional (Mahayana) worship, Kushana patronage and the yaksha and Greek traditions led to the image in the first centuries CE.

  4. What is the fundamental difference between the Gandhara and Mathura schools?
    Show answer

    Origin: Gandhara adapted Hellenistic style; Mathura grew from the indigenous yaksha tradition.

  5. Why is Gupta sculpture called classical?
    Show answer

    It balanced physical beauty with spiritual calm and set the ideal later sculptors followed, as in the Sarnath Buddha.

  6. Which dynasty created Arjuna's Penance, and what does it show?
    Show answer

    The Pallavas; the descent of the Ganga, with an ascetic in penance.

  7. What do the fire ring and the dwarf in the Chola Nataraja stand for?
    Show answer

    The ring is the cosmos; the dwarf Apasmara is ignorance, crushed by Shiva.

  8. How did Mughal painting change from Akbar to Jahangir?
    Show answer

    From crowded team-painted narratives (Hamzanama) to single portraits and nature studies by individual masters such as Mansur.

  9. Why did Mughal-trained painters move to Rajput and Pahari courts?
    Show answer

    Court patronage shrank under Aurangzeb, and Nadir Shah's sack of Delhi (1739) drove more artists to the hills.

  10. Against what did the Bengal School react?
    Show answer

    Western academic art and Ravi Varma's European-style realism.

Part V · Unit I50Music, Dance and TheatreVedic age – 1953 CE

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Origins: Samaveda, Bharata's Natyashastra; ragas and talas; Medieval music: Amir Khusrau, Sangita Ratnakara, Tansen, the Bhakti composers; Hindustani and Carnatic traditions; Classical dances recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi; Theatre: Sanskrit drama, Koodiyattam, folk theatre, modern and political theatre

Mains: GS-I Part B: Indian heritage — performing arts

Tier B. No RAS Mains (2016–2024) or RAS Prelims (2021–2024) question on music, dance or theatre so far, but Prelims PI7 names medieval music directly and IH1 (heritage) is the most-tested Mains history line, so a 5- or 10-mark question is possible. Rajasthan's folk dances, instruments and gharanas are in book 6.

The big picture

India's performing arts began as ritual and became, over two thousand years, a set of classical and folk traditions shaped by whoever paid for them. The hymns of the Samaveda were sung; Bharata's Natyashastra then treated drama, dance and music as one art whose purpose is to create rasa in the audience. For centuries north and south shared this theory. From the 13th century, Persian contact, Sultanate and Mughal courts and the Bhakti movement pulled the north towards Hindustani music, while temple and devotional patronage in the south produced Carnatic music. Dance lived in temples and courts until colonial reformers attacked it; it survived through a 20th-century revival that created the classical dances recognised today. Theatre moved from the Sanskrit stage to regional folk forms and, under colonial rule, to the political stage.

Exam focus

Read this unit as one story with three threads: theory (Natyashastra, rasa, raga), patronage (temple, court, Bhakti, colonial state, independent India) and change (each new patron reshaped the art). Most questions on performing arts are answered by placing a fact in one of these threads.

Core notes

I50.1 Roots: ritual, text and theory

Indian music begins with the Samaveda, which set Rigvedic verses to melody for chanting at sacrifices. Music here served ritual: the correct sound mattered as much as the words. The decisive step came with the Natyashastra, attributed to the sage Bharata and compiled over several centuries (broadly between the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE). It is a manual for the stage, covering the theatre building, acting, gesture, costume, dance, music and instruments, and it treats all of them as parts of one performance.

Concept

Rasa and bhava. The Natyashastra's central idea is that a performance exists to produce rasa (literally "juice" or "taste"), an aesthetic emotion felt by the audience. The performer shows a bhava (an emotional state such as love, grief or anger) through gesture, expression and music; a cultured viewer then "tastes" its universal form as rasa. Bharata named eight rasas (shringara, hasya, karuna, raudra, vira, bhayanaka, bibhatsa, adbhuta); later theorists added a ninth, shanta (peace). Why it matters: the theory explains why Indian arts aim at mood rather than realism, and it still guides classical dance and music.

The Natyashastra also classified instruments into four groups, a scheme still used: tata (stringed, such as the veena), sushira (wind, such as the flute), avanaddha (skin-covered drums, such as the mridangam) and ghana (solid, such as cymbals).

Concept

Raga and tala. A raga is not a tune but a melodic framework: a set of notes, rules for ascending and descending, characteristic phrases and a mood, within which a musician composes or improvises. A tala is a repeating rhythmic cycle of fixed beats. Every classical performance, north or south, combines the two. The word raga first appears as a technical term in Matanga's Brihaddeshi (c. 9th century), after the Natyashastra.

I50.2 How one tradition became two: Hindustani and Carnatic

Until the 13th century north and south shared one theory. Sharngadeva's Sangita Ratnakara, written at the Yadava court of Devagiri in the 13th century, is often called the last text both traditions treat as their own. After it the paths separated, for three reasons. First, Persian and Central Asian music reached north India with the Delhi Sultanate. Second, patrons differed: in the north music moved into Sultanate, Mughal and Rajput courts, where entertainment and display mattered; in the south it stayed tied to temples and devotional composition. Third, the Bhakti movement made regional languages the vehicle of song in both regions, so compositions grew in Hindi, Braj, Kannada, Telugu and Tamil rather than Sanskrit.

The northern line. Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), poet at the Delhi court and disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, is credited with qawwali and with forms that fed the khayal; historians treat claims that he invented the sitar or tabla as later legend. In the 15th century Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior patronised the austere, devotional dhrupad and had a treatise, Man Kutuhal, compiled on it. Swami Haridas of Vrindavan, a Bhakti musician, is remembered as the teacher of Tansen, whom Akbar brought to his court. In the 18th century Sadarang (Niyamat Khan), at the court of Muhammad Shah in Delhi, made the freer, more ornamented khayal popular, and in the 19th century the light-classical thumri flourished at Wajid Ali Shah's Lucknow. The change in form followed the change in setting: from temple and devotional dhrupad to the court khayal and the salon thumri.

The southern line. Purandara Dasa (16th century), a Vaishnava saint-composer of the Vijayanagara period, created graded lessons still used to teach beginners; he is called the father (pitamaha) of Carnatic music. In the 17th century Venkatamakhin's Chaturdandi Prakashika set out the 72 melakarta (parent scale) scheme that classifies Carnatic ragas. The Carnatic Trinity of the 18th–19th centuries, all from Tiruvarur in the Thanjavur region (Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri), composed the kritis that form the core of the concert repertoire.

FeatureHindustaniCarnatic
RegionNorth IndiaSouth India
InfluencesIndian base with Persian and court influencesLargely indigenous, temple and devotional
FormsDhrupad, khayal, thumri, tappa, taranaKriti, varnam, kirtanam
ImprovisationLarge scope; long raga elaboration (alap)Compositions central; improvisation within them
Raga systemRagas grouped into thaats (modern system by V.N. Bhatkhande)72 melakartas (Venkatamakhin)
Key figuresAmir Khusrau, Man Singh Tomar, Swami Haridas, Tansen, SadarangPurandara Dasa, Tyagaraja, Dikshitar, Syama Sastri
Concept

Gharana. A gharana ("household") is a lineage of musicians or dancers who share a style passed from teacher to pupil (the guru–shishya or ustad–shagird relationship), usually named after the court town where it took shape, such as Gwalior, Agra, Jaipur or Lucknow. Gharanas grew from court patronage: each court kept its own musicians, who guarded their style. When princely patronage ended after 1947, the gharanas moved to radio, concerts and music schools.

I50.3 Classical dance: from temple and court to the modern stage

Classical dance rests on the Natyashastra and on later texts such as Nandikeshvara's Abhinaya Darpana. Temple sculpture shows how old the vocabulary is: the gopurams of the Nataraja temple at Chidambaram carve the 108 karanas (dance units) the Natyashastra describes. For centuries dance was performed in temples by dedicated women (devadasis) and at courts by professional dancers.

Concept

Nritta, nritya and natya. Classical dance has three parts. Nritta is pure dance: rhythmic movement with no story. Nritya adds expression: gesture (mudra) and face convey meaning and bhava. Natya is drama: a full story told through dance. A Bharatanatyam recital moves through all three; Kathakali leans towards natya. Related pair: tandava (vigorous, associated with Shiva) and lasya (graceful, associated with Parvati).

Why the dances nearly disappeared. In the 19th century Victorian morality and Indian social reformers came to see temple and court dancers as immoral. An anti-nautch campaign from the 1890s pressed for an end to dedication of girls to temples, culminating in the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act, 1947. The hereditary performers lost their livelihood and status.

How they were revived. In the 20th century nationalists and artists reclaimed dance as heritage. E. Krishna Iyer campaigned for the dance of the devadasis, renamed Bharatanatyam; Rukmini Devi Arundale founded Kalakshetra (1936) at Madras and reshaped it for the concert stage. In Kerala the poet Vallathol Narayana Menon founded the Kerala Kalamandalam (1930) to revive Kathakali and Mohiniyattam. The revival changed who danced: forms once kept by hereditary communities were now learned by middle-class students in institutions. After independence the Sangeet Natak Akademi (1953) gave the dances official classical status; it now recognises eight.

DanceStateRemember it by
BharatanatyamTamil NaduDevadasi tradition; revived by E. Krishna Iyer and Rukmini Devi Arundale
KathakNorth IndiaStorytellers; Lucknow, Jaipur and Banaras gharanas; fast footwork and spins
KathakaliKeralaDance-drama of Ramayana and Mahabharata stories; elaborate make-up; revived at Kerala Kalamandalam
KuchipudiAndhra PradeshNamed after a village; tarangam danced on a brass plate
OdissiOdishaTribhanga (three-bend) posture; links with the Konark sculptures
ManipuriManipurVaishnava ras lila themes; gentle, flowing movement
MohiniyattamKeralaGraceful solo dance by women (lasya)
SattriyaAssamFrom Sankardeva's Vaishnava monasteries (sattras); recognised in 2000

How Kathak grew. The name comes from katha (story). Kathaks were a caste of temple storytellers in north India. With the Bhakti movement (15th–16th centuries) their gestures merged with the Radha–Krishna rasa lila folk plays. At the Mughal and later courts it gained fast footwork and rich costume. The Lucknow gharana grew under Wajid Ali Shah, the last Nawab of Awadh; the Jaipur gharana at the Rajput courts. Kathak is the main classical dance of north India, and its history shows both the temple and the court at work.

I50.4 Theatre: from the Sanskrit stage to the political stage

Sanskrit drama followed the Natyashastra's rules. Plays mixed languages by rank: kings and Brahmins spoke Sanskrit, while women and common characters spoke Prakrit. Tragic endings were avoided, since a play had to leave the audience with rasa, not despair. The great playwrights were Bhasa, Kalidasa (Abhijnanashakuntalam), Shudraka (Mrichchhakatika, a play about ordinary city life) and Vishakhadatta (Mudrarakshasa, a political play on Chanakya); see I51 for the historical plays. As Sanskrit lost its audience, this stage declined; Koodiyattam in Kerala is its one surviving form, performed in temple theatres (koothambalam), and UNESCO proclaimed it a masterpiece of intangible heritage in 2001.

Folk theatre filled the gap. Performed in regional languages for village audiences, often on religious themes spread by the Bhakti movement, it combined song, dance and comedy: Yakshagana (Karnataka), Jatra (Bengal), Nautanki (Uttar Pradesh), Tamasha (Maharashtra) and Bhavai (Gujarat); Rajasthan's Khyal and Gavari are in book 6.

Colonial theatre turned political. Commercial Parsi theatre companies in 19th-century Bombay toured widely and shaped later Hindi and Urdu drama and film. In Bengal, Dinabandhu Mitra's Nil Darpan (1860) exposed indigo planters' cruelty and fed the indigo protests. Alarmed by plays that mocked British rule, the government passed the Dramatic Performances Act (1876) to license and ban "seditious" plays. In 1943 the Indian People's Theatre Association (IPTA), linked to the left, took theatre to workers and peasants; Bijon Bhattacharya's Nabanna (1944) dramatised the Bengal famine.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Before it: Vedic religion and the Samaveda (I04); the Gupta age of Kalidasa (I10).
  • Art and architecture: dance poses carved at Chidambaram, Konark and Khajuraho (I48); Rajput and Pahari ragamala paintings, which illustrate ragas as moods and scenes (I49).
  • Religion: the Bhakti saints were composers: Purandara Dasa, Surdas, Mirabai and Sankardeva, whose sattras created Sattriya (I20); Amir Khusrau's link with the Chishti order (I20).
  • Courts: Tansen and Mughal patronage (I21, I22); Wajid Ali Shah's Lucknow and the annexation of Awadh (I32).
  • Colonial society: the anti-nautch campaign belongs with the social reform debates (I35) and women's history (I47); Nil Darpan with the indigo revolt (I33).
  • Rajasthan: the Jaipur gharana of Kathak, the Rajput courts' patronage, folk forms and instruments (book 6).

What historians say

Kapila Vatsyayan (Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts) links dance to sculpture and texts. Allyn Miner and Katherine Butler Brown study Mughal music and question many traditional attributions to Amir Khusrau; Brown also shows that musical writing continued under Aurangzeb despite the claim that he banned music. Davesh Soneji (Unfinished Gestures) studies how the devadasi reforms and the revival changed who performed dance. Sunil Kothari documents the classical dances.

Exam traps
  • Sangita Ratnakara (Sharngadeva) ≠ Natyashastra (Bharata).
  • Kathakali and Mohiniyattam are both from Kerala; Kuchipudi is from Andhra Pradesh.
  • Older NCERT texts say "six" classical dances; the current Sangeet Natak Akademi list has eight.
  • Sattriya comes from Sankardeva's monasteries in Assam, not Manipur.
  • Nil Darpan is a play (Dinabandhu Mitra), not a newspaper.

Previous-year questions (RAS)

No RAS Mains question on music, dance or theatre in 2016–2024, and none in the history sections of RAS Prelims 2021, 2023 and 2024. The 2016 question on historical plays of Sanskrit literature is covered in I51.

Mains answer writing

5 marks · 50 words

Distinguish between Hindustani and Carnatic music.

How to frame it: Region and influence → Forms → Improvisation → Figures

Model answer (41 words)

Hindustani music developed in the north with Persian and court influence; its forms include dhrupad, khayal and thumri, with wide improvisation (Tansen, Amir Khusrau). Carnatic music in the south is temple-based and centred on compositions such as kritis (Purandara Dasa, Tyagaraja).

5 marks · 50 words

What is the significance of the Natyashastra?

How to frame it: Author and date → Content → Rasa → Legacy

Model answer (34 words)

Attributed to Bharata, it is the oldest Indian treatise on drama, dance and music. It explains stagecraft, gestures, instruments and the theory of rasa, and remains the base of classical dance and aesthetic theory.

10 marks · 100 words

How did changing patronage shape Indian classical dance from the medieval period to independence?

How to frame it: Temple → Court → Colonial reform → Revival → State recognition

Model answer (94 words)

Dance first lived in temples, performed by devadasis on the Natyashastra base, as the Chidambaram karanas show. Courts then reshaped it: Kathak gained fast footwork and display at Mughal, Awadh and Rajput courts. Under colonial rule Victorian morality and reformers branded dancers immoral; the anti-nautch campaign led to the Madras Devadasis Act (1947), cutting off hereditary performers. Nationalist revivalists reclaimed it as heritage: E. Krishna Iyer and Rukmini Devi (Kalakshetra, 1936) recast Bharatanatyam, Vallathol (Kerala Kalamandalam, 1930) Kathakali. Finally the Sangeet Natak Akademi (1953) granted classical status. Each patron changed who danced and how.

2 marks · 15 words

What is Koodiyattam?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (11 words)

Kerala's surviving form of Sanskrit theatre, proclaimed by UNESCO in 2001.

Revision card

Remember
  • Samaveda → Natyashastra (Bharata; rasa; four instrument classes) → Sangita Ratnakara (Sharngadeva, 13th century).
  • Why two systems: Persian contact + different patrons (court vs temple) + Bhakti in regional languages.
  • Hindustani: Khusrau, Man Singh Tomar (dhrupad), Haridas, Tansen, Sadarang (khayal), Lucknow (thumri). Carnatic: Purandara Dasa, Venkatamakhin (72 melakartas), Trinity.
  • Dance: temple and court → anti-nautch (1890s) and Devadasis Act 1947 → revival (Kalamandalam 1930, Kalakshetra 1936) → SNA 1953, eight dances; Sattriya 2000.
  • Theatre: Sanskrit drama, Koodiyattam (UNESCO 2001), folk forms, Parsi theatre, Nil Darpan 1860, Act 1876, IPTA 1943.

Self-test

  1. Which Veda is the source of Indian music?
    Show answer

    The Samaveda.

  2. What is rasa, and how is it produced?
    Show answer

    The aesthetic emotion the audience feels; the performer shows a bhava through gesture, expression and music, and the viewer "tastes" its universal form.

  3. Name the four classes of instruments in the Natyashastra.
    Show answer

    Tata, sushira, avanaddha, ghana.

  4. Why did north and south Indian music separate after the 13th century?
    Show answer

    Persian influence in the north, different patrons (courts in the north, temples in the south) and Bhakti composition in regional languages.

  5. Why did dhrupad give way to khayal and thumri in the north?
    Show answer

    Music moved from temple and devotional settings to courts and salons that valued ornament and display; Sadarang (18th century) and Lucknow (19th century) mark the shift.

  6. Who are the Carnatic Trinity?
    Show answer

    Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri.

  7. Why did classical dance nearly disappear, and who revived it?
    Show answer

    The anti-nautch campaign branded hereditary dancers immoral, ending in the Devadasis Act (1947); E. Krishna Iyer, Rukmini Devi Arundale and Vallathol revived it through institutions.

  8. Distinguish nritta, nritya and natya.
    Show answer

    Pure rhythmic dance; dance with expression and meaning; dance-drama telling a story.

  9. How many classical dances does the Sangeet Natak Akademi recognise, and which came last?
    Show answer

    Eight; Sattriya of Assam, in 2000.

  10. Why did the British pass the Dramatic Performances Act (1876)?
    Show answer

    To license and ban plays that criticised British rule, after political plays such as Nil Darpan (1860).

Part V · Unit I51Literature: Vedic to the British Erac. 1500 BCE – 1913 CE

Where this fits in the syllabus

Prelims: Vedic literature; epics and Puranas; Buddhist and Jain texts in Pali and Prakrit; Sangam literature; Classical Sanskrit: Kalidasa, Bana, historical plays and chronicles; Medieval literature: Persian, Bhakti literature in regional languages; Modern literature: Bharatendu Harishchandra, Bankim Chandra, Tagore, Premchand

Mains: GS-I Part B: Indian heritage — literature; GS-I Part B: Socio-religious reform and the Renaissance (modern literature)

Tier B. RAS Mains asked about the historical plays of Sanskrit literature (2016, 5 marks) and Bharatendu Harishchandra as precursor of modern Hindi literature (2018, 5 marks). Rajasthani literature (Prithviraj Raso, dingal and pingal) is in book 6.

The big picture

India's literature is one of the longest continuous traditions in the world. The Vedas were transmitted orally for centuries; the epics and Puranas carried religious and social ideas to wider audiences. Buddhist and Jain texts used Pali and Prakrit, the language of the people. The Sangam poems record early Tamil society. Classical Sanskrit produced Kalidasa's plays, Bana's prose and Kalhana's chronicle. In the medieval period Persian became the court language while the Bhakti saints made regional languages literary. In the 19th century print, reform and nationalism produced modern prose, the novel and political poetry.

Exam focus

RAS Mains has asked short notes on the historical plays of Sanskrit literature (2016) and on Bharatendu Harishchandra (2018). Learn works with their authors and languages, and be ready to say what each tells the historian.

WhenWhat happened
