Core notes

I51.1 Ancient literature

The oldest Indian literature was not written but memorised. The four Vedas (Rig, Sama, Yajur, Atharva) were passed down orally with remarkable precision, each with its Brahmanas (ritual explanations), Aranyakas (forest texts) and Upanishads (philosophy). To preserve correct recitation and ritual, the six Vedangas developed: phonetics, ritual, grammar, etymology, metre and astronomy. These texts were shruti, "heard" or revealed; later texts were smriti, "remembered", and could be retold and expanded.

The epics, the Mahabharata (attributed to Vyasa, including the Bhagavad Gita) and the Ramayana (Valmiki), and the eighteen major Puranas grew over centuries as they were retold, and carried religious and social ideas to ordinary people. Buddhist and Jain teachers deliberately used the people's languages: the Buddhist Tripitaka and the Jataka tales are in Pali, and the Jain Agamas in Prakrit. In the far south, the Sangam anthologies (Ettuthogai, Pattuppattu) record early Tamil society, followed by the epics Silappadikaram and Manimekalai and Tiruvalluvar's Tirukkural.

Concept

Literature as a historical source. Most early texts were composed to teach, worship or entertain, not to record history. Historians use them carefully: they reveal beliefs, social customs, economy and geography, but dates and events must be checked against inscriptions, coins and archaeology. The Sangam poems, for instance, are prized for their picture of everyday life, trade and chiefdoms in early Tamilakam.

I51.2 Classical Sanskrit and historical plays

Classical Sanskrit reached its height under the Guptas and their successors, when royal courts patronised poets. Kalidasa wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta and Raghuvamsha; Shudraka's Mrichchhakatika showed city life; the Panchatantra taught statecraft through animal fables. Several plays and prose works took historical figures as their subject (RAS Mains 2016):

WorkAuthorHistorical subject
SvapnavasavadattaBhasaKing Udayana of Vatsa and Vasavadatta
MalavikagnimitramKalidasaAgnimitra, Shunga king, and Malavika
MudrarakshasaVishakhadattaChanakya's plan to win Rakshasa, minister of the Nandas, for Chandragupta Maurya
DevichandraguptamVishakhadatta (fragments only)Chandragupta II rescuing his brother Ramagupta's queen from the Shakas
Harshacharita (prose)BanabhattaEarly life of Harshavardhana
Rajatarangini (verse chronicle)KalhanaKings of Kashmir

These works mix history with drama and praise of patrons, so historians use them alongside inscriptions and coins. Kalhana's Rajatarangini (1148–49) stands apart: he consulted earlier chronicles and inscriptions and tried to judge kings impartially, which is why it is often called India's first true work of history.

I51.3 Medieval literature

In the medieval period two developments shaped literature. First, Persian became the language of courts and administration. Amir Khusrau wrote in Persian and Hindavi; Ziauddin Barani wrote the Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari. Akbar's court translated the Mahabharata into Persian (Razmnama), and Dara Shikoh translated the Upanishads (Sirr-i-Akbar). Babur wrote his memoirs, the Baburnama, in Turki.

Second, the Bhakti saints made regional languages literary, because they wanted to reach ordinary people directly: Kabir, Surdas and Tulsidas in Hindi dialects (Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, 1574–77, in Awadhi), Mirabai in Rajasthani and Braj, Tukaram and Jnaneshwar in Marathi, Chaitanya's followers in Bengali, Shankardev in Assamese, the Alvars and Nayanars in Tamil, and Basavanna's vachanas in Kannada. Southern courts produced Kamban's Tamil Ramayana, Pampa in Kannada and Krishnadevaraya's Amuktamalyada in Telugu.

Regional languages also grew through states and local traditions. The Chera kingdom of Mahodayapuram (9th century) used Malayalam language and script in its inscriptions, one of the earliest official uses of a regional language. The 14th-century Lilatilakam, on grammar and poetics, was written in Manipravalam ("diamonds and corals"), a blend of Sanskrit and the regional language. Bengali literature had two streams: one drew on Sanskrit (translations of the epics, Mangalakavyas on local deities, lives of Chaitanya); the other was oral and independent of it (Nath songs of Maynamati and Gopichandra, tales of Dharma Thakur, ballads).

I51.4 Modern literature and the Renaissance

In the 19th century the printing press, newspapers and reform debates changed literature. Prose, the novel and the journal became the main forms, and writers took up social reform and national pride.

Bharatendu Harishchandra (1850–1885) is called the father of modern Hindi literature (RAS Mains 2018). He made Khari Boli the language of Hindi prose, started the journals Kavivachan Sudha (1868) and Harishchandra Magazine, and wrote plays such as Andher Nagari and Bharat Durdasha that satirised colonial rule and social evils. The years 1868–1900 are called the Bharatendu Yug.

In Bengali, Bankim Chandra's Anandamath (1882) gave the nationalist movement Vande Mataram, and Rabindranath Tagore's Gitanjali won the Nobel Prize (1913), the first for an Asian. In Urdu, Ghalib, Altaf Hussain Hali (Musaddas) and Muhammad Iqbal shaped modern poetry. Premchand's realist stories and novels, such as Godan (1936), brought peasants and the poor to the centre of Hindi–Urdu fiction.

Concept

Why the modern period changed literature. Print made books cheap and created a reading public; the journal and newspaper gave writers a regular platform; and the questions of reform and colonial rule gave them urgent subjects. Literature moved from the court and temple to the public sphere, and became a vehicle of the Indian Renaissance (I35) and of nationalism.

Connections

How this unit connects.

  • Ancient: Vedic age (I04); Buddhism and Jainism (I06); Sangam age (I09); the Guptas (I10) and Harsha.
  • Medieval: Bhakti and Sufi movements (I20); Mughal sources (I21–I23).
  • Modern: socio-religious reform (I35); Swadeshi and nationalism (I37).
  • Rajasthan: Prithviraj Raso, dingal and pingal, Mirabai (Rajasthan art and culture book).

What historians say

A.L. Basham (The Wonder That Was India) surveys classical literature. Romila Thapar uses the historical plays and chronicles as sources while warning about their poetic purpose. Ramchandra Shukla (Hindi Sahitya ka Itihas, 1929) named the Bharatendu period and set the periods of Hindi literature.

  • Harshacharita is prose by Bana; Ratnavali and Nagananda are plays by Harsha himself.
  • Baburnama is in Turki, not Persian; its Persian translation was made under Akbar.
  • Ramcharitmanas is in Awadhi, not Braj; Surdas wrote in Braj.

Questions as printed in the RPSC Mains papers (GS Paper I), lightly edited for grammar.

Mains answer writing

10 marks · 100 words

How did the choice of language in Indian literature reflect changes in religion and society?

How to frame it: Sanskrit and the Vedas → Pali and Prakrit → Persian at court → Bhakti and regional languages → Print and modern prose

Model answer (102 words)

The Vedas were in Sanskrit and transmitted orally by Brahmins, reflecting a priestly, ritual religion. The Buddha and Mahavira taught in Pali and Prakrit to reach ordinary people. Classical Sanskrit flourished under royal patronage, as in Kalidasa and Bana. Persian became the language of Sultanate and Mughal courts, producing histories such as the Akbarnama, while the Bhakti saints made Hindi dialects, Marathi, Bengali, Tamil and Kannada literary in order to address the common people directly. In the 19th century print and reform created Khari Boli prose (Bharatendu), the novel (Bankim, Premchand) and nationalist poetry. Each shift in language marked a widening audience.

5 marks · 50 words

Write a short note on the historical plays of Sanskrit literature.

How to frame it: Examples with authors → Value as sources

Model answer (34 words)

Bhasa's Svapnavasavadatta (Udayana), Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram (Agnimitra Shunga), and Vishakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa (Chanakya and Chandragupta) and Devichandraguptam (Chandragupta II) dramatise history. They add political detail but mix fact with poetry, so must be checked against inscriptions.

5 marks · 50 words

Bharatendu Harishchandra was the precursor of modern trends in Hindi literature. Discuss.

How to frame it: Khari Boli prose → Journals → Plays with social and national themes → Legacy

Model answer (38 words)

He made Khari Boli the language of Hindi prose, founded journals like Kavivachan Sudha (1868), and wrote plays such as Bharat Durdasha and Andher Nagari attacking colonial exploitation and social evils. The period 1868–1900 is named after him.

2 marks · 15 words

What is the Rajatarangini?

How to frame it: Answer

Model answer (10 words)

Kalhana's 12th-century Sanskrit verse chronicle of the kings of Kashmir.

Revision card

Remember
  • Vedas → Brahmanas → Aranyakas → Upanishads; epics; Puranas; Pali Tripitaka; Sangam, Tirukkural.
  • Historical plays: Svapnavasavadatta (Bhasa), Malavikagnimitram (Kalidasa), Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam (Vishakhadatta); Harshacharita; Rajatarangini 1148.
  • Medieval: Persian (Khusrau, Barani, Abul Fazl), Turki Baburnama, Bhakti in regional languages, Ramcharitmanas (Awadhi).
  • Modern: Bharatendu (1868 journal), Anandamath 1882, Gitanjali Nobel 1913, Godan 1936.

    Show answer

    Show answer

    Bhasa.

  3. Which Shunga king appears in Malavikagnimitram?
    Show answer

  4. What is the subject of Mudrarakshasa?
    Show answer

  5. Who wrote the Harshacharita?

  6. When did Kalhana write the Rajatarangini?
    Show answer

    1148–49.

  7. In which language did Babur write his memoirs?
    Show answer

    Turki.

  8. Which journal did Bharatendu Harishchandra start in 1868?
    Show answer

    Kavivachan Sudha.

  9. For which work did Tagore win the Nobel Prize, and when?
    Show answer

    Gitanjali, 1913.

  10. Why did Buddhist and Jain teachers use Pali and Prakrit?
    Show answer

    To reach ordinary people in their own languages rather than priestly Sanskrit.

  11. Why must historians use Sanskrit historical plays carefully?
    Show answer

    They mix history with drama and praise of patrons, so must be checked against inscriptions and coins.

  12. Why did the Bhakti saints compose in regional languages?
    Show answer

    To speak directly to common people, bypassing Sanskrit and priests.
